paragraphs: The paper asks how many computational units a feedforward neural network needs to perform a given task. It studies this as a mathematical complexity problem, using harmonic analysis and rational approximation to establish lower bounds. A lower bound identifies a size below which networks in the relevant class cannot compute the target function.

The techniques cover networks whose individual units can be approximated piece by piece by low-degree rational functions. This gives a common framework for analyzing multiple kinds of neural elements. For the parity function, the paper derives size requirements for networks of sigmoid or linear-threshold units at specified depths.

The authors also construct networks that compute parity with sizes close to those requirements. The combination of lower bounds and constructions makes the results almost tight: the proven necessary size approaches what can actually be achieved. The abstract identifies these as the first known such size-complexity results for networks deeper than two layers, extending analysis beyond shallow architectures.
summary.tldr: Rational-approximation techniques yield nearly matching necessary and achievable network sizes for computing parity at multiple depths.

title: Computing with Almost Optimal Size Neural Networks

abstract: We demonstrate the use of a digital signal processing board to construct hybrid networks consisting of computer model neurons connected to a biological neural network. This system operates in real time. and the synaptic connections are realistic effective conductances. Therefore. the synapses made from the computer model neuron are integrated correctly by the postsynaptic biological neuron. This method provides us with the ability to add additional. completely known elements to a biological network and study their effect on network activity. Moreover. by changing the parameters of the model neuron. it is possible to assess the role of individual conductances in the activity of the neuron. and in the network in which it participates. paragraphs: The paper presents a method for joining simulated neurons to a biological neural network while that network is operating. A digital signal processing board runs the computer-model components in real time. The result is a hybrid circuit in which known computational elements can participate in the activity of living neurons.

The connections use realistic effective synaptic conductances. This feature matters because the biological neuron receiving a modeled synapse integrates its influence appropriately. The computer model therefore contributes through a biologically meaningful form of connection, allowing its effect to become part of the ongoing network dynamics.

The authors demonstrate this capability as an experimental method. Adding fully specified model elements makes it possible to study how those elements change biological network activity. Adjusting the modeled neuron's parameters also provides a way to assess the contribution of individual conductances, both to that neuron's behavior and to the surrounding network. The contribution is controlled intervention through real-time interaction between computation and biology.
summary.tldr: Real-time conductance-based connections let simulated neurons interact with biological networks for controlled studies of neural activity.

title: Hybrid Circuits of Interacting Computer Model and Biological Neurons

abstract: Boosting methods maximize a hard classification margin and are known as powerful techniques that do not exhibit overfitting for low noise cases. Also for noisy data boosting will try to enforce a hard margin and thereby give too much weight to outliers, which then leads to the dilemma of non-smooth fits and overfitting. Therefore we propose three algorithms to allow for soft margin classification by introducing regularization with slack variables into the boosting concept: (1) AdaBoostreg and regularized versions of (2) linear and (3) quadratic programming AdaBoost. Experiments show the usefulness of the proposed algorithms in comparison to another soft margin classifier: the support vector machine. 1

Also for noisy data boosting will try to enforce a hard margin and thereby give too much weight to outliers, which then leads to the dilemma of non-smooth fits and overfitting. Therefore we propose three algorithms to allow for soft margin classification by introducing regularization with slack variables into the boosting concept: (1) AdaBoostreg and regularized versions of (2) linear and (3) quadratic programming AdaBoost. paragraphs: The paper examines why boosting can overfit noisy data despite its strong behavior in low-noise settings. The authors explain the problem through hard classification margins: boosting continues trying to enforce a strict separation even when observations include outliers. Giving those points too much weight can produce irregular fits and overfitting.

Their response is to introduce regularization through slack variables, allowing a soft margin. This permits controlled departures from the margin requirement instead of forcing every difficult observation to satisfy it. The paper proposes three algorithms: AdaBoostreg, a regularized linear-programming version of AdaBoost, and a regularized quadratic-programming version. All three bring this relaxation into the boosting framework.

Experiments demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed methods in comparison with support vector machines, which also provide soft-margin classification. The result supports regularization as a response to the outlier sensitivity described by the authors. The contribution is a family of concrete boosting variants that balance fitting the data against the pressure to enforce a hard margin in noisy classification problems.
summary.tldr: Three regularized AdaBoost variants introduce soft margins to address excessive outlier weighting and overfitting in noisy data.

title: Regularizing AdaBoost

abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are currently the state-of-the-art models for many classification problems but they suffer from the complexity of their train(cid:173) ing algorithm which is at least quadratic with respect to the number of examples. Hence, it is hopeless to try to solve real-life problems having more than a few hundreds of thousands examples with SVMs. The present paper proposes a new mixture of SVMs that can be easily implemented in parallel and where each SVM is trained on a small subset of the whole dataset. Experiments on a large benchmark dataset (Forest) as well as a difficult speech database, yielded significant time improvement (time complexity appears empirically to locally grow linearly with the number of examples) . In addition, and that is a surprise, a significant improvement in generalization was observed on Forest.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the computational cost of training support vector machines on very large datasets. The authors describe training complexity that grows at least quadratically with the number of examples, making a single large training problem difficult to manage. Their aim is to retain SVM-based classification while changing how the training work is organized.

They propose a mixture of SVMs in which each component learns from a small subset of the complete dataset. The mixture is designed for straightforward parallel implementation. Dividing the data among smaller training problems addresses the size of each individual optimization task while also allowing those tasks to be carried out concurrently.

Experiments on the Forest benchmark and a difficult speech database show significant training-time improvements. Over the ranges examined, time complexity appears locally linear in dataset size; this is an empirical observation, not a general scaling guarantee. The authors also report a surprising improvement in generalization on Forest, showing that the observed benefit there extended beyond faster training.
summary.tldr: A parallel mixture of SVMs trained on smaller data subsets substantially reduces training time and also improves generalization on Forest.

title: A Parallel Mixture of SVMs for Very Large Scale Problems

abstract: If the promise of computational modeling is to be fully realized in higherlevel cognitive domains such as language processing, principled methods must be developed to construct the semantic representations used in such models. In this paper, we propose the use of an established formalism from mathematical psychology, additive clustering, as a means of automatically constructing binary representations for objects using only pairwise similarity data. However, existing methods for the unsupervised learning of additive clustering models do not scale well to large problems. We present a new algorithm for additive clustering, based on a novel heuristic technique for combinatorial optimization. The algorithm is simpler than previous formulations and makes fewer independence assumptions. Extensive empirical tests on both human and synthetic data suggest that it is more effective than previous methods and that it also scales better to larger problems. By making additive clustering practical, we take a significant step toward scaling connectionist models beyond hand-coded examples.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the construction of semantic representations for computational models of higher-level cognition, including language. Such models need a principled way to represent objects without relying entirely on hand-coded examples. The authors propose additive clustering, a formalism from mathematical psychology, to construct binary object representations automatically from pairwise similarity judgments.

The main obstacle is computational: existing unsupervised methods for learning additive clustering models do not scale well to large problems. The paper introduces an algorithm based on a new heuristic for combinatorial optimization. The formulation is simpler than earlier approaches and makes fewer independence assumptions, addressing both the practical difficulty of learning the representations and the assumptions imposed during that process.

Extensive tests using human and synthetic data suggest that the algorithm is more effective than previous methods and scales better as problems grow. These empirical findings support additive clustering as a more practical source of distributed representations. The broader significance is a route toward larger connectionist cognitive models whose representations can be learned from similarity data.
summary.tldr: A new additive clustering algorithm learns binary representations from similarity data, with empirical improvements in effectiveness and scalability.

title: Constructing Distributed Representations Using Additive Clustering

abstract: We give a fast rejection scheme that is based on image segments and demonstrate it on the canonical example of face detection. However, in- stead of focusing on the detection step we focus on the rejection step and show that our method is simple and fast to be learned, thus making it an excellent pre-processing step to accelerate standard machine learning classifiers, such as neural-networks, Bayes classifiers or SVM. We de- compose a collection of face images into regions of pixels with similar behavior over the image set. The relationships between the mean and variance of image segments are used to form a cascade of rejectors that can reject over 99.8% of image patches, thus only a small fraction of the image patches must be passed to a full-scale classifier. Moreover, the training time for our method is much less than an hour, on a standard PC. The shape of the features (i.e. image segments) we use is data-driven, they are very cheap to compute and they form a very low dimensional feature space in which exhaustive search for the best features is tractable.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates object detection by focusing on quickly rejecting image patches before they reach a full classifier. It demonstrates the idea with faces and presents the rejection stage as preprocessing for methods such as neural networks, Bayes classifiers, and support vector machines. The aim is to reduce how many patches require expensive classification.

The method groups pixels into image regions according to how similarly they behave across a collection of face images. Relationships between regional means and variances then form a cascade of rejection rules. The feature shapes are learned from data, are inexpensive to compute, and create a space small enough to search exhaustively for the best features.

The reported cascade rejects more than 99.8 percent of image patches, leaving only a small fraction for the full classifier. Training takes much less than an hour on a standard PC. These findings concern the efficiency of the learned filtering stage: the rejection percentage describes the amount of candidate processing removed, rather than a face-detection accuracy score.
summary.tldr: Learned image-segment features form a cheap rejection cascade that filters over 99.8 percent of patches before full classification.

title: The power of feature clustering: An application to object detection

abstract: A crucial technique for scaling kernel methods to very large data sets reaching or exceeding millions of instances is based on low-rank approximation of kernel matrices. We introduce a new family of algorithms based on mixtures of Nystrom approximations, ensemble Nystrom algorithms, that yield more accurate low-rank approximations than the standard Nystrom method. We give a detailed study of multiple variants of these algorithms based on simple averaging, an exponential weight method, or regression-based methods. We also present a theoretical analysis of these algorithms, including novel error bounds guaranteeing a better convergence rate than the standard Nystrom method. Finally, we report the results of extensive experiments with several data sets containing up to 1M points demonstrating the signiﬁcant performance improvements gained over the standard Nystrom approximation.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can become difficult to scale because they rely on a matrix of relationships among data points. A low-rank approximation replaces that matrix with a more compact representation. The paper develops ensemble Nystrom algorithms, which combine multiple Nystrom approximations to improve the accuracy of this representation.

The authors study several ways to form the ensemble. These include simple averaging, exponential weighting, and regression-based combinations. The shared idea is to use a mixture of approximations instead of relying on a single standard Nystrom approximation. Comparing these variants examines how the choice of combination method contributes to the resulting matrix approximation.

The paper supports the approach with both theoretical analysis and experiments. Its error bounds guarantee a better convergence rate than the standard Nystrom method, and evaluations on datasets with up to one million points show significant performance improvements over that method. These findings matter because low-rank approximation is a central tool for extending kernel methods to very large datasets, and the ensemble improves the approximation at the heart of that strategy.
summary.tldr: Combining Nystrom approximations improves low-rank kernel approximation, with stronger convergence guarantees and empirical gains on datasets up to one million points.

title: Ensemble Nystrom Method

abstract: Speaker comparison, the process of finding the speaker similarity between two speech signals, occupies a central role in a variety of applications---speaker verification, clustering, and identification. Speaker comparison can be placed in a geometric framework by casting the problem as a model comparison process. For a given speech signal, feature vectors are produced and used to adapt a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). Speaker comparison can then be viewed as the process of compensating and finding metrics on the space of adapted models. We propose a framework, inner product discriminant functions (IPDFs), which extends many common techniques for speaker comparison: support vector machines, joint factor analysis, and linear scoring. The framework uses inner products between the parameter vectors of GMM models motivated by several statistical methods. Compensation of nuisances is performed via linear transforms on GMM parameter vectors. Using the IPDF framework, we show that many current techniques are simple variations of each other. We demonstrate, on a 2006 NIST speaker recognition evaluation task, new scoring methods using IPDFs which produce excellent error rates and require significantly less computation than current techniques.

paragraphs: Speaker comparison estimates how similar the speakers in two speech recordings are, supporting verification, clustering, and identification. This paper treats comparison geometrically: features from each recording adapt a Gaussian mixture model, and the comparison is then performed in the space of those adapted models. The model parameters become the objects being compared.

The authors introduce inner product discriminant functions, or IPDFs, which use inner products between Gaussian-mixture parameter vectors. Linear transformations of these vectors compensate for nuisance variation. The framework extends support vector machines, joint factor analysis, and linear scoring, showing that many existing speaker-comparison techniques can be understood as relatively small variations within a shared representation.

This unified view also yields new scoring methods. On a 2006 NIST speaker-recognition evaluation task, the authors report excellent error rates with significantly less computation than existing techniques. The result links conceptual simplification with practical efficiency: expressing compensation and comparison through parameter transformations and inner products provides both a way to relate methods and a basis for developing new ones.
summary.tldr: A shared inner-product framework unifies speaker-comparison techniques and produces new scoring methods with strong reported accuracy and lower computation.

title: Speaker Comparison with Inner Product Discriminant Functions

abstract: Given a set $V$ of $n$ elements we wish to linearly order them using pairwise preference labels which may be non-transitive (due to irrationality or arbitrary noise). The goal is to linearly order the elements while disagreeing with as few pairwise preference labels as possible. Our performance is measured by two parameters: The number of disagreements (loss) and the query complexity (number of pairwise preference labels). Our algorithm adaptively queries at most $O(n\poly(\log n,\eps^{-1}))$ preference labels for a regret of $\eps$ times the optimal loss. This is strictly better, and often significantly better than what non-adaptive sampling could achieve. Our main result helps settle an open problem posed by learning-to-rank (from pairwise information) theoreticians and practitioners: What is a provably correct way to sample preference labels?

paragraphs: The paper studies how to rank a set of items when the available evidence consists of preferences between pairs. These preferences can be inconsistent: they need not fit together into a single coherent ordering. The objective is consequently to find a linear ranking that disagrees with as few pairwise labels as possible, while asking for relatively few labels.

The proposed algorithm chooses its queries adaptively, allowing the sampling process to respond to information already obtained. Its guarantee connects the cost of gathering evidence to the quality of the final ranking. For n items, it asks at most O(n poly(log n, ε⁻¹)) queries, with excess loss bounded by ε times the optimal loss.

The comparison point is the best achievable ordering under the supplied preferences, so the guarantee accommodates unavoidable disagreement. The authors show that adaptive querying is strictly better, and often substantially better, than non-adaptive sampling can achieve. This provides a principled answer to which preference labels should be collected when both ranking accuracy and annotation effort matter.
summary.tldr: Adaptive preference queries produce rankings close to the best possible ordering with almost optimal query complexity.

title: Active Learning Ranking from Pairwise Preferences with Almost Optimal Query Complexity

abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive impairment of memory and other cognitive functions. Regression analysis has been studied to relate neuroimaging measures to cognitive status. However, whether these measures have further predictive power to infer a trajectory of cognitive performance over time is still an under-explored but important topic in AD research. We propose a novel high-order multi-task learning model to address this issue. The proposed model explores the temporal correlations existing in data features and regression tasks by the structured sparsity-inducing norms. In addition, the sparsity of the model enables the selection of a small number of MRI measures while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The empirical studies, using the baseline MRI and serial cognitive data of the ADNI cohort, have yielded promising results.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether neuroimaging measurements can predict how cognitive performance changes over time in Alzheimer's disease research. Relating an image to cognitive status at one point is only part of that problem. Predicting a trajectory requires accounting for relationships among measurements and prediction tasks across time.

The authors propose a high-order multi-task learning model that uses structured sparsity-inducing norms to capture those temporal correlations. Such penalties encourage selective use of features while respecting relationships represented in the learning problem. By linking the regression tasks, the method uses their temporal structure as part of how it learns predictions.

Sparsity also allows the model to select a small collection of MRI measures while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The empirical study uses baseline MRI measurements and repeated cognitive observations from the ADNI cohort and reports promising results. The stated contribution is a structured prediction method that combines trajectory modeling with selection of a compact set of imaging measures relevant to the prediction task.
summary.tldr: A structured multi-task model uses baseline MRI measures to predict cognitive trajectories while selecting a small set of imaging features.

title: High-Order Multi-Task Feature Learning to Identify Longitudinal Phenotypic Markers for Alzheimer's Disease Progression Prediction

abstract: Principal components analysis (PCA) is a standard tool for identifying good low-dimensional approximations to data sets in high dimension. Many current data sets of interest contain private or sensitive information about individuals. Algorithms which operate on such data should be sensitive to the privacy risks in publishing their outputs. Differential privacy is a framework for developing tradeoffs between privacy and the utility of these outputs. In this paper we investigate the theory and empirical performance of differentially private approximations to PCA and propose a new method which explicitly optimizes the utility of the output. We demonstrate that on real data, there this a large performance gap between the existing methods and our method. We show that the sample complexity for the two procedures differs in the scaling with the data dimension, and that our method is nearly optimal in terms of this scaling.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks a useful low-dimensional approximation to high-dimensional data. When those data contain sensitive information about individuals, publishing the resulting components raises privacy concerns. This paper studies how to approximate PCA under differential privacy, a framework for balancing protection of individuals with the usefulness of released results.

The proposed method explicitly optimizes the utility of its output. This makes the quality of the private approximation a direct part of the method's design. The authors examine both theoretical properties and empirical performance, connecting the question of what privacy permits with the question of how well a private procedure works on real data.

Their experiments show a large performance gap favoring the proposed method over existing methods. The theory further shows that the compared procedures require different amounts of data as dimensionality grows. The new method is nearly optimal with respect to this dimensional scaling. That qualification matters: the near-optimality claim concerns how sample requirements depend on dimension.
summary.tldr: A utility-focused private PCA method improves empirical performance and achieves nearly optimal sample-complexity scaling with dimension.

title: Near-optimal Differentially Private Principal Components

abstract: Tensor factorizations have become popular methods for learning from multi-relational data. In this context, the rank of a factorization is an important parameter that determines runtime as well as generalization ability. To determine conditions under which factorization is an efficient approach for learning from relational data, we derive upper and lower bounds on the rank required to recover adjacency tensors. Based on our findings, we propose a novel additive tensor factorization model for learning from latent and observable patterns in multi-relational data and present a scalable algorithm for computing the factorization. Experimentally, we show that the proposed approach does not only improve the predictive performance over pure latent variable methods but that it also reduces the required rank --- and therefore runtime and memory complexity --- significantly.

In this context, the rank of a factorization is an important parameter that determines runtime as well as generalization ability. To determine conditions under which factorization is an efficient approach for learning from relational data, we derive upper and lower bounds on the rank required to recover adjacency tensors. Based on our findings, we propose a novel additive tensor factorization model for learning from latent and observable patterns in multi-relational data and present a scalable algorithm for computing the factorization. Experimentally, we show that the proposed approach does not only improve the predictive performance over pure latent variable methods but that it also reduces the required rank --- and therefore runtime and memory complexity --- significantly.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization represents data containing multiple kinds of relationships through shared components. The number of components, or rank, affects computational cost and the model’s ability to generalize. This paper asks when factorization can efficiently recover relational structure, making the required rank a central object of analysis.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds on the rank needed to recover adjacency tensors, which encode relationships in the data. Motivated by those findings, they propose an additive model that combines latent patterns with observable patterns. Explicitly representing observable structure gives the factorization another way to account for relationships alongside its hidden components.

A scalable algorithm computes the resulting factorization. Experiments show improved predictive performance over methods using only latent variables, together with a significant reduction in required rank. That reduction also lowers runtime and memory complexity. The stated findings therefore connect modeling choices to both prediction and efficiency: incorporating observable patterns can make the latent representation more economical while improving the quality of its predictions in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Combining observable and latent relational patterns improves reported predictions while reducing tensor rank, runtime, and memory complexity.

title: Reducing the Rank in Relational Factorization Models by Including Observable Patterns

abstract: We consider the problem of binary classification when the covariates conditioned on the each of the response values follow multivariate Gaussian distributions. We focus on the setting where the covariance matrices for the two conditional distributions are the same. The corresponding generative model classifier, derived via the Bayes rule, also called Linear Discriminant Analysis, has been shown to behave poorly in high-dimensional settings. We present a novel analysis of the classification error of any linear discriminant approach given conditional Gaussian models. This allows us to compare the generative model classifier, other recently proposed discriminative approaches that directly learn the discriminant function, and then finally logistic regression which is another classical discriminative model classifier. As we show, under a natural sparsity assumption, and letting $s$ denote the sparsity of the Bayes classifier, $p$ the number of covariates, and $n$ the number of samples, the simple ($\ell_1$-regularized) logistic regression classifier achieves the fast misclassification error rates of $O\left(\frac{s \log p}{n}\right)$, which is much better than the other approaches, which are either inconsistent under high-dimensional settings, or achieve a slower rate of $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{s \log p}{n}}\right)$.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of binary classification when the covariates conditioned on the each of the response values follow multivariate Gaussian distributions. We focus on the setting where the covariance matrices for the two conditional distributions are the same. The corresponding generative model classifier, derived via the Bayes rule, also called Linear Discriminant Analysis, has been shown to behave poorly in high-dimensional settings. We present a novel analysis of the classification error of any linear discriminant approach given conditional Gaussian models. This allows us to compare the generative model classifier, other recently proposed discriminative approaches that directly learn the discriminant function, and then finally logistic regression which is another classical discriminative model classifier. As we show, under a natural sparsity assumption, and letting $s$ denote the sparsity of the Bayes classifier, $p$ the number of covariates, and $n$ the number of samples, the simple ($\ell_1$-regularized) logistic regression classifier achieves the fast misclassification error rates of $O\left(\frac{s \log p}{n}\right)$, which is much better than the other approaches, which are either inconsistent under high-dimensional settings, or achieve a slower rate of $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{s \log p}{n}}\right)$.

paragraphs: This paper compares ways to classify data when each of two classes has a multivariate Gaussian feature distribution and both classes share the same covariance matrix. In this setting, Bayes' rule gives a linear classifier associated with Linear Discriminant Analysis. However, the usual generative estimation approach can behave poorly when the number of features is large.

The authors develop an analysis of classification error that applies to any linear discriminant approach under these Gaussian models. This provides a common basis for comparing generative estimation, methods that learn the discriminant function directly, and logistic regression. The comparison focuses on prediction error rather than simply how accurately each method estimates distributional parameters.

Under the stated sparsity assumption, ℓ1-regularized logistic regression achieves a rate of O(s log p / n), where s is the sparsity of the Bayes classifier, p the feature count, and n the sample count. The compared alternatives are either inconsistent in high dimensions or have the slower square-root rate. The advantage is established within this shared-covariance Gaussian and sparse-classifier setting.
summary.tldr: Under sparse, shared-covariance Gaussian class models, ℓ1-regularized logistic regression achieves faster classification rates than the compared approaches.

title: Fast Classification Rates for High-dimensional Gaussian Generative Models

abstract: Learning-from-crowds aims to design proper aggregation strategies to infer the unknown true labels from the noisy labels provided by ordinary web workers. This paper presents max-margin majority voting (M^3V) to improve the discriminative ability of majority voting and further presents a Bayesian generalization to incorporate the flexibility of generative methods on modeling noisy observations with worker confusion matrices. We formulate the joint learning as a regularized Bayesian inference problem, where the posterior regularization is derived by maximizing the margin between the aggregated score of a potential true label and that of any alternative label. Our Bayesian model naturally covers the Dawid-Skene estimator and M^3V. Empirical results demonstrate that our methods are competitive, often achieving better results than state-of-the-art estimators.

We formulate the joint learning as a regularized Bayesian inference problem, where the posterior regularization is derived by maximizing the margin between the aggregated score of a potential true label and that of any alternative label. Empirical results demonstrate that our methods are competitive, often achieving better results than state-of-the-art estimators.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can disagree because individual workers make mistakes. Learning from crowds therefore requires an aggregation rule that estimates the unknown true label from noisy responses. This paper introduces max-margin majority voting, or M³V, to improve how effectively aggregated votes distinguish competing labels.

The method encourages a margin between the score of a candidate true label and the scores of alternative labels. The authors then develop a Bayesian generalization that models noisy worker responses using worker confusion matrices. Joint learning becomes regularized Bayesian inference, with the margin requirement supplying the posterior regularization.

This construction combines discriminative separation with a generative account of worker errors. The resulting Bayesian model includes both M³V and the Dawid-Skene estimator, placing them within a shared framework. Empirical results show competitive performance, often exceeding state-of-the-art estimators in the reported evaluations. The contribution is a way to connect vote-based label separation with flexible modeling of how individual workers produce unreliable observations.
summary.tldr: Max-margin voting and a Bayesian extension combine stronger label separation with models of worker mistakes for crowdsourced annotation.

title: Max-Margin Majority Voting for Learning from Crowds

abstract: This paper studies the $k$-means++ algorithm for clustering as well as the class of $D^\ell$ sampling algorithms to which $k$-means++ belongs. It is shown that for any constant factor $\beta > 1$, selecting $\beta k$ cluster centers by $D^\ell$ sampling yields a constant-factor approximation to the optimal clustering with $k$ centers, in expectation and without conditions on the dataset. This result extends the previously known $O(\log k)$ guarantee for the case $\beta = 1$ to the constant-factor bi-criteria regime. It also improves upon an existing constant-factor bi-criteria result that holds only with constant probability.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well k-means++ and the broader family of D^ℓ sampling algorithms can initialize a clustering. Its central question is what happens when an algorithm may select more than the requested k centers. This changes the comparison: the algorithm receives extra centers, but its clustering quality is still judged against the best solution using only k.

The result allows any fixed multiplier β greater than one. Selecting βk centers gives an expected clustering cost within a constant factor of the optimal k-center cost, without imposing conditions on the dataset. The guarantee is therefore about average performance over the sampling randomness, rather than a promise about every individual run.

This is a bi-criteria approximation because it trades additional centers for a stronger cost guarantee. With exactly k centers, the previously known bound grew logarithmically with k. The new result establishes a constant-factor bound when extra centers are allowed, and strengthens an earlier bi-criteria result that held only with constant probability.
summary.tldr: Allowing a constant-factor increase in centers gives D^ℓ sampling a constant-factor expected approximation to optimal k-center clustering.

title: A Constant-Factor Bi-Criteria Approximation Guarantee for k-means++

abstract: We address the problem of aggregating an ensemble of predictors with known loss bounds in a semi-supervised binary classification setting, to minimize prediction loss incurred on the unlabeled data. We find the minimax optimal predictions for a very general class of loss functions including all convex and many non-convex losses, extending a recent analysis of the problem for misclassification error. The result is a family of semi-supervised ensemble aggregation algorithms which are as efficient as linear learning by convex optimization, but are minimax optimal without any relaxations. Their decision rules take a form familiar in decision theory -- applying sigmoid functions to a notion of ensemble margin -- without the assumptions typically made in margin-based learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine binary predictors when bounds on their losses are known and predictions are needed for unlabeled data. Its objective is minimax aggregation: choose predictions that minimize the worst-case loss allowed by the available information. This places the ensemble's guarantees, rather than a particular averaging rule, at the center of the problem.

The authors solve this problem for a broad class of losses that includes every convex loss and many nonconvex ones. This extends earlier analysis restricted to misclassification error. The resulting algorithms are minimax optimal without relaxations, while requiring computation comparable to linear learning through convex optimization.

Their decision rules apply sigmoid functions to a quantity resembling an ensemble margin. This familiar form emerges from the minimax analysis without the assumptions usually attached to margin-based learning. The result connects an interpretable prediction rule with an exact optimization guarantee. Its optimality is relative to the semi-supervised setting and the known loss bounds, which define the information available for aggregation.
summary.tldr: Known predictor loss bounds enable efficient, exactly minimax-optimal binary ensemble aggregation across all convex and many nonconvex losses.

title: Optimal Binary Classifier Aggregation for General Losses

abstract: Variational inference (VI) is widely used as an efficient alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo. It posits a family of approximating distributions $q$ and finds the closest member to the exact posterior $p$. Closeness is usually measured via a divergence $D(q || p)$ from $q$ to $p$. While successful, this approach also has problems. Notably, it typically leads to underestimation of the posterior variance. In this paper we propose CHIVI, a black-box variational inference algorithm that minimizes $D_{\chi}(p || q)$, the $\chi$-divergence from $p$ to $q$. CHIVI minimizes an upper bound of the model evidence, which we term the $\chi$ upper bound (CUBO). Minimizing the CUBO leads to improved posterior uncertainty, and it can also be used with the classical VI lower bound (ELBO) to provide a sandwich estimate of the model evidence. We study CHIVI on three models: probit regression, Gaussian process classification, and a Cox process model of basketball plays. When compared to expectation propagation and classical VI, CHIVI produces better error rates and more accurate estimates of posterior variance.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution by selecting a tractable distribution from a chosen family. The divergence commonly used for this selection can underestimate posterior variance, making the approximation appear too certain. This paper proposes CHIVI, a black-box inference algorithm that changes the divergence used to fit the approximation.

CHIVI minimizes a chi-divergence directed from the posterior toward the approximating distribution. It does so by minimizing an upper bound on model evidence, called CUBO. The authors report improved posterior uncertainty from this objective. Combined with the usual evidence lower bound, the upper bound also supplies a sandwich estimate that brackets the model evidence.

The evaluation covers probit regression, Gaussian process classification, and a Cox process model of basketball plays. Compared with expectation propagation and classical variational inference, CHIVI produces better error rates and more accurate posterior variance estimates in the reported studies. The results make uncertainty estimation a central criterion for evaluating the approximation, alongside prediction error and the ability to bound evidence.
summary.tldr: CHIVI minimizes a chi-divergence upper bound to improve posterior uncertainty estimates and complement the usual lower bound on model evidence.

title: Variational Inference via $\chi$ Upper Bound Minimization

abstract: The independence clustering problem is considered in the following formulation: given a set $S$ of random variables, it is required to find the finest partitioning $\{U_1,\dots,U_k\}$ of $S$ into clusters such that the clusters $U_1,\dots,U_k$ are mutually independent. Since mutual independence is the target, pairwise similarity measurements are of no use, and thus traditional clustering algorithms are inapplicable. The distribution of the random variables in $S$ is, in general, unknown, but a sample is available. Thus, the problem is cast in terms of time series. Two forms of sampling are considered: i.i.d.\ and stationary time series, with the main emphasis being on the latter, more general, case. A consistent, computationally tractable algorithm for each of the settings is proposed, and a number of fascinating open directions for further research are outlined.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering random variables into groups that are mutually independent. The desired answer is the finest such partition: separate the variables as much as possible while preserving independence between the resulting groups. The objects being clustered are variables, and the criterion concerns their joint distribution rather than ordinary geometric similarity.

Mutual independence makes this different from clustering based on pairwise measurements. A matrix of pairwise similarities does not capture the joint requirement the method must satisfy, so traditional clustering algorithms are inapplicable to the stated formulation. The distribution is generally unknown, and the method must infer its relevant structure from available observations.

The authors consider both independent sampling and stationary time series, emphasizing the more general time-series setting. They propose a computationally tractable, consistent algorithm for each case. Consistency gives an asymptotic correctness property as observations accumulate, while tractability addresses whether the procedure can be computed. The contribution establishes algorithms for a clustering objective whose defining statistical structure cannot be reduced to the usual pairwise matrix.
summary.tldr: The paper develops consistent, tractable methods for partitioning random variables into mutually independent groups without relying on pairwise similarity matrices.

title: Independence clustering (without a matrix)

abstract: Most recently proposed methods for Neural Program induction work under the assumption of having a large set of input/output (I/O) examples for learning any given input-output mapping. This paper aims to address the problem of data and computation efficiency of program induction by leveraging information from related tasks. Specifically, we propose two novel approaches for cross-task knowledge transfer to improve program induction in limited-data scenarios. In our first proposal, portfolio adaptation, a set of induction models is pretrained on a set of related tasks, and the best model is adapted towards the new task using transfer learning. In our second approach, meta program induction, a $k$-shot learning approach is used to make a model generalize to new tasks without additional training. To test the efficacy of our methods, we constructed a new benchmark of programs written in the Karel programming language. Using an extensive experimental evaluation on the Karel benchmark, we demonstrate that our proposals dramatically outperform the baseline induction method that does not use knowledge transfer. We also analyze the relative performance of the two approaches and study conditions in which they perform best. In particular, meta induction outperforms all existing approaches under extreme data sparsity (when a very small number of examples are available), i.e., fewer than ten. As the number of available I/O examples increase (i.e. a thousand or more), portfolio adapted program induction becomes the best approach. For intermediate data sizes, we demonstrate that the combined method of adapted meta program induction has the strongest performance.

paragraphs: Neural program induction learns an input-output mapping from examples, but learning each new task separately can demand substantial data and computation. This paper investigates transferring knowledge from related tasks. The aim is to make program induction more effective when a new task provides only a small collection of input-output examples.

The authors propose two approaches. Portfolio adaptation pretrains several induction models on related tasks, selects the best model, and adapts it to the new task. Meta program induction instead learns to handle new tasks from a few examples without additional training. They evaluate both using a newly constructed benchmark of Karel programs.

Both approaches strongly outperform the evaluated induction baseline without transfer, but their relative strengths depend on data availability. Meta induction performs best among the compared approaches with fewer than ten examples. Portfolio adaptation becomes strongest with a thousand or more examples. For intermediate amounts of data, adapting a meta-induction model performs best, showing that the most effective transfer strategy changes with the available evidence.
summary.tldr: Transferring knowledge across program-induction tasks improves learning, with different transfer strategies winning at different data sizes.

title: Neural Program Meta-Induction

abstract: We consider the problem of computing a restricted nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) of an m\times n matrix X. Specifically, we seek a factorization X\approx BC, where the k columns of B are a subset of those from X and C\in\Re_{\geq 0}^{k\times n}. Equivalently, given the matrix X, consider the problem of finding a small subset, S, of the columns of X such that the conic hull of S \eps-approximates the conic hull of the columns of X, i.e., the distance of every column of X to the conic hull of the columns of S should be at most an \eps-fraction of the angular diameter of X. If k is the size of the smallest \eps-approximation, then we produce an O(k/\eps^{2/3}) sized O(\eps^{1/3})-approximation, yielding the first provable, polynomial time \eps-approximation for this class of NMF problems, where also desirably the approximation is independent of n and m. Furthermore, we prove an approximate conic Carathéodory theorem, a general sparsity result, that shows that any column of X can be \eps-approximated with an O(1/\eps^2) sparse combination from S. Our results are facilitated by a reduction to the problem of approximating convex hulls, and we prove that both the convex and conic hull variants are d-sum-hard, resolving an open problem. Finally, we provide experimental results for the convex and conic algorithms on a variety of feature selection tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies a restricted matrix factorization in which representative columns must be selected from the original matrix. Every column is then approximated by a nonnegative combination of those representatives. Geometrically, the goal is to select a small set whose conic hull approximates the conic hull of all columns.

If the smallest ε-approximation uses k columns, the algorithm selects O(k/ε^(2/3)) columns and achieves O(ε^(1/3)) approximation. This explicitly trades a larger representative set and weaker approximation tolerance for a provable polynomial-time procedure. The approximation guarantee is independent of the matrix's row and column counts, a desirable feature when the dataset is large.

A separate sparsity theorem shows that an individual column can be ε-approximated using O(1/ε²) representatives from the selected set. The analysis reduces conic approximation to convex-hull approximation and establishes d-sum-hardness for both variants. Experiments apply the convex and conic algorithms to feature selection tasks. Together, the results address selecting a compact dictionary and representing each item sparsely within it.
summary.tldr: Polynomial-time conic-hull approximation selects representative matrix columns with explicit approximation and sparsity guarantees.

title: Sparse Approximate Conic Hulls

abstract: We present hash embeddings, an efficient method for representing words in a continuous vector form. A hash embedding may be seen as an interpolation between a standard word embedding and a word embedding created using a random hash function (the hashing trick). In hash embeddings each token is represented by $k$ $d$-dimensional embeddings vectors and one $k$ dimensional weight vector. The final $d$ dimensional representation of the token is the product of the two. Rather than fitting the embedding vectors for each token these are selected by the hashing trick from a shared pool of $B$ embedding vectors. Our experiments show that hash embeddings can easily deal with huge vocabularies consisting of millions tokens. When using a hash embedding there is no need to create a dictionary before training nor to perform any kind of vocabulary pruning after training. We show that models trained using hash embeddings exhibit at least the same level of performance as models trained using regular embeddings across a wide range of tasks. Furthermore, the number of parameters needed by such an embedding is only a fraction of what is required by a regular embedding. Since standard embeddings and embeddings constructed using the hashing trick are actually just special cases of a hash embedding, hash embeddings can be considered an extension and improvement over the existing regular embedding types.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent tokens as continuous vectors, but assigning each token its own full vector can require many parameters for large vocabularies. Hash embeddings reduce that burden by sharing a pool of embedding vectors across tokens while retaining a weighted representation for each token.

For a given token, hashing selects several vectors from the shared pool. A token-specific weight vector combines them into the final representation. This construction brings together ordinary learned embeddings and the hashing trick: both appear as special cases of the broader scheme. The resulting representation allows parameter sharing without reducing every token to just one hashed vector.

Experiments show that the approach handles vocabularies containing millions of tokens and uses only a fraction of the parameters required by regular embeddings. Across the evaluated tasks, models using hash embeddings achieve at least comparable performance. The method also removes the need to construct a dictionary before training or prune the vocabulary afterward, simplifying vocabulary handling alongside the reported parameter savings.
summary.tldr: Hash embeddings combine shared, hash-selected vectors with token-specific weights to represent large vocabularies with far fewer parameters.

title: Hash Embeddings for Efficient Word Representations

abstract: Time series classification using deep neural networks, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), operate on the spectral decomposition of the time series computed using a preprocessing step. This step can include a large number of hyperparameters, such as window length, filter widths, and filter shapes, each with a range of possible values that must be chosen using time and data intensive cross-validation procedures. We propose the wavelet deconvolution (WD) layer as an efficient alternative to this preprocessing step that eliminates a significant number of hyperparameters. The WD layer uses wavelet functions with adjustable scale parameters to learn the spectral decomposition directly from the signal. Using backpropagation, we show the scale parameters can be optimized with gradient descent. Furthermore, the WD layer adds interpretability to the learned time series classifier by exploiting the properties of the wavelet transform. In our experiments, we show that the WD layer can automatically extract the frequency content used to generate a dataset. The WD layer combined with a CNN applied to the phone recognition task on the TIMIT database achieves a phone error rate of 18.1\%, a relative improvement of 4\% over the baseline CNN. Experiments on a dataset where engineered features are not available showed WD+CNN is the best performing method. Our results show that the WD layer can improve neural network based time series classifiers both in accuracy and interpretability by learning directly from the input signal.

paragraphs: Time series classifiers often receive a spectral decomposition produced before neural network training. Choosing that preprocessing can require costly searches over window lengths, filter widths, and filter shapes. This paper introduces a wavelet deconvolution layer that learns a spectral representation directly from the signal, removing a substantial number of manually selected hyperparameters.

The layer uses wavelet functions with adjustable scales. Backpropagation supplies gradients for those scales, allowing gradient descent to tune the decomposition along with the classifier. These results support learning the spectral front end as a way to improve both accuracy and interpretability.
summary.tldr: A trainable wavelet layer learns spectral filter scales directly from signals, improving time series classification and making frequency use more interpretable.

title: Learning filter widths of spectral decompositions with wavelets

abstract: From a single image, humans are able to perceive the full 3D shape of an object by exploiting learned shape priors from everyday life. Contemporary single-image 3D reconstruction algorithms aim to solve this task in a similar fashion, but often end up with priors that are highly biased by training classes. Here we present an algorithm, Generalizable Reconstruction (GenRe), designed to capture more generic, class-agnostic shape priors. We achieve this with an inference network and training procedure that combine 2.5D representations of visible surfaces (depth and silhouette), spherical shape representations of both visible and non-visible surfaces, and 3D voxel-based representations, in a principled manner that exploits the causal structure of how 3D shapes give rise to 2D images. Experiments demonstrate that GenRe performs well on single-view shape reconstruction, and generalizes to diverse novel objects from categories not seen during training.

Contemporary single-image 3D reconstruction algorithms aim to solve this task in a similar fashion, but often end up with priors that are highly biased by training classes. Here we present an algorithm, Generalizable Reconstruction (GenRe), designed to capture more generic, class-agnostic shape priors. We achieve this with an inference network and training procedure that combine 2.5D representations of visible surfaces (depth and silhouette), spherical shape representations of both visible and non-visible surfaces, and 3D voxel-based representations, in a principled manner that exploits the causal structure of how 3D shapes give rise to 2D images. Experiments demonstrate that GenRe performs well on single-view shape reconstruction, and generalizes to diverse novel objects from categories not seen during training.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a complete three-dimensional object from one image requires reasoning about surfaces the image does not show. Learned shape priors can supply that information, but they may become strongly tied to the object categories used during training. This paper introduces Generalizable Reconstruction, or GenRe, to learn priors that are less category-specific.

GenRe combines several representations within its inference network and training procedure. Depth and silhouette describe visible surfaces in a 2.5D form. Spherical representations cover visible and hidden surfaces, while voxels represent three-dimensional shape. The combination is organized around the causal relationship between a three-dimensional object and the two-dimensional image it produces, giving the representations complementary roles.

The experiments show that GenRe performs well at single-view reconstruction and generalizes to diverse objects from categories absent during training. This supports the intended benefit of learning more generic shape knowledge: reconstruction can remain useful beyond the categories that supplied the training examples. The finding concerns demonstrated generalization to novel objects, without asserting that every unseen category will be reconstructed equally well.
summary.tldr: GenRe combines complementary geometric representations to reconstruct 3D shapes from single images and generalize to unseen object categories.

title: Learning to Reconstruct Shapes from Unseen Classes

abstract: Batch normalization (BN) is a technique to normalize activations in intermediate layers of deep neural networks. Its tendency to improve accuracy and speed up training have established BN as a favorite technique in deep learning. Yet, despite its enormous success, there remains little consensus on the exact reason and mechanism behind these improvements. In this paper we take a step towards a better understanding of BN, following an empirical approach. We conduct several experiments, and show that BN primarily enables training with larger learning rates, which is the cause for faster convergence and better generalization. For networks without BN we demonstrate how large gradient updates can result in diverging loss and activations growing uncontrollably with network depth, which limits possible learning rates. BN avoids this problem by constantly correcting activations to be zero-mean and of unit standard deviation, which enables larger gradient steps, yields faster convergence and may help bypass sharp local minima. We further show various ways in which gradients and activations of deep unnormalized networks are ill-behaved. We contrast our results against recent findings in random matrix theory, shedding new light on classical initialization schemes and their consequences.

paragraphs: Batch normalization is widely used because it often accelerates training and improves accuracy, but its mechanism has been debated. This paper investigates that mechanism experimentally. The authors find that its primary contribution is enabling larger learning rates, which in their analysis account for faster convergence and improved generalization.

Their experiments show how large updates can destabilize networks without normalization: the loss can diverge, and activations can grow uncontrollably with depth. Batch normalization repeatedly restores activations to zero mean and unit standard deviation. This correction allows larger gradient steps, providing a concrete connection between normalized activations and the learning rates training can sustain.

The paper also examines other problematic patterns in the gradients and activations of deep unnormalized networks. It compares these observations with findings from random matrix theory to reconsider classical initialization schemes. The authors suggest that larger steps may additionally help avoid sharp local minima, retaining that explanation as a possibility. The main account is empirical: normalization changes which update sizes remain workable during training.
summary.tldr: Experiments identify larger usable learning rates as a primary mechanism behind batch normalization’s training and generalization benefits.

title: Understanding Batch Normalization

abstract: Multi-response linear models aggregate a set of vanilla linear models by assuming correlated noise across them, which has an unknown covariance structure. To find the coefficient vector, estimators with a joint approximation of the noise covariance are often preferred than the simple linear regression in view of their superior empirical performance, which can be generally solved by alternating-minimization type procedures. Due to the non-convex nature of such joint estimators, the theoretical justification of their efficiency is typically challenging. The existing analyses fail to fully explain the empirical observations due to the assumption of resampling on the alternating procedures, which requires access to fresh samples in each iteration. In this work, we present a resampling-free analysis for the alternating minimization algorithm applied to the multi-response regression. In particular, we focus on the high-dimensional setting of multi-response linear models with structured coefficient parameter, and the statistical error of the parameter can be expressed by the complexity measure, Gaussian width, which is related to the assumed structure. More importantly, to the best of our knowledge, our result reveals for the first time that the alternating minimization with random initialization can achieve the same performance as the well-initialized one when solving this multi-response regression problem. Experimental results support our theoretical developments.

paragraphs: When several linear prediction problems have correlated noise, estimating them together can be more effective than treating each separately. The challenge is that both the prediction coefficients and the noise covariance are unknown. Alternating minimization updates these quantities in turn, but the resulting joint estimation problem is nonconvex, making its observed effectiveness difficult to justify theoretically.

This paper analyzes alternating minimization without requiring fresh observations at every iteration. That change matters because earlier analyses assumed repeated access to new samples, leaving a gap between their guarantees and procedures that reuse one dataset. The authors focus on high-dimensional models whose coefficients have an assumed structure, and express statistical error using Gaussian width, a measure connected to that structure.

The analysis also shows that random initialization can achieve the same performance as a carefully initialized procedure for this regression problem. Experiments support the theoretical results. Together, these findings strengthen the explanation for why alternating estimation can work while reusing data and avoiding a specially prepared starting point.
summary.tldr: A resampling-free analysis explains how alternating minimization can estimate structured multi-response regressions effectively even from random initialization.

title: An Improved Analysis of Alternating Minimization for Structured Multi-Response Regression

paragraphs: The supplied abstract introduces phase retrieval: recovering an unknown signal from measurements that retain only magnitudes. Each measurement is the absolute value of a known linear measurement of the signal. The measurement matrix is available, but the phase information is absent, which motivates reconstruction methods for situations where obtaining that information is expensive or infeasible.

The central opportunity described is that signals often have structure. The abstract names sparsity, low rank, and membership in a finite alphabet as examples. Such structure opens the possibility of recovering a signal with fewer measurements than its ambient dimension. This is presented as a possibility arising from structure, rather than a guarantee for every signal or measurement system.

The title identifies regularized PhaseMax and announces optimal sample complexity as the paper's subject. However, the supplied abstract stops during the problem setup, before describing the method or its findings. The supported explanation therefore centers on the reconstruction problem and its motivation; the conditions and meaning of the title's optimality claim are not available in this excerpt.
summary.tldr: The paper concerns structured signal recovery from magnitude-only measurements, but the supplied abstract ends before explaining its regularized PhaseMax result.

title: Learning without the Phase: Regularized PhaseMax Achieves Optimal Sample Complexity

abstract: Predicting the dependencies between observations from multiple time series is critical for applications such as anomaly detection, financial risk management, causal analysis, or demand forecasting. However, the computational and numerical difficulties of estimating time-varying and high-dimensional covariance matrices often limits existing methods to handling at most a few hundred dimensions or requires making strong assumptions on the dependence between series. We propose to combine an RNN-based time series model with a Gaussian copula process output model with a low-rank covariance structure to reduce the computational complexity and handle non-Gaussian marginal distributions. This permits to drastically reduce the number of parameters and consequently allows the modeling of time-varying correlations of thousands of time series. We show on several real-world datasets that our method provides significant accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and perform an ablation study analyzing the contributions of the different components of our model.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires modeling how their observations depend on one another. Allowing those relationships to change over time makes the problem harder, particularly when a covariance matrix must describe thousands of series. The paper addresses the computational and numerical burden that can restrict existing methods to much smaller collections.

The proposed model combines a recurrent neural network for time series with a Gaussian copula process output model. A low-rank covariance structure reduces the number of parameters used to represent dependencies. The copula formulation also accommodates non-Gaussian marginal distributions, so individual series need not each follow a Gaussian distribution.

Together, these choices make it possible to model changing correlations among thousands of series with substantially reduced computational complexity. Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant accuracy improvements over the compared state-of-the-art baselines. An ablation study examines the contributions of individual components. The results support combining temporal modeling, flexible marginal distributions, and a compact dependence representation within one forecasting system.
summary.tldr: A recurrent forecasting model with a low-rank Gaussian copula represents changing dependencies among thousands of non-Gaussian time series.

title: High-dimensional multivariate forecasting with low-rank Gaussian Copula Processes

abstract: In this paper, a bat-inspired high-resolution ultrasound 3D imaging system is presented. Live bats demonstrate that the properly used ultrasound can be used to perceive 3D space. With this in mind, a neural network referred to as a Bat-G network is implemented to reconstruct the 3D representation of target objects from the hyperbolic FM (HFM) chirped ultrasonic echoes. The Bat-G network consists of an encoder emulating a bat's central auditory pathway, and a 3D graphical visualization decoder. For the acquisition of the ultrasound data, a custom-made Bat-I sensor module is used. The Bat-G network shows the uniform 3D reconstruction results and achieves precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.896, 0.899 and 0.895, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the implementation feasibility of a high-resolution non-optical sound-based imaging system being used by live bats. The project web page (https://sites.google.com/view/batgnet) contains additional content summarizing our research.

paragraphs: Bats demonstrate that echoes can provide information about three-dimensional surroundings. This paper uses that observation to motivate a high-resolution imaging system that reconstructs target objects from ultrasound. Its central task is to turn recorded sound reflections into a spatial representation, providing an imaging route that does not depend on optical measurements.

The system combines a custom ultrasound acquisition module, called Bat-I, with a neural network called Bat-G. The inputs are echoes from hyperbolic frequency-modulated ultrasonic chirps. Within the network, an encoder emulates the bat's central auditory pathway, while a decoder converts the encoded information into a three-dimensional graphical representation of the target.

The authors report uniform reconstruction results, with precision of 0.896, recall of 0.899, and an F1-score of 0.895. Their experiments demonstrate the feasibility of implementing this bat-inspired, sound-based imaging approach. The contribution therefore joins specialized sensing hardware with a learned reconstruction system, showing how ultrasonic measurements can support the proposed three-dimensional imaging pipeline.
summary.tldr: Bat-G combines custom ultrasonic sensing with a bat-inspired neural network to reconstruct three-dimensional objects from echoes.

title: Bat-G net: Bat-inspired High-Resolution 3D Image Reconstruction using Ultrasonic Echoes

abstract: Cascading portfolio scheduling is a static algorithm selection strategy which uses a sample of test instances to compute an optimal ordering (a cascading schedule) of a portfolio of available algorithms. The algorithms are then applied to each future instance according to this cascading schedule, until some algorithm in the schedule succeeds. Cascading algorithm scheduling has proven to be effective in several applications, including QBF solving and the generation of ImageNet classification models. It is known that the computation of an optimal cascading schedule in the offline phase is NP-hard. In this paper we study the parameterized complexity of this problem and establish its fixed-parameter tractability by utilizing structural properties of the success relation between algorithms and test instances. Our findings are significant as they reveal that in spite of the intractability of the problem in its general form, one can indeed exploit sparseness or density of the success relation to obtain non-trivial runtime guarantees for finding an optimal cascading schedule.

paragraphs: Cascading portfolio scheduling chooses an order for trying a collection of algorithms. The schedule is learned from test instances, then applied to future instances until an algorithm succeeds. Computing an optimal schedule is NP-hard in general, even though the strategy has been useful in applications such as QBF solving and ImageNet model generation.

This paper studies whether structural features of the input make optimal scheduling tractable. Its focus is the success relation: which algorithms succeed on which test instances. Through parameterized complexity analysis, the authors establish fixed-parameter tractability by exploiting properties of this relation.

The findings show that both sparseness and density in the success relation can support nontrivial runtime guarantees for finding an optimal schedule. The general hardness result still applies, but these structural cases provide more informative guidance about computational difficulty. The contribution identifies properties of algorithm-instance performance that can be used to obtain exact scheduling guarantees despite the problem's worst-case intractability.
summary.tldr: Structural sparsity or density in algorithm successes enables fixed-parameter tractable approaches to otherwise NP-hard cascading portfolio scheduling.

title: The Parameterized Complexity of Cascading Portfolio Scheduling

abstract: Excitation-inhibition balance is ubiquitously observed in the cortex. Recent studies suggest an intriguing link between balance on fast timescales, tight balance, and efficient information coding with spikes. We further this connection by taking a principled approach to optimal balanced networks of excitatory (E) and inhibitory(I) neurons. By deriving E-I spiking neural networks from greedy spike-based optimizations of constrained minimax objectives, we show that tight balance arises from correcting for deviations from the minimax optima. We predict specific neuron firing rates in the networks by solving the minimax problems, going beyond statistical theories of balanced networks. We design minimax objectives for reconstruction of an input signal, associative memory, and storage of manifold attractors, and derive from them E-I networks that perform the computation. Overall, we present a novel normative modeling approach for spiking E-I networks, going beyond the widely-used energy-minimizing networks that violate Dale’s law. Our networks can be used to model cortical circuits and computations.

paragraphs: Excitatory and inhibitory activity often closely balance in the cortex, including over short timescales. This paper seeks a computational explanation for that tight balance. It starts from constrained minimax objectives and derives spiking networks whose excitatory and inhibitory neurons carry out greedy, spike-based optimization of those objectives.

Within this construction, tight balance emerges as the network corrects deviations from a minimax optimum. Solving the underlying optimization problem also predicts specific firing rates, connecting the desired computation to the activity of individual neurons. The approach therefore explains balance through an explicitly defined computational objective and provides predictions beyond a statistical description of network activity.

The authors construct objectives for reconstructing input signals, associative memory, and storing manifold attractors, then derive networks that perform these computations. Their framework provides a normative model of excitatory-inhibitory circuits that respects Dale's law, addressing a mismatch in widely used energy-minimizing networks. The resulting networks offer models for cortical computation grounded in the tasks their dynamics are designed to solve.
summary.tldr: Deriving spiking networks from minimax objectives explains tight excitation-inhibition balance and predicts firing rates for specified computations.

title: Minimax Dynamics of Optimally Balanced Spiking Networks of Excitatory and Inhibitory Neurons

abstract: In visual domain adaptation (DA), separating the domain-specific characteristics from the domain-invariant representations is an ill-posed problem. Existing methods apply different kinds of priors or directly minimize the domain discrepancy to address this problem, which lack flexibility in handling real-world situations. Another research pipeline expresses the domain-specific information as a gradual transferring process, which tends to be suboptimal in accurately removing the domain-specific properties. In this paper, we address the modeling of domain-invariant and domain-specific information from the heuristic search perspective. We identify the characteristics in the existing representations that lead to larger domain discrepancy as the heuristic representations. With the guidance of heuristic representations, we formulate a principled framework of Heuristic Domain Adaptation (HDA) with well-founded theoretical guarantees. To perform HDA, the cosine similarity scores and independence measurements between domain-invariant and domain-specific representations are cast into the constraints at the initial and final states during the learning procedure. Similar to the final condition of heuristic search, we further derive a constraint enforcing the final range of heuristic network output to be small. Accordingly, we propose Heuristic Domain Adaptation Network (HDAN), which explicitly learns the domain-invariant and domain-specific representations with the above mentioned constraints. Extensive experiments show that HDAN has exceeded state-of-the-art on unsupervised DA, multi-source DA and semi-supervised DA. The code is available at https://github.com/cuishuhao/HDA.
