paragraphs: Visual domain adaptation requires distinguishing information shared across domains from characteristics specific to a particular domain. The paper treats this separation as ill-posed and argues that existing priors, discrepancy reduction methods, and gradual transfer approaches lack flexibility or remove domain-specific information imperfectly. It proposes using ideas from heuristic search to guide the separation.

The key is to identify features associated with larger discrepancies between domains and use them as heuristic representations. The resulting Heuristic Domain Adaptation framework places constraints on the learning process using cosine similarity and independence measurements between shared and domain-specific representations. It also constrains the final range of the heuristic network's output to be small.

The authors implement these ideas in a network that explicitly learns both kinds of representation and provide theoretical guarantees for the framework. Experiments report performance beyond the state of the art in unsupervised, multi-source, and semi-supervised domain adaptation. The approach's significance is the structured guidance it gives to representation separation, with constraints governing both the beginning and the end of learning.
summary.tldr: Heuristic Domain Adaptation uses discrepancy-related features and learning constraints to separate domain-specific information from shared representations.

title: Heuristic Domain Adaptation

abstract: Weighted model integration (WMI) is a framework to perform advanced probabilistic inference on hybrid domains, i.e., on distributions over mixed continuous-discrete random variables and in presence of complex logical and arithmetic constraints. In this work, we advance the WMI framework on both the theoretical and algorithmic side. First, we exactly trace the boundaries of tractability for WMI inference by proving that to be amenable to exact and efficient inference a WMI problem has to posses a tree-shaped structure with logarithmic diameter. While this result deepens our theoretical understanding of WMI it hinders the practical applicability of exact WMI solvers to real-world problems. To overcome this, we propose the first approximate WMI solver that does not resort to sampling, but performs exact inference on one approximate models. Our solution performs message passing in a relaxed problem structure iteratively to recover certain lost dependencies and, as our experiments suggest, is competitive with other SOTA WMI solvers.

paragraphs: Weighted model integration supports probabilistic reasoning with both discrete and continuous variables, including logical and arithmetic constraints. This flexibility makes it useful for expressing complicated distributions, but exact inference can be computationally demanding. The paper studies the structural boundary between problems that permit efficient exact inference and those that require a more practical approximation.

The theoretical analysis identifies a tree-shaped structure with logarithmic diameter as necessary for exact, efficient inference in the tractability characterization. This places a substantial restriction on the problems covered by efficient exact solvers. The algorithmic contribution responds by relaxing the problem structure and carrying out exact inference on the resulting approximate model.

Unlike sampling-based approximations, the proposed solver uses iterative message passing to recover some dependencies lost during relaxation. Its answers are approximate because the model has been changed, even though inference on that model is exact. Experiments suggest competitiveness with other state-of-the-art WMI solvers, connecting the theoretical restrictions to a practical strategy for working beyond them.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes tractable weighted model integration and proposes a sampling-free approximation based on relaxed structures and iterative message passing.

title: Probabilistic Inference with Algebraic Constraints: Theoretical Limits and Practical Approximations

abstract: Similarity-based Hierarchical Clustering (HC) is a classical unsupervised machine learning algorithm that has traditionally been solved with heuristic algorithms like Average-Linkage. Recently, Dasgupta reframed HC as a discrete optimization problem by introducing a global cost function measuring the quality of a given tree. In this work, we provide the first continuous relaxation of Dasgupta's discrete optimization problem with provable quality guarantees. The key idea of our method, HypHC, is showing a direct correspondence from discrete trees to continuous representations (via the hyperbolic embeddings of their leaf nodes) and back (via a decoding algorithm that maps leaf embeddings to a dendrogram), allowing us to search the space of discrete binary trees with continuous optimization. Building on analogies between trees and hyperbolic space, we derive a continuous analogue for the notion of lowest common ancestor, which leads to a continuous relaxation of Dasgupta's discrete objective. We can show that after decoding, the global minimizer of our continuous relaxation yields a discrete tree with a (1+eps)-factor approximation for Dasgupta's optimal tree, where eps can be made arbitrarily small and controls optimization challenges. We experimentally evaluate HypHC on a variety of HC benchmarks and find that even approximate solutions found with gradient descent have superior clustering quality than agglomerative heuristics or other gradient based algorithms. Finally, we highlight the flexibility of HypHC using end-to-end training in a downstream classification task.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes observations into a tree of nested groups. Dasgupta's objective assigns a global cost to such a tree, but optimizing over discrete tree structures is challenging. HypHC creates a continuous version of this problem by representing the tree's leaves as points in hyperbolic space and decoding those points back into a clustering tree.

The method develops a continuous counterpart of the lowest common ancestor, the point where two branches meet in a tree. This supplies the bridge between the discrete objective and its continuous relaxation. The authors prove that decoding a global minimizer of the relaxation gives a tree within a factor of 1+epsilon of optimal; making epsilon smaller affects optimization difficulty.

The guarantee specifically concerns a global minimizer. Separately, experiments show that approximate solutions obtained with gradient descent outperform agglomerative heuristics and other gradient-based methods on the evaluated benchmarks. An end-to-end classification application demonstrates flexibility. Together, the results connect a principled tree objective with continuous optimization while distinguishing the theoretical optimum from practical solutions.
summary.tldr: HypHC optimizes hierarchical clustering through hyperbolic embeddings, with a near-optimal decoding guarantee for the relaxation's global minimizer.

title: From Trees to Continuous Embeddings and Back: Hyperbolic Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: We introduce Habitat 2.0 (H2.0), a simulation platform for training virtual robots in interactive 3D environments and complex physics-enabled scenarios. We make comprehensive contributions to all levels of the embodied AI stack – data, simulation, and benchmark tasks. Specifically, we present: (i) ReplicaCAD: an artist-authored, annotated, reconfigurable 3D dataset of apartments (matching real spaces) with articulated objects (e.g. cabinets and drawers that can open/close); (ii) H2.0: a high-performance physics-enabled 3D simulator with speeds exceeding 25,000 simulation steps per second (850x real-time) on an 8-GPU node, representing 100x speed-ups over prior work; and, (iii) Home Assistant Benchmark (HAB): a suite of common tasks for assistive robots (tidy the house, stock groceries, set the table) that test a range of mobile manipulation capabilities. These large-scale engineering contributions allow us to systematically compare deep reinforcement learning (RL) at scale and classical sense-plan-act (SPA) pipelines in long-horizon structured tasks, with an emphasis on generalization to new objects, receptacles, and layouts. We find that (1) flat RL policies struggle on HAB compared to hierarchical ones; (2) a hierarchy with independent skills suffers from ‘hand-off problems’, and (3) SPA pipelines are more brittle than RL policies.

paragraphs: Habitat 2.0 provides a simulation platform for training virtual robots to manipulate objects in interactive homes. Its contributions span environments, simulation, and evaluation tasks. ReplicaCAD supplies annotated, reconfigurable apartments matching real spaces, including articulated objects such as cabinets and drawers that can open and close.

The physics-enabled simulator exceeds 25,000 steps per second on an eight-GPU node, reported as 850 times real time and a hundredfold speedup over prior work. The Home Assistant Benchmark adds tasks such as tidying, stocking groceries, and setting a table. Together, these components support systematic comparisons on extended tasks requiring both movement and manipulation, including generalization to unfamiliar objects, receptacles, and layouts.

The comparisons reveal several distinct difficulties. Flat reinforcement-learning policies struggle relative to hierarchical policies, but independently learned skills in a hierarchy encounter problems when handing control from one skill to another. Classical sense-plan-act pipelines are more brittle than reinforcement-learning policies in the study. The benchmark therefore exposes coordination and robustness issues as well as testing individual robot capabilities.
summary.tldr: Habitat 2.0 combines interactive homes, fast physics simulation, and household benchmarks to reveal challenges in coordinating robust robot manipulation.

title: Habitat 2.0: Training Home Assistants to Rearrange their Habitat

abstract: Transformers are expensive to train due to the quadratic time and space complexity in the self-attention mechanism. On the other hand, although kernel machines suffer from the same computation bottleneck in pairwise dot products, several approximation schemes have been successfully incorporated to considerably reduce their computational cost without sacrificing too much accuracy. In this work, we leverage the computation methods for kernel machines to alleviate the high computational cost and introduce Skyformer, which replaces the softmax structure with a Gaussian kernel to stabilize the model training and adapts the Nyström method to a non-positive semidefinite matrix to accelerate the computation. We further conduct theoretical analysis by showing that the matrix approximation error of our proposed method is small in the spectral norm. Experiments on Long Range Arena benchmark show that the proposed method is sufficient in getting comparable or even better performance than the full self-attention while requiring fewer computation resources.

paragraphs: Transformer self-attention has quadratic time and memory costs, making training expensive as the number of elements grows. This paper draws on approximation methods from kernel machines, which face a related bottleneck from computing pairwise relationships. The aim is to reduce attention’s computational burden while retaining useful predictive performance.

Skyformer replaces the usual softmax structure with a Gaussian kernel to stabilize training. It then adapts the Nyström approximation method to a matrix that is not positive semidefinite, accelerating computation. These are linked design choices: the attention formulation changes, and a kernel-based approximation supplies the mechanism for computing it more cheaply.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing small matrix-approximation error in spectral norm. Experiments on the Long Range Arena benchmark find performance comparable to, or better than, full self-attention while using fewer computational resources. The theoretical result characterizes the approximation, while the benchmark results support its practical usefulness for the evaluated tasks. Together they motivate borrowing kernel-computation techniques when redesigning efficient attention.
summary.tldr: Skyformer combines Gaussian-kernel attention with a Nyström approximation to reduce computation while matching or improving benchmark performance.

title: Skyformer: Remodel Self-Attention with Gaussian Kernel and Nystr\"om Method

abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) is a widely-used approach to learn models that are robust against distribution shift. Compared with the standard optimization setting, the objective function in DRO is more difficult to optimize, and most of the existing theoretical results make strong assumptions on the loss function. In this work we bridge the gap by studying DRO algorithms for general smooth non-convex losses. By carefully exploiting the specific form of the DRO objective, we are able to provide non-asymptotic convergence guarantees even though the objective function is possibly non-convex, non-smooth and has unbounded gradient noise. In particular, we prove that a special algorithm called the mini-batch normalized gradient descent with momentum, can find an $\epsilon$-first-order stationary point within $\mathcal O(\epsilon^{-4})$ gradient complexity. We also discuss the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) setting, where we propose a penalized DRO objective based on a smoothed version of the CVaR that allows us to obtain a similar convergence guarantee. We finally verify our theoretical results in a number of tasks and find that the proposed algorithm can consistently achieve prominent acceleration.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains models to account for distribution shift, but its objective can be harder to optimize than an ordinary training loss. This paper studies the problem for general smooth nonconvex losses, seeking guarantees without the strong loss assumptions used in much previous theory.

The authors exploit the structure of the robust objective even when that objective is nonconvex, nonsmooth, and subject to unbounded gradient noise. They prove that mini-batch normalized gradient descent with momentum reaches an epsilon first-order stationary point using O(epsilon^-4) gradient evaluations. This is a finite-computation guarantee for approximate stationarity, rather than a claim of reaching a global optimum.

The paper also considers conditional value-at-risk, introducing a penalized objective based on a smoothed version of that criterion and obtaining a similar convergence guarantee. Experiments across several tasks report consistent acceleration from the proposed algorithm. Together, the theory and evaluations support an optimization method tailored to the structure of robust objectives, extending convergence analysis to settings with several simultaneous sources of difficulty.
summary.tldr: Normalized gradient descent with momentum has a finite gradient-complexity guarantee for approximate stationarity in challenging nonconvex DRO problems.

title: Non-convex Distributionally Robust Optimization: Non-asymptotic Analysis

abstract: We propose the Motion Capsule Autoencoder (MCAE), which addresses a key challenge in the unsupervised learning of motion representations: transformation invariance. MCAE models motion in a two-level hierarchy. In the lower level, a spatio-temporal motion signal is divided into short, local, and semantic-agnostic snippets. In the higher level, the snippets are aggregated to form full-length semantic-aware segments. For both levels, we represent motion with a set of learned transformation invariant templates and the corresponding geometric transformations by using capsule autoencoders of a novel design. This leads to a robust and efficient encoding of viewpoint changes. MCAE is evaluated on a novel Trajectory20 motion dataset and various real-world skeleton-based human action datasets. Notably, it achieves better results than baselines on Trajectory20 with considerably fewer parameters and state-of-the-art performance on the unsupervised skeleton-based action recognition task.

paragraphs: Motion can look different when viewed from another angle, even when the underlying action stays the same. Learning a useful motion representation without labels therefore requires handling transformations. The Motion Capsule Autoencoder, or MCAE, addresses this through a hierarchy that separates learned motion templates from the geometric transformations associated with them.

At the lower level, the model divides a motion signal into short local snippets that do not yet represent full action semantics. At the higher level, it combines these snippets into full-length segments that capture semantic structure. Both levels use specially designed capsule autoencoders with transformation-invariant templates and corresponding transformations, supporting efficient encoding of viewpoint changes.

The authors evaluate MCAE on the new Trajectory20 dataset and several real-world datasets of skeleton-based human actions. It outperforms baselines on Trajectory20 with considerably fewer parameters and achieves state-of-the-art results for unsupervised skeleton-based action recognition. These findings support the combination of hierarchical motion structure and explicit treatment of geometric transformations.
summary.tldr: MCAE learns hierarchical motion templates and their transformations, improving unsupervised action recognition while handling viewpoint changes.

title: Unsupervised Motion Representation Learning with Capsule Autoencoders

abstract: We propose a framework for comparing data manifolds, aimed, in particular, towards the evaluation of deep generative models. We describe a novel tool, Cross-Barcode(P,Q), that, given a pair of distributions in a high-dimensional space, tracks multiscale topology spacial discrepancies between manifolds on which the distributions are concentrated. Based on the Cross-Barcode, we introduce the Manifold Topology Divergence score (MTop-Divergence) and apply it to assess the performance of deep generative models in various domains: images, 3D-shapes, time-series, and on different datasets: MNIST, Fashion MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10, FFHQ, market stock data, ShapeNet. We demonstrate that the MTop-Divergence accurately detects various degrees of mode-dropping, intra-mode collapse, mode invention, and image disturbance. Our algorithm scales well (essentially linearly) with the increase of the dimension of the ambient high-dimensional space. It is one of the first TDA-based methodologies that can be applied universally to datasets of different sizes and dimensions, including the ones on which the most recent GANs in the visual domain are trained. The proposed method is domain agnostic and does not rely on pre-trained networks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves comparing generated data with the structure of the target data. This paper approaches that comparison through the topology of the manifolds on which two distributions concentrate. Its goal is to detect structural differences across multiple scales, including discrepancies that reflect missing or distorted parts of the generated distribution.

The central tool, Cross-Barcode, tracks these multiscale discrepancies for a pair of distributions in a high-dimensional space. The authors turn this tool into the Manifold Topology Divergence score and evaluate it across images, three-dimensional shapes, and time series. The method does not depend on pretrained networks and is designed to work across domains.

The experiments show detection of different degrees of mode dropping, collapse within modes, invented modes, and image disturbance. The algorithm also scales essentially linearly with ambient dimension. Together, these findings support a broadly applicable topology-based assessment tool: it can distinguish several forms of generative failure while accommodating varied data dimensions and types, without requiring a domain-specific pretrained representation.
summary.tldr: Manifold Topology Divergence compares multiscale data structure to detect generative-model failures across domains without pretrained networks.

title: Manifold Topology Divergence: a Framework for Comparing Data Manifolds.

abstract: Controllable generation is one of the key requirements for successful adoption of deep generative models in real-world applications, but it still remains as a great challenge. In particular, the compositional ability to generate novel concept combinations is out of reach for most current models. In this work, we use energy-based models (EBMs) to handle compositional generation over a set of attributes. To make them scalable to high-resolution image generation, we introduce an EBM in the latent space of a pre-trained generative model such as StyleGAN. We propose a novel EBM formulation representing the joint distribution of data and attributes together, and we show how sampling from it is formulated as solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Given a pre-trained generator, all we need for controllable generation is to train an attribute classifier. Sampling with ODEs is done efficiently in the latent space and is robust to hyperparameters. Thus, our method is simple, fast to train, and efficient to sample. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in both conditional sampling and sequential editing. In compositional generation, our method excels at zero-shot generation of unseen attribute combinations. Also, by composing energy functions with logical operators, this work is the first to achieve such compositionality in generating photo-realistic images of resolution 1024x1024.

paragraphs: Controllable image generation requires a model to follow requested attributes, including combinations it has not previously encountered. This paper uses energy-based models to express those attribute preferences within the latent space of a pretrained generator. Working in that space makes the approach applicable to high-resolution image synthesis.

The proposed energy formulation describes data and attributes jointly, and sampling is expressed as solving an ordinary differential equation. Given a pretrained generator such as StyleGAN, the additional training requirement is an attribute classifier. The authors report efficient latent-space sampling that is robust to hyperparameter choices, alongside a simple and fast training procedure.

Experiments show better conditional sampling and sequential editing than the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The approach also performs strongly when generating unseen attribute combinations without examples of those combinations. By combining energy functions through logical operators, the authors demonstrate compositional generation of photorealistic images at 1024 by 1024 resolution and claim the first such result. The contribution connects reusable attribute controls with an existing generator's image-production capabilities.
summary.tldr: Latent-space energy models enable efficient attribute-controlled generation and unseen attribute combinations with a pretrained image generator.

title: Controllable and Compositional Generation with Latent-Space Energy-Based Models

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms have had great success in recent years in limited labeled data regimes. However, the current state-of-the-art SSL algorithms are computationally expensive and entail significant compute time and energy requirements. This can prove to be a huge limitation for many smaller companies and academic groups. Our main insight is that training on a subset of unlabeled data instead of entire unlabeled data enables the current SSL algorithms to converge faster, significantly reducing computational costs. In this work, we propose RETRIEVE, a coreset selection framework for efficient and robust semi-supervised learning. RETRIEVE selects the coreset by solving a mixed discrete-continuous bi-level optimization problem such that the selected coreset minimizes the labeled set loss. We use a one-step gradient approximation and show that the discrete optimization problem is approximately submodular, enabling simple greedy algorithms to obtain the coreset. We empirically demonstrate on several real-world datasets that existing SSL algorithms like VAT, Mean-Teacher, FixMatch, when used with RETRIEVE, achieve a) faster training times, b) better performance when unlabeled data consists of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) data and imbalance. More specifically, we show that with minimal accuracy degradation, RETRIEVE achieves a speedup of around $3\times$ in the traditional SSL setting and achieves a speedup of $5\times$ compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) robust SSL algorithms in the case of imbalance and OOD data. RETRIEVE is available as a part of the CORDS toolkit: https://github.com/decile-team/cords.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning can make good use of limited labels, but repeatedly training on a large unlabeled collection is computationally expensive. RETRIEVE asks which unlabeled examples are most useful to retain. Its central idea is that a carefully chosen subset can make existing learning algorithms converge faster and reduce their training costs.

The subset is selected through a bi-level optimization problem that combines discrete example choices with continuous model training. The selection objective is the loss on labeled data, tying the choice of unlabeled examples to the supervised task. A one-step gradient approximation makes the problem more tractable, and approximate submodularity supports using simple greedy selection algorithms.

Experiments combine RETRIEVE with VAT, Mean-Teacher, and FixMatch on several real-world datasets. The authors report around threefold training speedup in conventional semi-supervised learning with minimal accuracy degradation. Under unlabeled-data imbalance and out-of-distribution contamination, they report improved performance and a fivefold speedup relative to state-of-the-art robust methods. These results suggest that selective use of unlabeled data can improve both training efficiency and robustness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: RETRIEVE selects useful subsets of unlabeled data to accelerate semi-supervised training and improve robustness to imbalance and out-of-distribution data.

title: RETRIEVE: Coreset Selection for Efficient and Robust Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We present neural radiance fields for rendering and temporal (4D) reconstruction of humans in motion (H-NeRF), as captured by a sparse set of cameras or even from a monocular video. Our approach combines ideas from neural scene representation, novel-view synthesis, and implicit statistical geometric human representations, coupled using novel loss functions. Instead of learning a radiance field with a uniform occupancy prior, we constrain it by a structured implicit human body model, represented using signed distance functions. This allows us to robustly fuse information from sparse views and generalize well beyond the poses or views observed in training. Moreover, we apply geometric constraints to co-learn the structure of the observed subject -- including both body and clothing -- and to regularize the radiance field to geometrically plausible solutions. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the robustness and the accuracy of our approach, its generalization capabilities significantly outside a small training set of poses and views, and statistical extrapolation beyond the observed shape.

paragraphs: H-NeRF reconstructs and renders moving humans over time from sparse camera views or even a single-camera video. The method combines neural scene representations, synthesis of new viewpoints, and an implicit statistical representation of human geometry. Its task involves recovering a person's changing structure as well as the appearance needed to render that person.

The key design is to constrain the radiance field with a structured human-body model represented through signed distance functions. This supplies geometric structure when combining information from limited views. Additional geometric constraints jointly learn the observed person's body and clothing while steering the radiance field toward geometrically plausible solutions. Loss functions connect these components during learning.

Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate accuracy, robustness, and generalization substantially beyond the small set of training poses and views. The authors also report statistical extrapolation beyond the observed shape. These findings support the use of a structured human model to guide reconstruction and rendering when the available visual observations are sparse.
summary.tldr: H-NeRF combines radiance fields with structured human geometry to reconstruct and render moving people from sparse views or monocular video.

title: H-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Rendering and Temporal Reconstruction of Humans in Motion

abstract: Most of the existing neural video compression methods adopt the predictive coding framework, which first generates the predicted frame and then encodes its residue with the current frame. However, as for compression ratio, predictive coding is only a sub-optimal solution as it uses simple subtraction operation to remove the redundancy across frames. In this paper, we propose a deep contextual video compression framework to enable a paradigm shift from predictive coding to conditional coding. In particular, we try to answer the following questions: how to define, use, and learn condition under a deep video compression framework. To tap the potential of conditional coding, we propose using feature domain context as condition. This enables us to leverage the high dimension context to carry rich information to both the encoder and the decoder, which helps reconstruct the high-frequency contents for higher video quality. Our framework is also extensible, in which the condition can be flexibly designed. Experiments show that our method can significantly outperform the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep video compression methods. When compared with x265 using veryslow preset, we can achieve 26.0% bitrate saving for 1080P standard test videos.

paragraphs: Many neural video compressors predict a frame and then encode the difference between that prediction and the actual frame. The paper argues that removing information shared across frames through simple subtraction leaves compression opportunities unused. It proposes conditional coding, in which learned context directly informs how the current frame is encoded and reconstructed.

The key design choice is to express that context in a feature space. These higher-dimensional features can carry rich information to both the encoder and decoder, giving the compression system more useful conditioning information. The authors connect this richer context to improved reconstruction of high-frequency image content, which matters for preserving fine visual detail.

The framework addresses how to define, use, and learn the conditioning information, while allowing its design to be changed within the same general approach. Experiments report substantial improvements over previous leading neural video compression methods. Against x265 with its veryslow preset, the method achieves a 26.0% bitrate saving on standard 1080P test videos. This result supports learned feature context as an effective way to exploit information shared across video frames.
summary.tldr: Learned feature context improves conditional video compression, delivering a reported 26.0% bitrate saving against x265 veryslow on standard 1080P videos.

title: Deep Contextual Video Compression

abstract: The recently-introduced class of ordinary differential equation networks (ODE-Nets) establishes a fruitful connection between deep learning and dynamical systems. In this work, we reconsider formulations of the weights as continuous-in-depth functions using linear combinations of basis functions which enables us to leverage parameter transformations such as function projections. In turn, this view allows us to formulate a novel stateful ODE-Block that handles stateful layers. The benefits of this new ODE-Block are twofold: first, it enables incorporating meaningful continuous-in-depth batch normalization layers to achieve state-of-the-art performance; second, it enables compressing the weights through a change of basis, without retraining, while maintaining near state-of-the-art performance and reducing both inference time and memory footprint. Performance is demonstrated by applying our stateful ODE-Block to (a) image classification tasks using convolutional units and (b) sentence-tagging tasks using transformer encoder units.

In turn, this view allows us to formulate a novel stateful ODE-Block that handles stateful layers. paragraphs: ODE-Nets connect neural networks with dynamical systems by treating depth continuously. This paper represents their depth-dependent weights as linear combinations of basis functions. Viewing weights as functions in this way makes transformations such as function projection available and provides the foundation for a new ODE block that supports stateful layers.

One benefit is the ability to incorporate meaningful continuous-in-depth batch normalization. Another is weight compression through a change of basis. The latter can be performed without retraining, allowing the weight representation to be altered after learning while retaining near state-of-the-art performance in the reported results. The method therefore connects the functional description of weights with both architectural support and compression.

The authors demonstrate the stateful block on image classification with convolutional units and sentence tagging with Transformer encoder units. They report state-of-the-art performance with the normalization-enabled design, while compression reduces inference time and memory use. These findings show how the same basis-function perspective can support stateful computation and provide a practical means of reducing deployment costs.
summary.tldr: Basis-function representations enable stateful ODE blocks with batch normalization and weight compression without retraining.

title: Stateful ODE-Nets using Basis Function Expansions

abstract: Graph embedding maps a graph into a convenient vector-space representation for graph analysis and machine learning applications. Many graph embedding methods hinge on a sampling of context nodes based on random walks. However, random walks can be a biased sampler due to the structural properties of graphs. Most notably, random walks are biased by the degree of each node, where a node is sampled proportionally to its degree. The implication of such biases has not been clear, particularly in the context of graph representation learning. Here, we investigate the impact of the random walks' bias on graph embedding and propose residual2vec, a general graph embedding method that can debias various structural biases in graphs by using random graphs. We demonstrate that this debiasing not only improves link prediction and clustering performance but also allows us to explicitly model salient structural properties in graph embedding.

Here, we investigate the impact of the random walks' bias on graph embedding and propose residual2vec, a general graph embedding method that can debias various structural biases in graphs by using random graphs. paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes and their relationships into vectors for analysis and machine learning. Many methods learn from context nodes sampled through random walks. This paper examines how the graph's structure biases that sampling process and, in turn, influences the representations that are learned.

A prominent example is degree bias: random walks sample nodes in proportion to their degree. As a result, the contexts used for embedding reflect this structural sampling preference. The authors propose residual2vec, a general embedding method that uses random graphs to account for various structural biases. The choice to model those biases explicitly is central to the approach.

The reported demonstrations show improved link prediction and clustering after debiasing. They also show that the method enables explicit modeling of salient structural graph properties in the embedding. This makes the contribution broader than a correction for node degree alone. It provides a way to account for structural effects in context sampling while retaining graph representations useful for the downstream tasks examined.
summary.tldr: Residual2vec uses random graphs to account for structural sampling biases and improves graph link prediction and clustering.

title: Residual2Vec: Debiasing graph embedding with random graphs

abstract: Designing spectral convolutional networks is a challenging problem in graph learning. ChebNet, one of the early attempts, approximates the spectral graph convolutions using Chebyshev polynomials. GCN simplifies ChebNet by utilizing only the first two Chebyshev polynomials while still outperforming it on real-world datasets. GPR-GNN and BernNet demonstrate that the Monomial and Bernstein bases also outperform the Chebyshev basis in terms of learning the spectral graph convolutions. Such conclusions are counter-intuitive in the field of approximation theory, where it is established that the Chebyshev polynomial achieves the optimum convergent rate for approximating a function. In this paper, we revisit the problem of approximating the spectral graph convolutions with Chebyshev polynomials. We show that ChebNet's inferior performance is primarily due to illegal coefficients learnt by ChebNet approximating analytic filter functions, which leads to over-fitting. We then propose ChebNetII, a new GNN model based on Chebyshev interpolation, which enhances the original Chebyshev polynomial approximation while reducing the Runge phenomenon. We conducted an extensive experimental study to demonstrate that ChebNetII can learn arbitrary graph convolutions and achieve superior performance in both full- and semi-supervised node classification tasks. Most notably, we scale ChebNetII to a billion graph ogbn-papers100M, showing that spectral-based GNNs have superior performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/ivam-he/ChebNetII.

paragraphs: Chebyshev polynomials have strong approximation properties, yet graph neural networks using them have sometimes performed worse than simpler or alternative polynomial constructions. This paper investigates that apparent contradiction in ChebNet, which approximates spectral graph convolutions using a Chebyshev basis. The question is whether the basis itself explains the disappointing results.

The authors attribute ChebNet's weaker performance primarily to learned coefficients that are unsuitable for approximating analytic filter functions, leading to overfitting. They introduce ChebNetII, which uses Chebyshev interpolation to improve the approximation. The design also reduces the Runge phenomenon, an unwanted oscillatory behavior associated with polynomial approximation. This shifts attention from the choice of polynomial family to how its coefficients and resulting filters are constructed.

Experiments show that ChebNetII can learn arbitrary graph convolutions and achieves superior performance in the evaluated fully supervised and semi-supervised node classification tasks. The authors also scale it to ogbn-papers100M. Together, these results support revisiting spectral graph networks with improved approximation design, rather than treating earlier ChebNet results as evidence against the Chebyshev basis.
summary.tldr: ChebNetII improves spectral graph learning through Chebyshev interpolation, addressing coefficient-related overfitting in the original ChebNet.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks on Graphs with Chebyshev Approximation, Revisited

abstract: A common lens to theoretically study neural net architectures is to analyze the functions they can approximate. However, the constructions from approximation theory often have unrealistic aspects, for example, reliance on infinite precision to memorize target function values. To address this issue, we propose a formal definition of statistically meaningful approximation which requires the approximating network to exhibit good statistical learnability. We present case studies on statistically meaningful approximation for two classes of functions: boolean circuits and Turing machines. We show that overparameterized feedforward neural nets can statistically meaningfully approximate boolean circuits with sample complexity depending only polynomially on the circuit size, not the size of the approximating network. In addition, we show that transformers can statistically meaningfully approximate Turing machines with computation time bounded by T, requiring sample complexity polynomial in the alphabet size, state space size, and log(T). Our analysis introduces new tools for generalization bounds that provide much tighter sample complexity guarantees than the typical VC-dimension or norm-based bounds, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Showing that a neural network can represent a function does not by itself establish that the function can be learned statistically. Some approximation constructions depend on unrealistic features such as infinite numerical precision. This paper introduces a definition of statistically meaningful approximation that also requires good statistical learnability.

The authors study Boolean circuits and time-bounded Turing machines. For Boolean circuits, they show that overparameterized feed-forward networks can provide meaningful approximations with sample complexity polynomial in circuit size, independent of the approximating network's size. The guarantee therefore connects the needed data to the target computation rather than the potentially much larger network.

For Turing machines with computation time bounded by T, transformers achieve sample complexity polynomial in alphabet size, state-space size, and log(T). The analysis introduces tools for generalization bounds that yield much tighter guarantees than typical VC-dimension or norm-based bounds in these studies. The contribution strengthens expressivity analysis by asking whether an approximating construction also comes with favorable guarantees about how much data learning requires.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens neural approximation theory with learnability requirements and derives sample-complexity guarantees for circuits and time-bounded Turing machines.

title: Statistically Meaningful Approximation: a Case Study on Approximating Turing Machines with Transformers

abstract: In meta reinforcement learning (meta RL), an agent learns from a set of training tasks how to quickly solve a new task, drawn from the same task distribution. The optimal meta RL policy, a.k.a.~the Bayes-optimal behavior, is well defined, and guarantees optimal reward in expectation, taken with respect to the task distribution. The question we explore in this work is how many training tasks are required to guarantee approximately optimal behavior with high probability. Recent work provided the first such PAC analysis for a model-free setting, where a history-dependent policy was learned from the training tasks. In this work, we propose a different approach: directly learn the task distribution, using density estimation techniques, and then train a policy on the learned task distribution. We show that our approach leads to bounds that depend on the dimension of the task distribution. In particular, in settings where the task distribution lies in a low-dimensional manifold, we extend our analysis to use dimensionality reduction techniques and account for such structure, obtaining significantly better bounds than previous work, which strictly depend on the number of states and actions. The key of our approach is the regularization implied by the kernel density estimation method. We further demonstrate that this regularization is useful in practice, when `plugged in' the state-of-the-art VariBAD meta RL algorithm.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning trains an agent across tasks so it can quickly solve a new task drawn from the same distribution. This paper asks how many training tasks are needed to guarantee approximately optimal expected reward with high probability. The target is behavior optimized for the underlying distribution of tasks.

The proposed approach first estimates that task distribution and then trains a policy using the estimate. Its theoretical bounds depend on the distribution's dimension. When tasks lie on a low-dimensional manifold, the analysis incorporates dimensionality reduction and obtains substantially better bounds than earlier results that depend directly on the numbers of states and actions.

Kernel density estimation supplies the regularization central to the approach. The authors also incorporate that regularization into VariBAD and demonstrate its practical usefulness. The theoretical advantage is tied to exploitable structure in the task distribution, especially low dimensionality. The work therefore links how tasks are distributed to how much training experience is needed, while connecting the analysis to an existing meta-learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Estimating the task distribution yields meta-RL guarantees that can improve substantially when tasks have low-dimensional structure.

title: Meta Reinforcement Learning with Finite Training Tasks - a Density Estimation Approach

abstract: We propose an information-theoretic knowledge distillation approach for the compression of generative adversarial networks, which aims to maximize the mutual information between teacher and student networks via a variational optimization based on an energy-based model. Because the direct computation of the mutual information in continuous domains is intractable, our approach alternatively optimizes the student network by maximizing the variational lower bound of the mutual information. To achieve a tight lower bound, we introduce an energy-based model relying on a deep neural network to represent a flexible variational distribution that deals with high-dimensional images and consider spatial dependencies between pixels, effectively. Since the proposed method is a generic optimization algorithm, it can be conveniently incorporated into arbitrary generative adversarial networks and even dense prediction networks, e.g., image enhancement models. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves outstanding performance in model compression of generative adversarial networks consistently when combined with several existing models.

Because the direct computation of the mutual information in continuous domains is intractable, our approach alternatively optimizes the student network by maximizing the variational lower bound of the mutual information. To achieve a tight lower bound, we introduce an energy-based model relying on a deep neural network to represent a flexible variational distribution that deals with high-dimensional images and consider spatial dependencies between pixels, effectively. paragraphs: Compressing a generative adversarial network involves transferring useful behavior from a teacher network to a smaller student. This paper formulates that transfer in information-theoretic terms: training should maximize mutual information between teacher and student. The objective is to preserve information shared by their outputs during compression.

Directly computing mutual information in continuous domains is intractable, so the method optimizes a variational lower bound instead. A deep energy-based model represents a flexible variational distribution intended to make this bound tight. Its flexibility is used to handle high-dimensional images and account for spatial relationships among pixels, which are relevant to transferring image-generation behavior.

The resulting procedure is presented as a generic optimization method that can be incorporated into arbitrary GAN architectures and extended to dense prediction networks, including image enhancement models. Experiments combining it with several existing models report consistently strong GAN compression performance. The contribution connects an information-preservation objective to a tractable training procedure, with the energy-based model supplying the distributional flexibility needed for image outputs.
summary.tldr: This GAN compression method trains students through a variational mutual-information objective supported by a flexible energy-based model.

title: Information-Theoretic GAN Compression with Variational Energy-based Model

abstract: The fundamental model of all solid crystalline materials is a periodic set of atomic centers considered up to rigid motion in Euclidean space. The major obstacle to materials discovery was highly ambiguous representations of periodic crystals that didn't allow fast and reliable comparisons and led to numerous (near-) duplicates in many databases of experimental and simulated crystals. This paper exemplarily resolves the ambiguity by invariants, which are descriptors without false negatives.The new Pointwise Distance Distributions (PDD) is a numerical matrix with a near-linear time complexity and an exactly computable metric. The strongest theoretical result is generic completeness (absence of false positives) for all finite and periodic sets of points in any dimension. The strength of PDD is shown by 200B+ pairwise comparisons of all periodic structures in the world's largest collection (Cambridge Structural Database) of existing materials over two days on a modest desktop.

paragraphs: A crystal can be modeled as a repeating set of atomic centers, with rigidly moved versions representing the same structure. Ambiguous representations make reliable comparison difficult and allow duplicate or nearly duplicate entries to accumulate in materials databases. This paper develops descriptors intended to make those comparisons both dependable and fast.

The proposed Pointwise Distance Distribution, or PDD, represents a point set as a numerical matrix. It is an invariant, so equivalent structures do not become false negatives merely through their representation. PDD has near-linear computational complexity and an exactly computable comparison metric. The strongest theoretical result is generic completeness for finite and periodic point sets in any dimension: the absence of false positives is qualified as generic, rather than universal.

The authors demonstrate practical scale through more than 200 billion pairwise comparisons of periodic structures in the Cambridge Structural Database, completed over two days on a modest desktop. This combines a theoretical account of discrimination with evidence that the representation can support very large collections of structural comparisons.
summary.tldr: Pointwise Distance Distributions support fast crystal comparisons with invariant descriptors and a generic completeness guarantee.

title: Resolving the data ambiguity for periodic crystals

abstract: We consider 1-dimensional location estimation, where we estimate a parameter $\lambda$ from $n$ samples $\lambda + \eta_i$, with each $\eta_i$ drawn i.i.d. from a known distribution $f$. For fixed $f$ the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) is well-known to be optimal in the limit as $n \to \infty$: it is asymptotically normal with variance matching the Cramer-Rao lower bound of $\frac{1}{n\mathcal{I}}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ is the Fisher information of $f$. However, this bound does not hold for finite $n$, or when $f$ varies with $n$. We show for arbitrary $f$ and $n$ that one can recover a similar theory based on the Fisher information of a smoothed version of $f$, where the smoothing radius decays with $n$.

paragraphs: The paper studies a basic estimation problem: each observation is an unknown numerical location plus random noise. The noise samples are independent, share the same distribution, and come from a known distribution. The goal is to estimate the common location from a finite collection of these noisy observations.

For a fixed noise distribution, classical maximum-likelihood theory describes what happens as the sample count becomes arbitrarily large. Its limiting variance matches a bound determined by Fisher information, a measure of how informative the distribution is about the location. That asymptotic benchmark does not directly hold for finite samples or when the noise distribution changes with the sample count.

The authors recover a similar theory for arbitrary noise distributions and sample counts by using the Fisher information of a smoothed distribution. The smoothing radius shrinks as more observations become available. This changes which version of the noise distribution supplies the information benchmark, providing a way to extend the classical perspective to settings where its limiting formulation does not apply.
summary.tldr: Using Fisher information from a smoothed noise distribution extends location-estimation theory beyond the classical infinite-sample setting.

title: Finite-Sample Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Location

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) enables generalizing a learning machine from multiple seen source domains to an unseen target one. The general objective of DG methods is to learn semantic representations that are independent of domain labels, which is theoretically sound but empirically challenged due to the complex mixture of common and domain-specific factors. Although disentangling the representations into two disjoint parts has been gaining momentum in DG, the strong presumption over the data limits its efficacy in many real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose Mix and Reason (MiRe), a new DG framework that learns semantic representations via enforcing the structural invariance of semantic topology. MiRe consists of two key components, namely, Category-aware Data Mixing (CDM) and Adaptive Semantic Topology Refinement (ASTR). CDM mixes two images from different domains in virtue of activation maps generated by two complementary classification losses, making the classifier focus on the representations of semantic objects. ASTR introduces relation graphs to represent semantic topology, which is progressively refined via the interactions between local feature aggregation and global cross-domain relational reasoning. Experiments on multiple DG benchmarks validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed MiRe.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to transfer learning from several observed domains to an unseen one. Separating shared meaning from domain-specific variation is difficult because these factors can be intertwined. Mix and Reason approaches the problem by encouraging stable relationships among semantic features, described as the structural invariance of semantic topology.

Its first component, Category-aware Data Mixing, combines images from different domains using activation maps generated by two complementary classification losses. This encourages attention to semantic objects. Its second component, Adaptive Semantic Topology Refinement, represents semantic relationships with graphs and progressively refines them through local feature aggregation and global reasoning across domains.

The two components address related aspects of generalization: the image mixing directs learning toward meaningful content, while graph-based reasoning refines how that content is related across domains. Experiments on multiple domain-generalization benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness and robustness. The approach offers a way to pursue shared semantic structure without relying on a clean division of representations into two disjoint parts, an assumption the authors identify as restrictive.
summary.tldr: Mix and Reason combines category-aware image mixing with graph-based semantic refinement to improve generalization to unseen domains.

title: Mix and Reason: Reasoning over Semantic Topology with Data Mixing for Domain Generalization

abstract: We study counterfactual classification as a new tool for decision-making under hypothetical (contrary to fact) scenarios. We propose a doubly-robust nonparametric estimator for a general counterfactual classifier, where we can incorporate flexible constraints by casting the classification problem as a nonlinear mathematical program involving counterfactuals. We go on to analyze the rates of convergence of the estimator and provide a closed-form expression for its asymptotic distribution. Our analysis shows that the proposed estimator is robust against nuisance model misspecification, and can attain fast $\sqrt{n}$ rates with tractable inference even when using nonparametric machine learning approaches. We study the empirical performance of our methods by simulation and apply them for recidivism risk prediction.

We propose a doubly-robust nonparametric estimator for a general counterfactual classifier, where we can incorporate flexible constraints by casting the classification problem as a nonlinear mathematical program involving counterfactuals. We go on to analyze the rates of convergence of the estimator and provide a closed-form expression for its asymptotic distribution. paragraphs: Counterfactual classification asks how to make predictions under a hypothetical scenario that differs from what actually occurred. This changes the prediction problem because the quantities used to guide a decision concern an alternative situation. The paper develops a general statistical approach to constructing classifiers for such scenarios while allowing flexible constraints on the resulting decision rule.

The authors express the classification task as a nonlinear optimization problem involving counterfactual quantities. They then propose a doubly robust, nonparametric estimator. Its robustness concerns misspecification in supporting statistical models used by the estimator, providing protection against certain modeling errors. The nonparametric formulation also allows flexible machine learning methods to participate in estimation.

The analysis establishes convergence rates and gives an explicit expression for the estimator's limiting distribution. The authors show that fast square-root-of-sample-size rates and tractable statistical inference can be attainable even with nonparametric learning. Simulations and an application to recidivism risk prediction examine empirical behavior. Together, these contributions connect constrained hypothetical decision-making with a framework for estimating classifiers and assessing their statistical uncertainty.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a doubly robust estimator for constrained classification under hypothetical scenarios, with convergence and inference guarantees.

title: Doubly Robust Counterfactual Classification

abstract: Correctly capturing intraoperative brain shift in image-guided neurosurgical procedures is a critical task for aligning preoperative data with intraoperative geometry for ensuring accurate surgical navigation. While the finite element method (FEM) is a proven technique to effectively approximate soft tissue deformation through biomechanical formulations, their degree of success boils down to a trade-off between accuracy and speed. To circumvent this problem, the most recent works in this domain have proposed leveraging data-driven models obtained by training various machine learning algorithms---e.g., random forests, artificial neural networks (ANNs)---with the results of finite element analysis (FEA) to speed up tissue deformation approximations by prediction. These methods, however, do not account for the structure of the finite element (FE) mesh during training that provides information on node connectivities as well as the distance between them, which can aid with approximating tissue deformation based on the proximity of force load points with the rest of the mesh nodes. Therefore, this work proposes a novel framework, PhysGNN, a data-driven model that approximates the solution of the FEM by leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs), which are capable of accounting for the mesh structural information and inductive learning over unstructured grids and complex topological structures. Empirically, we demonstrate that the proposed architecture, PhysGNN, promises accurate and fast soft tissue deformation approximations, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms while promising enhanced computational feasibility, therefore suitable for neurosurgical settings.

paragraphs: Brain tissue can shift during surgery, changing the geometry that surgical navigation must align with preoperative images. Finite element methods approximate this deformation through biomechanical models, but their use involves a trade-off between speed and accuracy. Learned predictors offer a way to approximate those calculations more quickly.

PhysGNN uses a graph neural network to approximate finite element solutions while accounting for the structure of the finite element mesh. That structure records which nodes connect and how far apart they are. These relationships can help represent how force applied at one part of the mesh relates to deformation elsewhere.

The approach addresses a weakness of earlier learned predictors that did not incorporate mesh structure during training. Graph neural networks also accommodate unstructured grids and complex connectivity, matching the form of the underlying representation. Empirical results indicate accurate, fast deformation approximations that are competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms and promise improved computational feasibility. The paper presents this as a promising approach for neurosurgical settings, with its evidence centered on the performance of the deformation approximation.
summary.tldr: PhysGNN incorporates finite element mesh structure into a graph neural network for fast, competitive soft-tissue deformation prediction.

title: PhysGNN: A Physics--Driven Graph Neural Network Based Model for Predicting Soft Tissue Deformation in Image--Guided Neurosurgery

abstract: Text-conditioned image generation models often generate incorrect associations between entities and their visual attributes. This reflects an impaired mapping between linguistic binding of entities and modifiers in the prompt and visual binding of the corresponding elements in the generated image. As one example, a query like ``a pink sunflower and a yellow flamingo'' may incorrectly produce an image of a yellow sunflower and a pink flamingo. To remedy this issue, we propose SynGen, an approach which first syntactically analyses the prompt to identify entities and their modifiers, and then uses a novel loss function that encourages the cross-attention maps to agree with the linguistic binding reflected by the syntax. Specifically, we encourage large overlap between attention maps of entities and their modifiers, and small overlap with other entities and modifier words. The loss is optimized during inference, without retraining or fine-tuning the model. Human evaluation on three datasets, including one new and challenging set, demonstrate significant improvements of SynGen compared with current state of the art methods. This work highlights how making use of sentence structure during inference can efficiently and substantially improve the faithfulness of text-to-image generation.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models may recognize all the objects and attributes in a prompt yet attach an attribute to the wrong object. This paper treats that error as a mismatch between grammatical relationships in language and visual relationships in the generated image. SynGen aims to preserve those relationships during image generation.

The approach first analyzes the prompt's syntax to identify entities and their modifiers. It then applies a loss to cross-attention maps, encouraging an entity and its modifiers to attend to overlapping image regions while discouraging overlap with unrelated entities and modifiers. This translates grammatical associations into a spatial alignment objective inside the generation process.

SynGen optimizes that objective during inference, without retraining or fine-tuning the underlying model. Human evaluations on three datasets, including a newly introduced challenging dataset, show significant improvements over leading methods. The findings indicate that sentence structure can provide useful generation-time guidance, improving how faithfully images preserve which visual properties belong to which objects in a prompt.
summary.tldr: SynGen aligns diffusion-model attention with prompt syntax to improve object–attribute correspondence without retraining.

title: Linguistic Binding in Diffusion Models: Enhancing Attribute Correspondence through Attention Map Alignment

abstract: With rapid development and deployment of generative language models in global settings, there is an urgent need to also scale our measurements of harm, not just in the number and types of harms covered, but also how well they account for local cultural contexts, including marginalized identities and the social biases experienced by them.Current evaluation paradigms are limited in their abilities to address this, as they are not representative of diverse, locally situated but global, socio-cultural perspectives. It is imperative that our evaluation resources are enhanced and calibrated by including people and experiences from different cultures and societies worldwide, in order to prevent gross underestimations or skews in measurements of harm. In this work, we demonstrate a socio-culturally aware expansion of evaluation resources in the Indian societal context, specifically for the harm of stereotyping. We devise a community engaged effort to build a resource which contains stereotypes for axes of disparity that are uniquely present in India. The resultant resource increases the number of stereotypes known for and in the Indian context by over 1000 stereotypes across many unique identities. We also demonstrate the utility and effectiveness of such expanded resources for evaluations of language models.CONTENT WARNING: This paper contains examples of stereotypes that may be offensive.

paragraphs: Evaluating stereotyping in language models requires knowing which stereotypes matter in the societies where those models are used. The paper argues that existing evaluation resources do not adequately represent diverse local perspectives, particularly the experiences of marginalized identities. As a result, assessments can underestimate harm or give a distorted picture of its distribution.

The authors develop a community-engaged approach to expanding stereotype evaluation resources in the Indian social context. Their work includes axes of disparity specific to India and adds more than 1,000 stereotypes across numerous identities. Community participation connects the resource-building process to locally situated experiences rather than relying solely on the coverage of existing evaluations.

The paper also demonstrates that the expanded resource is useful for evaluating language models. Its contribution is both a concrete collection and an example of how evaluation coverage can become more culturally informed. The stated result concerns improved resources for measuring stereotyping; it does not establish that the evaluated models themselves become less harmful.
summary.tldr: Community engagement adds over 1,000 India-context stereotypes to resources for more culturally informed language-model evaluation.

title: Building Socio-culturally Inclusive Stereotype Resources with Community Engagement

abstract: This paper investigates new families of compositional optimization problems, called non-smooth weakly-convex finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (NSWC FCCO). There has been a growing interest in FCCO due to its wide-ranging applications in machine learning and AI, as well as its ability to address the shortcomings of stochastic algorithms based on empirical risk minimization. However, current research on FCCO presumes that both the inner and outer functions are smooth, limiting their potential to tackle a more diverse set of problems. Our research expands on this area by examining non-smooth weakly-convex FCCO, where the outer function is weakly convex and non-decreasing, and the inner function is weakly-convex. We analyze a single-loop algorithm and establish its complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the Moreau envelop of the objective function. Additionally, we also extend the algorithm for solving novel non-smooth weakly-convex tri-level finite-sum coupled compositional optimization problems, which feature a nested arrangement of three functions. Lastly, we explore the applications of our algorithms in deep learning for two-way partial AUC maximization and multi-instance two-way partial AUC maximization, using empirical studies to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine functions inside other functions and sum many such coupled terms. Existing work on finite-sum coupled compositional optimization assumes smooth inner and outer functions. This paper broadens the setting to nonsmooth, weakly convex functions, allowing a class of objectives excluded by those smoothness requirements.

The analyzed setting requires a weakly convex, non-decreasing outer function and a weakly convex inner function. The authors study a single-loop algorithm and bound the work needed to find an approximately stationary point of the objective's Moreau envelope, a smoothed representation used in the analysis. This is a stationarity guarantee, rather than a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The algorithm is also extended to a three-level composition, where three functions are nested. Applications include deep-learning objectives for two-way partial AUC maximization and its multi-instance version. Empirical studies demonstrate effectiveness on these applications, linking the broader optimization theory to concrete learning objectives while retaining explicit structural assumptions on the functions.
summary.tldr: The paper extends coupled compositional optimization to nonsmooth weakly convex objectives and analyzes algorithms for two-level and three-level compositions.

title: Non-Smooth Weakly-Convex Finite-sum Coupled Compositional Optimization

abstract: The well-established practice of time series analysis involves estimating deterministic, non-stationary trend and seasonality components followed by learning the residual stochastic, stationary components. Recently, it has been shown that one can learn the deterministic non-stationary components accurately using multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (mSSA) in the absence of a correlated stationary component; meanwhile, in the absence of deterministic non-stationary components, the Autoregressive (AR) stationary component can also be learnt readily, e.g. via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). However, a theoretical underpinning of multi-stage learning algorithms involving both deterministic and stationary components has been absent in the literature despite its pervasiveness. We resolve this open question by establishing desirable theoretical guarantees for a natural two-stage algorithm, where mSSA is first applied to estimate the non-stationary components despite the presence of a correlated stationary AR component, which is subsequently learned from the residual time series. We provide a finite-sample forecasting consistency bound for the proposed algorithm, SAMoSSA, which is data-driven and thus requires minimal parameter tuning. To establish theoretical guarantees, we overcome three hurdles: (i) we characterize the spectra of Page matrices of stable AR processes, thus extending the analysis of mSSA; (ii) we extend the analysis of AR process identification in the presence of arbitrary bounded perturbations; (iii) we characterize the out-of-sample or forecasting error, as opposed to solely considering model identification. Through representative empirical studies, we validate the superior performance of SAMoSSA compared to existing baselines. Notably, SAMoSSA's ability to account for AR noise structure yields improvements ranging from 5% to 37% across various benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting often separates changing trends and seasonality from a remaining stationary random component. Each stage has established methods, but analyzing them together is harder because estimation errors and correlated noise interact. SAMoSSA provides theoretical support for a two-stage procedure that combines multivariate singular spectrum analysis with autoregressive modeling.

The first stage estimates deterministic, nonstationary components using multivariate singular spectrum analysis, even when correlated autoregressive noise is present. The second stage learns that noise structure from the residual series. The authors establish a finite-sample forecasting consistency bound, addressing predictions beyond the observed data rather than only whether fitted parameters resemble the underlying model.

The analysis handles the matrix spectra of stable autoregressive processes and autoregressive identification under bounded perturbations. These results connect the two learning stages despite imperfect separation. The resulting procedure is data-driven and requires little parameter tuning. summary.tldr: SAMoSSA gives forecasting guarantees for jointly handling nonstationary trends and correlated autoregressive residuals through a two-stage procedure.

title: SAMoSSA: Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis with Stochastic Autoregressive Noise

abstract: The human brain rewires itself for neuroplasticity in the presence of new tasks. We are inspired to harness this key process in continual reinforcement learning, prioritizing adaptation to non-stationary environments. In distinction to existing rewiring approaches that rely on pruning or dynamic routing, which may limit network capacity and plasticity, this work presents a novel rewiring scheme by permuting hidden neurons. Specifically, the neuron permutation is parameterized to be end-to-end learnable and can rearrange all available synapses to explore a large span of weight space, thereby promoting adaptivity. In addition, we introduce two main designs to steer the rewiring process in continual reinforcement learning: first, a multi-mode rewiring strategy is proposed which diversifies the policy and encourages exploration when encountering new environments. Secondly, to ensure stability on history tasks, the network is devised to cache each learned wiring while subtly updating its weights, allowing for retrospective recovery of any previous state appropriate for the task. Meanwhile, an alignment mechanism is curated to achieve better plasticity-stability tradeoff by jointly optimizing cached wirings and weights. Our proposed method is comprehensively evaluated on 18 continual reinforcement learning scenarios ranging from locomotion to manipulation, demonstrating its advantages over state-of-the-art competitors in performance-efficiency tradeoffs. Code is available at https://github.com/feifeiobama/RewireNeuron.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning requires adapting to changing environments while retaining useful behavior from earlier tasks. The permutation mechanism is trained end to end and can rearrange available synapses, opening up a broad range of weight configurations for adaptation.

An alignment mechanism jointly optimizes the cached wirings and weights to balance adaptation with stability.

The method is evaluated in eighteen continual reinforcement-learning scenarios covering locomotion and manipulation. The authors report advantages over leading competitors in the tradeoff between performance and efficiency. The contribution connects exploration and retention through learnable connectivity: new wirings support adaptation, while cached wirings and alignment provide a way to maintain access to earlier task behavior.
summary.tldr: Learnable neuron permutations and cached wirings help reinforcement-learning networks adapt to new environments while retaining earlier task behavior.

title: Rewiring Neurons in Non-Stationary Environments

abstract: With the widespread digitization of finance and the increasing popularity of cryptocurrencies, the sophistication of fraud schemes devised by cybercriminals is growing. Money laundering -- the movement of illicit funds to conceal their origins -- can cross bank and national boundaries, producing complex transaction patterns. The UN estimates 2-5\% of global GDP or \$0.8 - \$2.0 trillion dollars are laundered globally each year. Unfortunately, real data to train machine learning models to detect laundering is generally not available, and previous synthetic data generators have had significant shortcomings. A realistic, standardized, publicly-available benchmark is needed for comparing models and for the advancement of the area.To this end, this paper contributes a synthetic financial transaction dataset generator and a set of synthetically generated AML (Anti-Money Laundering) datasets. We have calibrated this agent-based generator to match real transactions as closely as possible and made the datasets public. We describe the generator in detail and demonstrate how the datasets generated can help compare different machine learning models in terms of their AML abilities. In a key way, using synthetic data in these comparisons can be even better than using real data: the ground truth labels are complete, whilst many laundering transactions in real data are never detected.
