paragraphs: Money laundering can involve complex transaction patterns across banks and countries, yet real transaction data for training detection models are generally unavailable. This paper addresses the need for a public, standardized way to compare anti-money-laundering models. It contributes both a synthetic transaction generator and datasets produced by that generator.

The generator is agent-based and calibrated to resemble real financial transactions as closely as possible. The authors describe how it works and demonstrate how the generated datasets can support comparisons of machine-learning models’ laundering-detection abilities. Public datasets give those comparisons a shared foundation instead of requiring access to private financial records.

A particular advantage is the completeness of the synthetic ground-truth labels. In real records, laundering that has never been detected can remain unlabeled, complicating evaluation. In generated data, the laundering labels are complete by construction. The paper argues that this can make synthetic data better for this aspect of model comparison, while the realism of the simulated transactions remains part of the generator’s design objective.
summary.tldr: An agent-based transaction generator supplies public anti-money-laundering benchmarks with complete labels and calibration toward realistic financial activity.

title: Realistic Synthetic Financial Transactions for Anti-Money Laundering Models

abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) is a recently proposed method that minimizes the sharpness of the training loss of a neural network. While its generalization improvement is well-known and is the primary motivation, we uncover an additional intriguing effect of SAM: reduction of the feature rank which happens at different layers of a neural network. We show that this low-rank effect occurs very broadly: for different architectures such as fully-connected networks, convolutional networks, vision transformers and for different objectives such as regression, classification, language-image contrastive training. To better understand this phenomenon, we provide a mechanistic understanding of how low-rank features arise in a simple two-layer network. We observe that a significant number of activations gets entirely pruned by SAM which directly contributes to the rank reduction. We confirm this effect theoretically and check that it can also occur in deep networks, although the overall rank reduction mechanism can be more complex, especially for deep networks with pre-activation skip connections and self-attention layers.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, trains a neural network by minimizing the sharpness of its training loss. Its established motivation is improved generalization. This paper investigates an additional effect: features at different network layers become lower rank, meaning their representations span fewer independent directions.

The authors observe this effect across fully connected networks, convolutional networks, and vision Transformers. It also appears across regression, classification, and language–image contrastive objectives. To explain the phenomenon, they examine a simple two-layer network and find that SAM entirely prunes a substantial number of activations, directly contributing to the reduced feature rank.

They support this mechanism theoretically and check that activation pruning can also occur in deeper networks. The paper explicitly notes that the full explanation can be more complex in architectures with pre-activation skip connections and self-attention. Its contribution is therefore both a broad observation about learned representations and a concrete mechanism explaining part of it, with the simpler analysis providing a starting point for understanding more elaborate networks.
summary.tldr: SAM reduces feature rank across diverse networks and objectives, with activation pruning explaining part of the effect.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization Leads to Low-Rank Features

abstract: In this research, we investigate the high-dimensional linear contextual bandit problem where the number of features $p$ is greater than the budget $T$, or it may even be infinite. Differing from the majority of previous works in this field, we do not impose sparsity on the regression coefficients. Instead, we rely on recent findings on overparameterized models, which enables us to analyze the performance of the minimum-norm interpolating estimator when data distributions have small effective ranks. We propose an explore-then-commit (EtC) algorithm to address this problem and examine its performance. Through our analysis, we derive the optimal rate of the ETC algorithm in terms of $T$ and show that this rate can be achieved by balancing exploration and exploitation. Moreover, we introduce an adaptive explore-then-commit (AEtC) algorithm that adaptively finds the optimal balance. We assess the performance of the proposed algorithms through a series of simulations.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit must choose actions while learning from their rewards, balancing information gathering with using what it already knows. This paper studies a linear version in which the number of features exceeds the interaction budget and may even be infinite. It does not assume that only a few regression coefficients are nonzero.

Instead, the analysis uses a small-effective-rank condition on the data distribution. This provides structure for studying a minimum-norm interpolating estimator in the overparameterized setting. The proposed explore-then-commit algorithm first gathers information and then commits to decisions based on what it has learned.

The authors derive an optimal rate for this explore-then-commit algorithm as a function of the budget and show how balancing exploration and exploitation achieves it. They also introduce an adaptive version that finds the balance automatically and assess both algorithms through simulations. The work shows how distributional structure can support analysis without coefficient sparsity in this high-dimensional bandit setting.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes high-dimensional contextual bandits without coefficient sparsity by using small effective rank and adaptively balancing exploration with commitment.

title: High-dimensional Contextual Bandit Problem without Sparsity

abstract: Algorithms for the minimum-cost bipartite matching can be used to estimate Wasserstein distance between two distributions.Given two sets $A$ and $B$ of $n$ points in a $2$-dimensional Euclidean space, one can use a fast implementation of the Hungarian method to compute a minimum-cost bipartite matching of $A$ and $B$ in $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ time. Let $\Delta$ be the spread, i.e., the ratio of the distance of the farthest to the closest pair of points in $A\cup B$. In this paper, we present a new algorithm to compute a minimum-cost bipartite matching of $A$ and $B$ with a similar worst-case execution time of $\tilde{O}(n^2 \log \Delta)$. However, when $A$ and $B$ are drawn independently and identically from a fixed distribution that is not known to the algorithm, the execution time of our algorithm is, in expectation, $\tilde{O}(n^{7/4}\log \Delta)$.To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm is the first one to achieve a sub-quadratic execution time even for stochastic point sets with real-valued coordinates.Our algorithm extends to any dimension $d$, where it runs in $\tilde{O}(n^{2-\frac{1}{2d}}\Phi(n))$ time for stochastic point sets $A$ and $B$; here $\Phi(n)$ is the query/update time of a dynamic weighted nearest neighbor data structure. Our algorithm can be seen as a careful adaptation of the Hungarian method in the geometric divide-and-conquer framework.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to pair two equally sized sets of points while minimizing the total distance between matched points. This minimum-cost matching problem also supports estimation of Wasserstein distance between distributions. The goal is an exact answer, with faster computation when the point sets have a particular statistical structure.

The algorithm adapts the Hungarian method within a geometric divide-and-conquer framework. In two dimensions, its worst-case running time is roughly quadratic in the number of points, with an additional dependence on the logarithm of the spread: the ratio between the largest and smallest pairwise distances. When both sets are sampled independently from the same fixed distribution, its expected running time improves to a power of 7/4, again with logarithmic factors.

That improvement depends on the sampling setting, but the algorithm does not need to know the distribution. The method also extends to higher dimensions, where its running time depends on dimension and the efficiency of a dynamic weighted nearest-neighbor data structure.
summary.tldr: An exact geometric matching algorithm achieves subquadratic expected running time for independently sampled point sets without knowing their distribution.

title: A Robust Exact Algorithm for the Euclidean Bipartite Matching Problem

abstract: Video self-supervised learning (VSSL) has made significant progress in recent years. However, the exact behavior and dynamics of these models under different forms of distribution shift are not yet known. In this paper, we comprehensively study the behavior of six popular self-supervised methods (v-SimCLR, v-MoCo, v-BYOL, v-SimSiam, v-DINO, v-MAE) in response to various forms of natural distribution shift, i.e., (i) context shift, (ii) viewpoint shift, (iii) actor shift, (iv) source shift, (v) generalizability to unknown classes (zero-shot), and (vi) open-set recognition. To perform this extensive study, we carefully craft a test bed consisting of 17 in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmark pairs using available public datasets and a series of evaluation protocols to stress-test the different methods under the intended shifts. Our study uncovers a series of intriguing findings and interesting behaviors of VSSL methods. For instance, we observe that while video models generally struggle with context shifts, v-MAE and supervised learning exhibit more robustness. Moreover, our study shows that v-MAE is a strong temporal learner, whereas contrastive methods, v-SimCLR and v-MoCo, exhibit strong performances against viewpoint shifts. When studying the notion of open-set recognition, we notice a trade-off between closed-set and open-set recognition performance if the pretrained VSSL encoders are used without finetuning. We hope that our work will contribute to the development of robust video representation learning frameworks for various real-world scenarios. The project page and code are available at: https://pritamqu.github.io/OOD-VSSL.

paragraphs: Strong video representations on familiar data may behave differently when the context, viewpoint, actor, or data source changes. This paper systematically studies six self-supervised video methods under these shifts, as well as zero-shot generalization and open-set recognition. It constructs 17 pairs of in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks from public datasets.

The results show that robustness depends on the kind of shift. Video models generally struggle with changes in context, although v-MAE and supervised learning are more robust in that comparison. The study identifies v-MAE as a strong temporal learner, while the contrastive methods v-SimCLR and v-MoCo perform strongly under viewpoint changes.

Another finding concerns recognizing unfamiliar classes: when pretrained encoders are used without fine-tuning, closed-set and open-set recognition performance exhibit a tradeoff. This qualification matters because the observation applies to that encoder-use setting. Overall, the benchmark reveals distinct strengths across learning methods and evaluation conditions, helping characterize what standard video representation performance can leave unresolved about distribution shift.
summary.tldr: A study of six video self-supervised methods finds shift-specific strengths and a closed-set versus open-set tradeoff without fine-tuning.

title: Uncovering the Hidden Dynamics of Video Self-supervised Learning under Distribution Shifts

abstract: Flexibly quantifying both irreducible aleatoric and model-dependent epistemic uncertainties plays an important role for complex regression problems. While deep neural networks in principle can provide this flexibility and learn heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainties through non-linear functions, recent works highlight that maximizing the log likelihood objective parameterized by mean and variance can lead to compromised mean fits since the gradient are scaled by the predictive variance, and propose adjustments in line with this premise. We instead propose to use the natural parametrization of the Gaussian, which has been shown to be more stable for heteroscedastic regression based on non-linear feature maps and Gaussian processes. Further, we emphasize the significance of principled regularization of the network parameters and prediction. We therefore propose an efficient Laplace approximation for heteroscedastic neural networks that allows automatic regularization through empirical Bayes and provides epistemic uncertainties, both of which improve generalization.We showcase on a range of regression problems—including a new heteroscedastic image regression benchmark—that our methods are scalable, improve over previous approaches for heteroscedastic regression, and provide epistemic uncertainty without requiring hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Regression models often need to predict both an outcome and how uncertain that prediction is. This paper distinguishes uncertainty inherent in observations from uncertainty about the model itself. It focuses on heteroscedastic regression, where the amount of observation noise changes with the input rather than remaining constant across all examples.

Training a Gaussian predictor directly through its mean and variance can compromise the mean prediction because predictive variance scales the training gradients. The authors instead use the Gaussian’s natural parameterization, drawing on its established stability in related settings. They also emphasize regularization of both network parameters and predictions, rather than treating the parameterization change as the entire solution.

An efficient Laplace approximation supplies model uncertainty and enables automatic regularization through empirical Bayes. Across regression problems, including a new image regression benchmark with varying noise, the authors report scalability and improvements over previous approaches. Their method provides epistemic uncertainty without requiring hyperparameter tuning, connecting uncertainty estimation with a practical mechanism for improving generalization.
summary.tldr: A different Gaussian parameterization and efficient Bayesian approximation improve regression with input-dependent noise and model uncertainty.

title: Effective Bayesian Heteroscedastic Regression with Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Human perception of the empirical world involves recognizing the diverse appearances, or 'modalities', of underlying objects. Despite the longstanding consideration of this perspective in philosophy and cognitive science, the study of multimodality remains relatively under-explored within the field of machine learning. Nevertheless, current studies of multimodal machine learning are limited to empirical practices, lacking theoretical foundations beyond heuristic arguments. An intriguing finding from the practice of multimodal learning is that a model trained on multiple modalities can outperform a finely-tuned unimodal model, even on unimodal tasks. This paper provides a theoretical framework that explains this phenomenon, by studying generalization properties of multimodal learning algorithms. We demonstrate that multimodal learning allows for a superior generalization bound compared to unimodal learning, up to a factor of $O(\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ represents the sample size. Such advantage occurs when both connection and heterogeneity exist between the modalities.
originalAbstract: Human perception of the empirical world involves recognizing the diverse appearances, or 'modalities', of underlying objects. Despite the longstanding consideration of this perspective in philosophy and cognitive science, the study of multimodality remains relatively under-explored within the field of machine learning. Nevertheless, current studies of multimodal machine learning are limited to empirical practices, lacking theoretical foundations beyond heuristic arguments. An intriguing finding from the practice of multimodal learning is that a model trained on multiple modalities can outperform a finely-tuned unimodal model, even on unimodal tasks. This paper provides a theoretical framework that explains this phenomenon, by studying generalization properties of multimodal learning algorithms. We demonstrate that multimodal learning allows for a superior generalization bound compared to unimodal learning, up to a factor of $O(\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ represents the sample size. Such advantage occurs when both connection and heterogeneity exist between the modalities.

paragraphs: A model trained with several kinds of information can sometimes outperform a carefully tuned model trained with just one kind, even when the final task uses only one modality. This paper develops a theoretical explanation for that observation by studying generalization: how learning from available examples supports performance on unseen examples.

The analysis compares generalization bounds for multimodal and unimodal learning. It shows that the multimodal bound can be better by a factor of up to O(√n), where n is the number of training samples. This is a statement about theoretical bounds, rather than a guarantee that every multimodal model will achieve that improvement in measured accuracy.

The advantage depends on modalities having both connections and differences. Their relationship makes information transferable, while their heterogeneity supplies something beyond repeated versions of the same signal. The contribution is therefore a conditional account of why multiple modalities can help: their combination can support stronger generalization when they offer related but distinct information.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework shows how connected but heterogeneous modalities can improve generalization bounds over unimodal learning.

title: A Theory of Multimodal Learning

abstract: Millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar has emerged as an attractive and cost-effective alternative for human activity sensing compared to traditional camera-based systems. mmWave radars are also non-intrusive, providing better protection for user privacy. However, as a Radio Frequency based technology, mmWave radars rely on capturing reflected signals from objects, making them more prone to noise compared to cameras. This raises an intriguing question for the deep learning community: Can we develop more effective point set-based deep learning methods for such attractive sensors? To answer this question, our work, termed MiliPoint, delves into this idea by providing a large-scale, open dataset for the community to explore how mmWave radars can be utilised for human activity recognition. Moreover, MiliPoint stands out as it is larger in size than existing datasets, has more diverse human actions represented, and encompasses all three key tasks in human activity recognition. We have also established a range of point-based deep neural networks such as DGCNN, PointNet++ and PointTransformer, on MiliPoint, which can serve to set the ground baseline for further development.

The authors report that it is larger than existing datasets, represents a wider variety of human actions, and covers all three key tasks in human activity recognition. summary.tldr: MiliPoint provides an open mmWave radar point-cloud dataset and neural-network baselines for studying human activity recognition.

title: MiliPoint: A Point Cloud Dataset for mmWave Radar

abstract: Modern Deep Neural Network (DNN) frameworks use tensor operators as the main building blocks of DNNs. However, we observe that operator-based construction of DNNs incurs significant drawbacks in parallelism in the form of synchronization barriers. Synchronization barriers of operators confine the scope of parallel computation to each operator and obscure the rich parallel computation opportunities that exist across operators. To this end, we present ASPEN, a novel parallel computation solution for DNNs that achieves fine-grained dynamic execution of DNNs, which (1) removes the operator barriers and expresses DNNs in dataflow graphs of fine-grained tiles to expose the parallel computation opportunities across operators, and (2) exploits these opportunities by dynamically locating and scheduling them in runtime. This novel approach of ASPEN enables opportunistic parallelism, a new class of parallelism for DNNs that is unavailable in the existing operator-based approaches. ASPEN also achieves high resource utilization and memory reuse by letting each resource asynchronously traverse depthwise in the DNN graph to its full computing potential. We provide challenges and solutions to our approach and show that our proof-of-concept implementation of ASPEN on CPU shows exceptional performance, outperforming state-of-the-art inference systems of TorchScript and TVM by up to 3.2$\times$ and 4.3$\times$, respectively.

paragraphs: Deep learning frameworks commonly organize computation around tensor operators. The paper identifies a parallelism problem with this organization: synchronization barriers restrict concurrent work to the boundaries of individual operators. Useful work across different operators can consequently remain hidden, even when the underlying data dependencies would permit it to proceed.

ASPEN replaces those coarse boundaries with a dataflow graph of small computational tiles. During execution, it dynamically finds and schedules available work across operators. The authors call this opportunistic parallelism because the runtime can exploit opportunities that operator-based execution does not expose. Computing resources can also progress asynchronously through the depth of the network, supporting resource utilization and memory reuse.

The paper develops solutions to the challenges of this execution model and evaluates a proof-of-concept CPU implementation. It reports speedups of up to 3.2 times over TorchScript and 4.3 times over TVM for inference. These maximum reported gains show the potential value of changing execution granularity and scheduling, rather than treating each operator as the fixed unit of parallel work.
summary.tldr: ASPEN exposes and dynamically schedules parallel work across neural-network operators, achieving substantial reported CPU inference speedups.

title: ASPEN: Breaking Operator Barriers for Efficient Parallelization of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Optimizing proper loss functions is popularly believed to yield predictors with good calibration properties; the intuition being that for such losses, the global optimum is to predict the ground-truth probabilities, which is indeed calibrated. However, typical machine learning models are trained to approximately minimize loss over restricted families of predictors, that are unlikely to contain the ground truth. Under what circumstances does optimizing proper loss over a restricted family yield calibrated models? What precise calibration guarantees does it give? In this work, we provide a rigorous answer to these questions. We replace the global optimality with a local optimality condition stipulating that the (proper) loss of the predictor cannot be reduced much by post-processing its predictions with a certain family of Lipschitz functions. We show that any predictor with this local optimality satisfies smooth calibration as defined in [Kakade and Foster, 2008, Błasiok et al., 2023]. Local optimality is plausibly satisfied by well-trained DNNs, which suggests an explanation for why they are calibrated from proper loss minimization alone. Finally, we show that the connection between local optimality and calibration error goes both ways: nearly calibrated predictors are also nearly locally optimal.

paragraphs: Proper losses favor predicting the true outcome probabilities at their global optimum. That motivates the belief that minimizing such a loss produces calibrated predictions. Real models, however, optimize approximately within restricted predictor families that may not contain the true probabilities. This paper asks what calibration guarantee can survive that practical gap.

The authors replace global optimality with a local condition: applying functions from a specified Lipschitz post-processing family cannot substantially reduce the predictor's proper loss. They prove that a predictor satisfying this condition has smooth calibration. The guarantee therefore follows from resistance to a particular class of prediction adjustments, rather than requiring recovery of the globally optimal predictor.

The connection also runs in the reverse direction: nearly calibrated predictors are nearly locally optimal. This makes calibration error and improvement through post-processing closely related quantities. The authors suggest that well-trained deep networks plausibly satisfy the local condition, offering a possible explanation for calibration from proper-loss training alone. That explanation is explicitly plausible; the theorem does not establish that every trained neural network satisfies its premise.
summary.tldr: Limited improvement under Lipschitz post-processing implies smooth calibration for proper losses, with a corresponding guarantee in the reverse direction.

title: When Does Optimizing a Proper Loss Yield Calibration?

abstract: We initiate the study of smoothed analysis for the sequential probability assignment problem with contexts. We study information-theoretically optimal minmax rates as well as a framework for algorithmic reduction involving the maximum likelihood estimator oracle. Our approach establishes a general-purpose reduction from minimax rates for sequential probability assignment for smoothed adversaries to minimax rates for transductive learning. This leads to optimal (logarithmic) fast rates for parametric classes and classes with finite VC dimension. On the algorithmic front, we develop an algorithm that efficiently taps into the MLE oracle, for general classes of functions. We show that under general conditions this algorithmic approach yields sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Sequential probability assignment involves making probabilistic predictions as observations arrive, using available contextual information. This paper studies the problem through smoothed analysis, focusing on the performance possible against smoothed adversaries. It addresses both information-theoretic limits and the algorithmic question of how to obtain useful performance through access to a maximum likelihood estimation oracle.

The theoretical contribution is a general reduction connecting minimax rates in this sequential setting to rates for transductive learning. That connection yields optimal logarithmic fast rates for parametric function classes and classes with finite VC dimension. In effect, the reduction makes results from another learning setting available for analyzing sequential probability assignment.

The authors also develop an algorithm that efficiently uses the maximum likelihood oracle for general function classes. Under general conditions, they prove that this approach achieves sublinear regret. The distinction matters: the optimal rate results describe what is statistically achievable for specified classes, while the oracle-based algorithm provides a computational framework with its own conditional regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper connects smoothed sequential probability prediction to transductive learning and develops an MLE-oracle algorithm with conditional sublinear regret guarantees.

title: Smoothed Analysis of Sequential Probability Assignment

abstract: Large language models can solve tasks that were not present in the training set. This capability is believed to be due to in-context learning and skill composition. In this work, we study the emergence of in-context learning and skill composition in a collection of modular arithmetic tasks. Specifically, we consider a finite collection of linear modular functions $z = a x + b y \text{ mod } p$ labeled by the vector $(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}_p^2$. We use some of these tasks for pre-training and the rest for out-of-distribution testing. We empirically show that a GPT-style transformer exhibits a transition from in-distribution to out-of-distribution generalization as the number of pre-training tasks increases. We find that the smallest model capable of out-of-distribution generalization requires two transformer blocks, while for deeper models, the out-of-distribution generalization phase is *transient*, necessitating early stopping. Finally, we perform an interpretability study of the pre-trained models, revealing highly structured representations in both attention heads and MLPs; and discuss the learned algorithms. Notably, we find an algorithmic shift in deeper models, as we go from few to many in-context examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a transformer begins solving tasks outside its pre-training collection using a controlled family of modular arithmetic problems. Each task computes ax + by modulo p, with the coefficient pair defining the task. Some coefficient pairs are used during pre-training, while the remaining tasks test out-of-distribution generalization.

The experiments show a transition as the number of pre-training tasks increases: the model moves from generalizing within its training distribution to succeeding on held-out tasks. In the studied setting, the smallest model capable of this broader generalization has two transformer blocks. For deeper models, the successful out-of-distribution phase is temporary, making early stopping necessary to retain it.

An interpretability analysis finds highly structured representations in both attention heads and multilayer perceptrons. The authors examine the algorithms those representations support and find that deeper models change algorithms as the number of in-context examples increases. The study links task diversity, model depth, and example availability to distinct learned behaviors within this arithmetic setting.
summary.tldr: Controlled modular-arithmetic experiments reveal transitions in transformer generalization and algorithm choice as training-task diversity and in-context examples increase.

title: Learning to grok: Emergence of in-context learning and skill composition in modular arithmetic tasks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance on downstream tasks by in-context learning (ICL), which heavily relies on the quality of demonstrations selected from a large set of annotated examples. Recent works claim that in-context learning is robust to noisy demonstrations in text classification. In this work, we show that, on text generation tasks, noisy annotations significantly hurt the performance of in-context learning. To circumvent the issue, we propose a simple and effective approach called Local Perplexity Ranking (LPR), which replaces the "noisy" candidates with their nearest neighbors that are more likely to be clean. Our method is motivated by analyzing the perplexity deviation caused by noisy labels and decomposing perplexity into inherent perplexity and matching perplexity. Our key idea behind LPR is thus to decouple the matching perplexity by performing the ranking among the neighbors in semantic space. Our approach can prevent the selected demonstrations from including mismatched input-label pairs while preserving the effectiveness of the original selection methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LPR, improving the EM score by up to 18.75 on common benchmarks with noisy annotations.

paragraphs: In-context learning depends on examples placed in a model's prompt. Although earlier work reported robustness to noisy demonstrations in classification, this paper finds that noisy annotations substantially harm text-generation tasks. The distinction matters because selecting relevant examples does not ensure that their inputs and labels actually match.

The authors introduce Local Perplexity Ranking, or LPR, to replace suspect candidate demonstrations with nearby examples that are more likely to be clean. Their motivation comes from separating perplexity into an inherent component and a matching component. Ranking within semantic neighborhoods helps isolate the signal associated with input-label compatibility rather than relying on an undifferentiated perplexity score.

The approach aims to prevent mismatched pairs from entering the prompt while preserving the usefulness of the original demonstration-selection method. Experiments on common benchmarks with noisy annotations show exact-match score improvements of up to 18.75. That figure is the largest reported improvement, not a uniform gain across tasks. The findings show that local checking of candidate demonstrations can improve generation when the example pool contains annotation noise.
summary.tldr: Local Perplexity Ranking replaces suspect demonstrations with cleaner semantic neighbors, improving text-generation performance under annotation noise.

title: On the Noise Robustness of In-Context Learning for Text Generation

abstract: Scaling deep learning models has been at the heart of recent revolutions in language modelling and image generation. Practitioners have observed a strong relationship between model size, dataset size, and performance. However, structure-based architectures such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are yet to show the benefits of scale mainly due to lower efficiency of sparse operations, large data requirements, and lack of clarity about the effectiveness of various architectures. We address this drawback of GNNs by studying their scaling behavior. Specifically, we analyze message-passing networks, graph Transformers, and hybrid architectures on the largest public collection of 2D molecular graphs for supervised pretraining. For the first time, we observe that GNNs benefit tremendously from the increasing scale of depth, width, number of molecules and associated labels. A major factor is the diversity of the pretraining data that comprises thousands of labels per molecule derived from bio-assays, quantum simulations, transcriptomics and phenomic imaging. We further demonstrate strong finetuning scaling behavior on 38 highly competitive downstream tasks, outclassing previous large models. This gives rise to MolGPS, a new graph foundation model that allows to navigate the chemical space, outperforming the previous state-of-the-arts on 26 out the 38 downstream tasks. We hope that our work paves the way for an era where foundational GNNs drive pharmaceutical drug discovery.

Sparse computation is relatively inefficient, large datasets are needed, and architectural choices remain uncertain. This paper studies whether molecular graph models improve as their depth, width, training molecules, and available labels increase.

The authors compare message-passing networks, graph transformers, and hybrid architectures using the largest public collection of two-dimensional molecular graphs for supervised pretraining. summary.tldr: Large-scale molecular graph pretraining with diverse supervision yields strong scaling gains and a model that leads on 26 of 38 downstream tasks.

title: On the Scalability of GNNs for Molecular Graphs

abstract: With the rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), their evaluation has become increasingly comprehensive. However, understanding long multimodal content, as a foundational ability for real-world applications, remains underexplored. In this work, we present Needle In A Multimodal Haystack (MM-NIAH), the first benchmark specifically designed to systematically evaluate the capability of existing MLLMs to comprehend long multimodal documents. Our benchmark includes three types of evaluation tasks: multimodal retrieval, counting, and reasoning. In each task, the model is required to answer the questions according to different key information scattered throughout the given multimodal document. Evaluating the leading MLLMs on MM-NIAH, we observe that existing models still have significant room for improvement on these tasks, especially on vision-centric evaluation. We hope this work can provide a platform for further research on long multimodal document comprehension and contribute to the advancement of MLLMs. Code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/MM-NIAH.

paragraphs: Understanding a long document containing both text and images requires locating and using relevant information across the document. The paper argues that this ability remains underexplored despite increasingly comprehensive evaluations of multimodal language models. It introduces Needle In A Multimodal Haystack, or MM-NIAH, as a benchmark specifically designed to examine long multimodal document comprehension.

The benchmark contains three kinds of tasks: retrieval, counting, and reasoning. In each, questions depend on key information scattered throughout a multimodal document. These tasks examine different demands on comprehension, from finding relevant content to keeping track of it and using it to answer questions. The shared challenge is that useful information is distributed across a long input.

Evaluations of leading multimodal models reveal substantial room for improvement, especially when the tasks center on visual information. This finding identifies long-document visual comprehension as a particular weakness in the evaluated systems. By releasing the code and benchmark, the authors provide a common platform for investigating that weakness and assessing future progress on the broader capability.
summary.tldr: MM-NIAH tests retrieval, counting, and reasoning across long multimodal documents and reveals particular weaknesses on visual tasks.

title: Needle In A Multimodal Haystack

abstract: We propose a video editing framework, NaRCan, which integrates a hybrid deformation field and diffusion prior to generate high-quality natural canonical images to represent the input video. Our approach utilizes homography to model global motion and employs multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to capture local residual deformations, enhancing the model’s ability to handle complex video dynamics. By introducing a diffusion prior from the early stages of training, our model ensures that the generated images retain a high-quality natural appearance, making the produced canonical images suitable for various downstream tasks in video editing, a capability not achieved by current canonical-based methods. Furthermore, we incorporate low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning and introduce a noise and diffusion prior update scheduling technique that accelerates the training process by 14 times. Extensive experimental results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in various video editing tasks and produces coherent and high-quality edited video sequences. See our project page for video results: [koi953215.github.io/NaRCan_page](https://koi953215.github.io/NaRCan_page/).

paragraphs: NaRCan represents a video using canonical images designed to look natural and support subsequent editing. The challenge is to connect this representation to frames containing motion and deformation while keeping the representative images visually suitable for editing. The framework combines a model of video deformation with a diffusion prior that guides image appearance.

Global motion is modeled with a homography, while multilayer perceptrons capture local deformations left over after that global transformation. This division helps the model represent complex video dynamics. The diffusion prior is introduced early in training so that natural appearance influences how the canonical images are formed.

The framework also incorporates low-rank adaptation and schedules changes to noise and diffusion-prior updates. The authors report a fourteenfold acceleration of training from these techniques. Across the evaluated video-editing tasks, NaRCan outperforms existing approaches and produces coherent, high-quality edited sequences. The findings support combining motion modeling and appearance guidance to obtain canonical representations that are useful for downstream video editing.
summary.tldr: NaRCan combines motion modeling and diffusion guidance to create natural canonical images for coherent video editing.

title: NaRCan: Natural Refined Canonical Image with Integration of Diffusion Prior for Video Editing

abstract: Motivated by the problem of compressing point sets into as few bits as possible while maintaining information about approximate distances between points, we construct random nonlinear maps $\varphi_\ell$ that compress point sets in the following way. For a point set $S$, the map $\varphi_\ell:\mathbb{R}^d \to N^{-1/2}\{-1,1\}^N$ has the property that storing $\varphi_\ell(S)$ (a sketch of $S$) allows one to report squared distances between points up to some multiplicative $(1\pm \epsilon)$ error with high probability. The maps $\varphi_\ell$ are the $\ell$-fold composition of a certain type of random feature mapping. Compared to existing techniques, our maps offer several advantages. The standard method for compressing point sets by random mappings relies on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma and involves compressing point sets with a random linear map. The main advantage of our maps $\varphi_\ell$ over random linear maps is that ours map point sets directly into the discrete cube $N^{-1/2}\{-1,1\}^N$ and so there is no additional step needed to convert the sketch to bits. For some range of parameters, our maps $\varphi_\ell$ produce sketches using fewer bits of storage space. We validate the method with experiments, including an application to nearest neighbor search.

The authors construct random nonlinear maps that produce compact sketches. With high probability, the sketches allow squared distances to be reported within a specified multiplicative error of one plus or minus epsilon.

The maps are built by repeatedly composing a particular random feature transformation. Each output coordinate takes one of two scaled values, so the result already has a binary representation. This distinguishes the construction from the usual Johnson–Lindenstrauss approach based on random linear maps, whose outputs need an additional conversion into bits before they become a digital sketch.

The direct binary output is a practical advantage of the construction, and the authors establish that it also uses fewer storage bits for some parameter ranges. That storage benefit is explicitly conditional rather than universal. Experiments, including nearest-neighbor search, validate the method and connect its distance-preservation properties with a task that depends on identifying nearby points.
summary.tldr: Repeated random nonlinear mappings produce binary sketches that preserve approximate squared distances and can reduce storage for some parameter ranges.

title: Euclidean distance compression via deep random features

abstract: For many graph-related problems, it can be essential to have a set of structurally diverse graphs. For instance, such graphs can be used for testing graph algorithms or their neural approximations. However, to the best of our knowledge, the problem of generating structurally diverse graphs has not been explored in the literature. In this paper, we fill this gap. First, we discuss how to define diversity for a set of graphs, why this task is non-trivial, and how one can choose a proper diversity measure. Then, for a given diversity measure, we propose and compare several algorithms optimizing it: we consider approaches based on standard random graph models, local graph optimization, genetic algorithms, and neural generative models. We show that it is possible to significantly improve diversity over basic random graph generators. Additionally, our analysis of generated graphs allows us to better understand the properties of graph distances: depending on which diversity measure is used for optimization, the obtained graphs may possess very different structural properties which gives a better understanding of the graph distance underlying the diversity measure.

This paper treats the construction of such collections as an explicit optimization problem. Its starting point is that structural diversity needs a definition: choosing how to measure differences between graphs also determines what kinds of variation a generator will be encouraged to produce.

The authors discuss how to select a suitable diversity measure, then compare several ways to optimize it. These include standard random graph models, local changes to graphs, genetic algorithms, and neural generative models. Their comparisons show that deliberately optimizing diversity can produce substantially more diverse collections than basic random graph generators under the measures considered.

The generated collections also reveal properties of the measures themselves. Optimizing different diversity measures can yield graphs with very different structures, exposing which distinctions the underlying graph distances emphasize. The work therefore offers both methods for building varied test collections and a way to examine whether a chosen notion of diversity captures the structural differences of interest.
summary.tldr: Explicitly optimizing graph diversity improves on basic random generators and reveals how diversity measures favor different structures.

title: Challenges of Generating Structurally Diverse Graphs

abstract: Rigorously establishing the safety of black-box machine learning models with respect to critical risk measures is important for providing guarantees about the behavior of the model.Recently, a notion of a risk controlling prediction set (RCPS) has been introduced by Bates et. al. (JACM '24) for producing prediction sets that are statistically guaranteed to have low risk from machine learning models.Our method extends this notion to the sequential setting, where we provide guarantees even when the data is collected adaptively, and ensures the risk guarantee is anytime-valid, i.e., simultaneously holds at all time steps. Further, we propose a framework for constructing RCPSes for active labeling, i.e., allowing one to use a labeling policy that chooses whether to query the true label for each received data point, and ensures the expected proportion data points whose labels are queried are below a predetermined label budget. We also describe how to use predictors (e.g., the machine learning model we are providing risk control guarantees for) to further improve the utility of our RCPSes by estimating the expected risk conditioned on the covariates.We characterize the optimal choices of label policy under a fixed label budget, and predictor, and show a regret result that relates the estimation error of the optimal labeling policy and predictor to the wealth process that underlies our RCPSes.Lastly, we present practical ways of formulating label policies and we empirically show that our label policies use fewer labels to reach higher utility than naive baseline labeling strategies on both simulations and real data.

paragraphs: A risk controlling prediction set lets a model return a set of possible answers while providing a statistical guarantee about a chosen risk measure. This paper extends that idea to data arriving sequentially. Its guarantees accommodate adaptive data collection and hold simultaneously across time steps, so their validity does not depend on assessing the procedure at one predetermined moment.

The method also supports active labeling: a policy decides whether to request the true label for each incoming example. It constrains the expected proportion of requested labels to a specified budget. Predictions of risk conditional on the input information can further improve the usefulness of the resulting prediction sets.

The authors characterize optimal labeling policies and risk predictors, and connect errors in estimating them to the statistical evidence process supporting the guarantees. Experiments on simulated and real data show that practical versions of their policies achieve higher utility with fewer labels than naive labeling strategies. The contribution therefore combines sequential statistical protection with more selective use of labeling resources.
summary.tldr: The method builds prediction sets with risk guarantees that remain valid over time while selectively requesting labels within an expected budget.

title: Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) problems in which agents observe the reward or transition realizations at their current state _before deciding which action to take_. Such observations are available in many applications, including transactions, navigation and more. When the environment is known, previous work shows that this lookahead information can drastically increase the collected reward. However, outside of specific applications, existing approaches for interacting with unknown environments are not well-adapted to these observations. In this work, we close this gap and design provably-efficient learning algorithms able to incorporate lookahead information. To achieve this, we perform planning using the empirical distribution of the reward and transition observations, in contrast to vanilla approaches that only rely on estimated expectations. We prove that our algorithms achieve tight regret versus a baseline that also has access to lookahead information -- linearly increasing the amount of collected reward compared to agents that cannot handle lookahead information.

paragraphs: This paper considers reinforcement learning where an agent sees realized rewards or transitions at its current state before choosing an action. Such lookahead information changes the decision problem because the agent can respond to observations that ordinary action selection does not use. Previous work established large benefits when the environment is already known.

The authors address unknown environments by designing learning algorithms that incorporate these observations. Their planning procedure uses the empirical distribution of observed rewards and transitions, rather than relying only on estimated expectations. This retains distributional information needed to plan decisions that depend on what the agent gets to observe before acting.

The theoretical comparison uses a baseline that also receives lookahead information. This is significant because it evaluates learning against a decision-maker with the same informational advantage. The authors prove tight regret guarantees and report a linear increase in collected reward relative to agents that cannot handle lookahead information. The contribution is an efficient learning framework tailored to this observation structure, extending the usefulness of lookahead beyond settings where the environment is known in advance.
summary.tldr: Distribution-based planning enables provably efficient reinforcement learning when reward or transition realizations are visible before action selection.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Lookahead Information

abstract: Instruction tuning plays a crucial role in shaping the outputs of language models (LMs) to desired styles. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective method, Instruction Modelling (IM), which trains LMs by applying a loss function to the instruction and prompt part rather than solely to the output part. Through experiments across 21 diverse benchmarks, we show that, in many scenarios, IM can effectively improve the LM performance on both NLP tasks (*e.g.,* MMLU, TruthfulQA, and HumanEval) and open-ended generation benchmarks (*e.g.,* MT-Bench and AlpacaEval). Remarkably, in the most advantageous case, IM boosts model performance on AlpacaEval 1.0 by over 100%. We identify two key factors influencing the effectiveness of IM: (1) The ratio between instruction length and output length in the training data; and (2) The number of training examples. We observe that IM is especially beneficial when trained on datasets with lengthy instructions paired with brief outputs, or under the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis (SAH) where a small amount of training examples are used for instruction tuning. Further analysis substantiates our hypothesis that our improvement can be attributed to reduced overfitting to instruction tuning datasets. It is worth noting that we are not proposing \ours as a replacement for the current instruction tuning process.Instead, our work aims to provide practical guidance for instruction tuning LMs, especially in low-resource scenarios.Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhengxiangShi/InstructionModelling.

summary.tldr: Including instructions and prompts in the training loss can improve instruction tuning, particularly with few examples or long instructions and short answers.

title: Instruction Tuning With Loss Over Instructions

abstract: In steganography, selecting an optimal cover image—referred to as cover selection—is pivotal for effective message concealment. Traditional methods have typically employed exhaustive searches to identify images that conform to specific perceptual or complexity metrics. However, the relationship between these metrics and the actual message hiding efficacy of an image is unclear, often yielding less-than-ideal steganographic outcomes. Inspired by recent advancements in generative models, we introduce a novel cover selection framework, which involves optimizing within the latent space of pretrained generative models to identify the most suitable cover images, distinguishing itself from traditional exhaustive search methods. Our method shows significant advantages in message recovery and image quality. We also conduct an information-theoretic analysis of the generated cover images, revealing that message hiding predominantly occurs in low-variance pixels, reflecting the waterfilling algorithm's principles in parallel Gaussian channels.

paragraphs: Image steganography hides a message inside an image, making the choice of that image an important part of the task. Traditional cover selection searches through images using perceptual or complexity measurements. The difficulty is that an image scoring well on those measurements may not actually be well suited to concealing and recovering a message.

This paper replaces exhaustive cover searching with optimization in the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The latent space provides a way to search among images represented by the generator and identify suitable covers. This makes the generative model part of the cover-selection process, addressing the uncertain relationship between conventional selection measurements and actual hiding effectiveness.

The authors report significant advantages in message recovery and image quality. They also analyze the generated covers from an information-theoretic perspective and find that message hiding occurs mainly in low-variance pixels. They relate this pattern to waterfilling in parallel Gaussian channels. This observation offers an interpretation of where the message is carried in the generated covers, alongside the empirical performance findings.
summary.tldr: Optimizing within a pretrained generator's latent space finds cover images with improved message recovery and image quality.

title: Neural Cover Selection for Image Steganography

abstract: Achieving the no-regret property for Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems in continuous state and action-space environments is one of the major open problems in the field. Existing solutions either work under very specific assumptions or achieve bounds that are vacuous in some regimes. Furthermore, many structural assumptions are known to suffer from a provably unavoidable exponential dependence on the time horizon $H$ in the regret, which makes any possible solution unfeasible in practice. In this paper, we identify _local linearity_ as the feature that makes Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) both _learnable_ (sublinear regret) and _feasible_ (regret that is polynomial in $H$). We define a novel MDP representation class, namely _Locally Linearizable MDPs_, generalizing other representation classes like Linear MDPs and MDPS with low inherent Belmman error. Then, i) we introduce **Cinderella**, a no-regret algorithm for this general representation class, and ii) we show that all known learnable and feasible MDP families are representable in this class. We first show that all known feasible MDPs belong to a family that we call _Mildly Smooth MDPs_. Then, we show how any mildly smooth MDP can be represented as a Locally Linearizable MDP by an appropriate choice of representation. This way, **Cinderella** is shown to achieve state-of-the-art regret bounds for all previously known (and some new) continuous MDPs for which RL is learnable and feasible.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces needs structure to make learning manageable. Even when regret grows sublinearly with experience, a bound can be impractical if it depends exponentially on the planning horizon. This paper seeks a representation that supports both sublinear regret and polynomial dependence on that horizon.

The authors define Locally Linearizable MDPs, a class that generalizes linear MDPs and models with low inherent Bellman error. They introduce Cinderella, a no-regret algorithm for this representation class. Local linearity provides the organizing structure for the analysis, allowing the paper to connect several previously studied settings within one framework.

The authors show that all known learnable and feasible MDP families fit this class. Their argument passes through a family called Mildly Smooth MDPs, whose members admit suitable locally linearizable representations. Cinderella consequently obtains state-of-the-art regret bounds for previously known and some new continuous settings with these properties. The result unifies known positive cases; it does not establish that every possible learnable continuous environment must satisfy this representation.
summary.tldr: Cinderella achieves no-regret learning for locally linearizable MDPs, unifying known continuous settings with feasible dependence on the planning horizon.

title: Local Linearity: the Key for No-regret Reinforcement Learning in Continuous MDPs

abstract: Stochastic second-order methods are known to achieve fast local convergence in strongly convex optimization by relying on noisy Hessian estimates to precondition the gradient. Yet, most of these methods achieve superlinear convergence only when the stochastic Hessian noise diminishes, requiring an increase in the per-iteration cost as time progresses. Recent work in \cite{na2022hessian} addressed this issue via a Hessian averaging scheme that achieves a superlinear convergence rate without increasing the per-iteration cost. However, the considered method exhibits a slow global convergence rate, requiring up to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\kappa^2)$ iterations to reach the superlinear rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((1/t)^{t/2})$, where $\kappa$ is the problem's condition number. In this paper, we propose a novel stochastic Newton proximal extragradient method that significantly improves these bounds, achieving a faster global linear rate and reaching the same fast superlinear rate in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\kappa)$ iterations. We achieve this by developing a novel extension of the Hybrid Proximal Extragradient (HPE) framework, which simultaneously achieves fast global and local convergence rates for strongly convex functions with access to a noisy Hessian oracle.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization methods use curvature information to guide updates and can converge rapidly near a solution. With noisy Hessian estimates, however, many methods require increasingly costly iterations to obtain superlinear convergence. Earlier Hessian averaging work avoided that growing cost, but could take many iterations to reach its fast local regime.

This paper proposes a stochastic Newton proximal extragradient method for strongly convex functions with access to noisy Hessian information. It extends the Hybrid Proximal Extragradient framework to combine faster global progress with rapid local convergence. The distinction matters because a strong local rate is less useful if reaching the region where it applies is slow.

The method reaches the same stated superlinear rate after roughly κ iterations, up to logarithmic factors, compared with roughly κ² for the earlier method, where κ is the condition number. It also improves the global linear convergence rate. These bounds strengthen both phases of the optimization process under the paper's strongly convex, noisy-Hessian setting.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Newton method improves global convergence and reaches its superlinear phase in roughly κ rather than κ² iterations.

title: Stochastic Newton Proximal Extragradient Method

abstract: Most existing prompting methods suffer from the issues of generalizability and consistency, as they often rely on instance-specific solutions that may not be applicable to other instances and lack task-level consistency across the selected few-shot examples. To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive framework, StrategyLLM, allowing LLMs to perform inductive reasoning, deriving general strategies from specific task instances, and deductive reasoning, applying these general strategies to particular task examples, for constructing generalizable and consistent few-shot prompts. It employs four LLM-based agents: strategy generator, executor, optimizer, and evaluator, working together to generate, evaluate, and select promising strategies for a given task. Experimental results demonstrate that StrategyLLM outperforms the competitive baseline CoT-SC that requires human-annotated solutions on 13 datasets across 4 challenging tasks without human involvement, including math reasoning (34.2\% $\rightarrow$ 38.8\%), commonsense reasoning (70.3\% $\rightarrow$ 72.5\%), algorithmic reasoning (73.7\% $\rightarrow$ 85.0\%), and symbolic reasoning (30.0\% $\rightarrow$ 79.2\%). Further analysis reveals that StrategyLLM is applicable to various LLMs and demonstrates advantages across numerous scenarios.

paragraphs: Few-shot prompts often show solutions to individual examples, but those solutions may not express a consistent approach that transfers across a task. StrategyLLM addresses this by having language models derive general strategies from particular examples and then apply those strategies to new examples. It combines inductive reasoning about shared patterns with deductive use of the resulting strategy.

The framework assigns four roles to language-model agents: generating strategies, executing them, optimizing them, and evaluating them. Together, these agents produce and select promising task-level strategies for constructing few-shot prompts. The approach aims to make the examples reflect a coherent method instead of an assortment of instance-specific solutions.

Across 13 datasets covering mathematical, commonsense, algorithmic, and symbolic reasoning, StrategyLLM outperforms the CoT-SC baseline without human involvement, while that baseline uses human-annotated solutions. The largest reported change is in symbolic reasoning, from 30.0% to 79.2%. Further analysis finds applicability across several language models and advantages in numerous scenarios, supporting the value of explicit strategy development in prompting.
summary.tldr: StrategyLLM uses four language-model agents to develop and apply reusable task strategies, improving reasoning results without human-annotated solutions.

title: StrategyLLM: Large Language Models as Strategy Generators, Executors, Optimizers, and Evaluators for Problem Solving

abstract: Feature attributions attempt to highlight what inputs drive predictive power. Good attributions or explanations are thus those that produce inputs that retain this predictive power; accordingly, evaluations of explanations score their quality of prediction. However, evaluations produce scores better than what appears possible from the values in the explanation for a class of explanations, called encoding explanations. Probing for encoding remains a challenge because there is no general characterization of what gives the extra predictive power. We develop a deﬁnition of encoding that identiﬁes this extra predictive power via conditional dependence and show that the deﬁnition ﬁts existing examples of encoding. This deﬁnition implies, in contrast to encoding explanations, that non-encoding explanations contain all the informative inputs used to produce the explanation, giving them a “what you see is what you get” property, which makes them transparent and simple to use. Next, we prove that existing scores (ROAR, FRESH, EVAL-X) do not rank non-encoding explanations above encoding ones, and develop STRIPE-X which ranks them correctly. After empirically demonstrating the theoretical insights, we use STRIPE-X to show that despite prompting an LLM to produce non-encoding explanations for a sentiment analysis task, the LLM-generated explanations encode.

paragraphs: Feature-attribution explanations highlight inputs intended to account for a prediction. Evaluations often reward explanations that preserve predictive information. The problem studied here is that some explanations carry extra information beyond what their displayed input values appear to contain, allowing them to achieve deceptively strong prediction-based scores. The paper calls these encoding explanations.

The authors define encoding through conditional dependence and show that this definition captures existing examples. It also characterizes a desirable property of non-encoding explanations: they contain all informative inputs used to produce the explanation. That makes the visible explanation a transparent account of the information involved in constructing it.

The paper proves that ROAR, FRESH, and EVAL-X do not rank non-encoding explanations above encoding ones, then introduces STRIPE-X to obtain the correct ranking. Empirical demonstrations support the theoretical analysis. Applying STRIPE-X to a sentiment-analysis task reveals encoding in LLM-generated explanations even when the model was explicitly prompted to avoid it, showing why instructions alone did not ensure transparency in that setting.
summary.tldr: A formal definition of explanation encoding leads to STRIPE-X, which distinguishes transparent explanations from those carrying extra predictive information.

title: Explanations that reveal all through the deﬁnition of encoding

abstract: Machine learning has driven an exponential increase in computational demand, leading to massive data centers that consume significant amounts of energy and contribute to climate change. This makes sustainable data center control a priority. In this paper, we introduce SustainDC, a set of Python environments for benchmarking multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms for data centers (DC). SustainDC supports custom DC configurations and tasks such as workload scheduling, cooling optimization, and auxiliary battery management, with multiple agents managing these operations while accounting for the effects of each other. We evaluate various MARL algorithms on SustainDC, showing their performance across diverse DC designs, locations, weather conditions, grid carbon intensity, and workload requirements. Our results highlight significant opportunities for improvement of data center operations using MARL algorithms. Given the increasing use of DC due to AI, SustainDC provides a crucial platform for the development and benchmarking of advanced algorithms essential for achieving sustainable computing and addressing other heterogeneous real-world challenges.

paragraphs: SustainDC provides Python environments for studying sustainable data center control with multi-agent reinforcement learning. The motivation is the energy consumption and climate impact associated with growing computational demand. Its focus is a setting where several operational decisions interact, so evaluating each controller independently would miss part of the control problem.

The environments support custom data center configurations and tasks including workload scheduling, cooling optimization, and auxiliary battery management. Multiple agents manage these operations while accounting for one another’s effects. This makes coordinated decision making part of the benchmark rather than treating workload, cooling, and storage as unrelated tasks.

The authors evaluate reinforcement learning algorithms across different data center designs, locations, weather conditions, grid carbon intensities, and workload requirements. Their results highlight substantial opportunities to improve operations using multi-agent methods. SustainDC’s main contribution is a configurable platform for developing and comparing such algorithms across varied operating conditions, with sustainability motivating both the control tasks and the evaluation setting.
summary.tldr: SustainDC benchmarks coordinated reinforcement learning for workload scheduling, cooling, and battery control across varied data center conditions.

title: SustainDC: Benchmarking for Sustainable Data Center Control

abstract: While Tensor-based Multi-view Subspace Clustering (TMSC) has garnered significant attention for its capacity to effectively capture high-order correlations among multiple views, three notable limitations in current TMSC methods necessitate consideration: 1) high computational complexity and reliance on dictionary completeness resulting from using observed data as the dictionary, 2) inaccurate subspace representation stemming from the oversight of local geometric information and 3) under-penalization of noise-related singular values within tensor data caused by treating all singular values equally. To address these limitations, this paper presents a \textbf{S}calable TMSC framework with \textbf{T}riple inf\textbf{O}rmatio\textbf{N} \textbf{E}nhancement (\textbf{STONE}). Notably, an enhanced anchor dictionary learning mechanism has been utilized to recover the low-rank anchor structure, resulting in reduced computational complexity and increased resilience, especially in scenarios with inadequate dictionaries. Additionally, we introduce an anchor hypergraph Laplacian regularizer to preserve the inherent geometry of the data within the subspace representation. Simultaneously, an improved hyperbolic tangent function has been employed as a precise approximation for tensor rank, effectively capturing the significant variations in singular values. Extensive experimentation on a variety of datasets demonstrates that our approach surpasses SOTA methods in both effectiveness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Multi-view subspace clustering groups observations using several representations of the same data. Tensor-based approaches capture relationships across those views, but existing methods can be expensive, depend heavily on complete dictionaries, and lose local geometric information. The paper also identifies a problem with treating all tensor singular values equally when some are associated with noise.

STONE addresses these issues through three connected changes. An enhanced anchor dictionary mechanism recovers a low-rank anchor structure, reducing computation and improving resilience when dictionaries are inadequate. An anchor hypergraph Laplacian regularizer preserves the data’s geometry within the learned subspace representation, helping retain relationships that a purely global representation can overlook.

Together, these changes improve the dictionary, geometric structure, and tensor representation. Experiments across several datasets report better clustering effectiveness and efficiency than state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined framework’s scalability and representation quality.
summary.tldr: STONE improves multi-view clustering through anchor dictionary learning, geometry preservation, and a more discriminating tensor-rank approximation.

title: From Dictionary to Tensor: A Scalable Multi-View Subspace Clustering Framework with Triple Information Enhancement

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have garnered significant attention for their remarkable capabilities across various domains, whose vast parameter scales present challenges for practical deployment. Structured pruning is an effective method to balance model performance with efficiency, but performance restoration under computational resource constraints is a principal challenge in pruning LLMs. Therefore, we present a low-cost and fast structured pruning method for LLMs named SlimGPT based on the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework. We propose Batched Greedy Pruning for rapid and near-optimal pruning, which enhances the accuracy of head-wise pruning error estimation through grouped Cholesky decomposition and improves the pruning efficiency of FFN via Dynamic Group Size, thereby achieving approximate local optimal pruning results within one hour. Besides, we explore the limitations of layer-wise pruning from the perspective of error accumulation and propose Incremental Pruning Ratio, a non-uniform pruning strategy to reduce performance degradation. Experimental results on the LLaMA benchmark show that SlimGPT outperforms other methods and achieves state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Structured pruning reduces a language model's size by removing organized components, but retaining performance under tight computational budgets remains difficult. SlimGPT proposes a fast, low-cost pruning method based on the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework. It focuses on choosing removals carefully enough to limit the damage introduced during compression.

Its Batched Greedy Pruning procedure combines two mechanisms. Grouped Cholesky decomposition improves estimates of the error caused by pruning attention heads, while Dynamic Group Size makes pruning feed-forward networks more efficient. The authors report obtaining approximately locally optimal pruning results within one hour. This is a claim about the pruning procedure's reported results, rather than a guarantee of a globally best compressed model.

The paper also examines how errors accumulate when layers are pruned separately. Its Incremental Pruning Ratio strategy varies pruning across layers to reduce performance degradation. On the LLaMA benchmark, SlimGPT outperforms other methods and achieves reported state-of-the-art results. Together, the contributions address both the immediate quality of component-removal decisions and the accumulated effect of those decisions across the model.
summary.tldr: SlimGPT combines efficient component selection with nonuniform layer pruning to compress language models while reducing accumulated performance loss.

title: SlimGPT: Layer-wise Structured Pruning for Large Language Models

abstract: Stochastic compositional optimization (SCO) problem constitutes a class of optimization problems characterized by the objective function with a compositional form, including the tasks with known derivatives, such as AUC maximization, and the derivative-free tasks exemplified by black-box vertical federated learning (VFL). From the learning theory perspective, the learning guarantees of SCO algorithms with known derivatives have been studied in the literature. However, the potential impacts of the derivative-free setting on the learning guarantees of SCO remains unclear and merits further investigation. This paper aims to reveal the impacts by developing a theoretical analysis for two derivative-free algorithms, black-box SCGD and SCSC. Specifically, we first provide the sharper generalization upper bounds of convex SCGD and SCSC based on a new stability analysis framework more effective than prior work under some milder conditions, which is further developed to the non-convex case using the almost co-coercivity property of smooth function. Then, we derive the learning guarantees of three black-box variants of non-convex SCGD and SCSC with additional optimization analysis. Comparing these results, we theoretically uncover the impacts that a better gradient estimation brings a tighter learning guarantee and a larger proportion of unknown gradients may lead to a stronger dependence on the gradient estimation quality. Finally, our analysis is applied to two SCO algorithms, FOO-based vertical VFL and VFL-CZOFO, to build the first learning guarantees for VFL that align with the findings of SCGD and SCSC.

paragraphs: Stochastic compositional optimization studies objectives built by composing functions, with applications ranging from AUC maximization to vertical federated learning. Some settings provide derivatives directly, while black-box settings require their estimation. This paper asks how losing access to derivatives changes the learning guarantees of two optimization algorithms, SCGD and SCSC.

The analysis first develops a new stability framework that gives sharper generalization upper bounds in convex settings under some milder conditions. It then extends the reasoning to non-convex objectives using a property of smooth functions called almost co-coercivity. Combining this framework with optimization analysis produces learning guarantees for three black-box variants of non-convex SCGD and SCSC.
