It also shows that a larger proportion of unknown gradients may increase dependence on estimation quality. The authors apply the analysis to FOO-based vertical VFL and VFL-CZOFO, establishing learning guarantees consistent with these findings. The contribution clarifies theoretically how the quality and extent of missing derivative information affect what these methods can guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper derives black-box compositional optimization guarantees showing how gradient-estimation quality and the proportion of unknown gradients affect learning bounds.

title: How Does Black-Box Impact the Learning Guarantee of Stochastic Compositional Optimization?

abstract: Offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) enhances data efficiency by utilizing pre-collected datasets to learn models and policies, especially in scenarios where exploration is costly or infeasible. Nevertheless, its performance often suffers from the objective mismatch between model and policy learning, resulting in inferior performance despite accurate model predictions. This paper first identifies the primary source of this mismatch comes from the underlying confounders present in offline data for MBRL. Subsequently, we introduce **B**ilin**E**ar **CAUS**al r**E**presentation (BECAUSE), an algorithm to capture causal representation for both states and actions to reduce the influence of the distribution shift, thus mitigating the objective mismatch problem. Comprehensive evaluations on 18 tasks that vary in data quality and environment context demonstrate the superior performance of BECAUSE over existing offline RL algorithms. We show the generalizability and robustness of BECAUSE under fewer samples or larger numbers of confounders. Additionally, we offer theoretical analysis of BECAUSE to prove its error bound and sample efficiency when integrating causal representation into offline MBRL. See more details in our project page: [https://sites.google.com/view/be-cause](https://sites.google.com/view/be-cause).

paragraphs: Offline model-based reinforcement learning learns an environment model and a decision policy from previously collected data. This is valuable when further exploration is expensive or impossible. However, an environment model can predict accurately while supporting a poor policy. The paper investigates this mismatch between learning to predict and learning to make useful decisions.

The authors identify underlying confounders in offline data as the primary source of the mismatch they study. Their algorithm, BECAUSE, learns a bilinear causal representation for both states and actions. The purpose is to reduce the influence of distribution shifts and thereby bring model learning and policy learning into better agreement.

Evaluations cover 18 tasks with differing data quality and environmental contexts, reporting better performance than existing offline reinforcement-learning algorithms. Additional results support robustness and generalization when fewer samples are available or more confounders are present. The paper also provides theoretical analysis of error bounds and sample efficiency. Together, these contributions connect a causal explanation of the learning mismatch with an algorithm evaluated under varied data conditions.
summary.tldr: BECAUSE learns causal representations of states and actions to reduce the mismatch between accurate environment models and effective offline policies.

title: BECAUSE: Bilinear Causal Representation for Generalizable Offline Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has led to the adoption of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures that dynamically leverage specialized subnetworks for improved efficiency and performance. Despite their benefits, MoE models face significant challenges during inference, including inefficient memory management and suboptimal batching, due to misaligned design choices between the model architecture and the system policies. Furthermore, the conventional approach of training MoEs from scratch is increasingly prohibitive in terms of cost. In this paper, we propose a novel framework $\textit{Read-ME}$ that transforms pre-trained dense LLMs into smaller MoE models (in contrast to ``upcycling" generalist MoEs), avoiding the high costs of ground-up training. Our approach employs activation sparsity to extract experts. To compose experts, we examine the widely-adopted layer-wise router design and show its redundancy, and thus we introduce the pre-gating router decoupled from the MoE backbone that facilitates system-friendly pre-computing and lookahead scheduling, enhancing expert-aware batching and caching.Our codesign therefore addresses critical gaps on both the algorithmic and system fronts, establishing a scalable and efficient alternative for LLM inference in resource-constrained settings.$\textit{Read-ME}$ outperforms other popular open-source dense models of similar scales, achieving improvements of up to 10.1\% on MMLU, and improving mean end-to-end latency up to 6.1\%. Codes are available at: \url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/READ-ME}.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models activate specialized subnetworks, but their inference efficiency depends on how expert selection interacts with memory management and batching. This paper introduces Read-ME, a framework that converts pretrained dense language models into smaller expert models. Reusing a pretrained model avoids the cost of training the mixture-of-experts architecture from scratch.

Read-ME extracts experts using activation sparsity. It also examines redundancy in conventional layer-wise routing and introduces a pre-gating router separate from the expert backbone. Computing routing decisions ahead of time enables lookahead scheduling, expert-aware batching, and caching. The architecture and execution policies are therefore designed together to address both model computation and system-level overhead.

The reported comparisons with popular open-source dense models of similar scale show MMLU improvements of up to 10.1% and mean end-to-end latency improvements of up to 6.1%. These are reported upper-end gains rather than uniform benefits for every case. The findings support converting existing dense models and reorganizing routing as a combined approach to efficient inference in resource-constrained settings.
summary.tldr: Read-ME converts dense language models into smaller expert models and separates routing to improve inference scheduling and reported performance.

title: $\textit{Read-ME}$: Refactorizing LLMs as Router-Decoupled Mixture of Experts with System Co-Design

abstract: Conformal prediction is an uncertainty quantification method that constructs a prediction set for a previously unseen datum, ensuring the true label is included with a predetermined coverage probability. Adaptive conformal prediction has been developed to address data distribution shifts in dynamic environments. However, the efficiency of prediction sets varies depending on the learning model used. Employing a single fixed model may not consistently offer the best performance in dynamic environments with unknown data distribution shifts. To address this issue, we introduce a novel adaptive conformal prediction framework, where the model used for creating prediction sets is selected ‘on the fly’ from multiple candidate models. The proposed algorithm is proven to achieve strongly adaptive regret over all intervals while maintaining valid coverage. Experiments on both real and synthetic datasets corroborate that the proposed approach consistently yields more efficient prediction sets while maintaining valid coverage, outperforming alternative methods.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty through a set of possible labels designed to include the correct label at a specified coverage level. Adaptive methods extend this idea to changing data distributions. This paper addresses a further difficulty: the model that produces efficient prediction sets at one time may become a poor choice after the environment changes.

The proposed framework chooses among multiple candidate models as new data arrives. Instead of committing permanently to one model, it selects the model used to construct prediction sets on the fly. This adds adaptation at the model-selection level, allowing the prediction procedure to respond when unknown distribution shifts change which candidate works best.

The authors prove strongly adaptive regret over all intervals while maintaining valid coverage. This provides a theoretical performance statement across time intervals alongside the coverage result. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets report more efficient prediction sets than alternative methods while preserving valid coverage. The stated benefit is improved usefulness of the uncertainty sets without giving up their coverage objective.
summary.tldr: Selecting conformal prediction models on the fly improves prediction-set efficiency under distribution shifts while maintaining valid coverage.

title: Multi-model Ensemble Conformal Prediction in Dynamic Environments

abstract: Since deep learning models are usually deployed in non-stationary environments, it is imperative to improve their robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. A common approach to mitigate distribution shift is to regularize internal representations or predictors learned from in-distribution (ID) data to be domain invariant. Past studies have primarily learned pairwise invariances, ignoring the intrinsic structure and high-order dependencies of the data. Unlike machines, human recognizes objects by first dividing them into major components and then identifying the topological relation of these components. Motivated by this, we propose Reconstruct and Match (REMA), a general learning framework for object recognition tasks to endow deep models with the capability of capturing the topological homogeneity of objects without human prior knowledge or fine-grained annotations. To identify major components from objects, REMA introduces a selective slot-based reconstruction module to dynamically map dense pixels into a sparse and discrete set of slot vectors in an unsupervised manner. Then, to model high-order dependencies among these components, we propose a hypergraph-based relational reasoning module that models the intricate relations of nodes (slots) with structural constraints. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that REMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in OOD generalization and test-time adaptation settings.

paragraphs: Object-recognition models often face data that differ from their training examples. Methods for handling this shift commonly encourage representations or predictors to stay invariant across domains. This paper argues that approaches centered on pairwise relationships overlook the internal structure of objects and dependencies involving multiple components.

Reconstruct and Match, or REMA, learns object components and their relationships without human-specified prior knowledge or fine-grained annotations. A selective slot-based reconstruction module maps dense image pixels into a small, discrete collection of slot vectors through unsupervised learning. These vectors provide a representation of major components that the next module can reason about.

A hypergraph-based relational module then models higher-order relationships among the slots under structural constraints. Experiments on standard benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both out-of-distribution generalization and test-time adaptation. The findings support learning component structure and multi-component relationships as useful ingredients for robustness.
summary.tldr: REMA learns object components and higher-order relationships to improve recognition under distribution shifts.

title: Reconstruct and Match: Out-of-Distribution Robustness via Topological Homogeneity

abstract: Novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes is becoming important in various applications, including augmented and virtual reality.We propose a novel 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) algorithm for dynamic scenes from casually recorded monocular videos. To overcome the overfitting problem of existing work for these real-world videos, we introduce an uncertainty-aware regularization that identifies uncertain regions with few observations and selectively imposes additional priors based on diffusion models and depth smoothness on such regions.This approach improves both the performance of novel view synthesis and the quality of training image reconstruction. We also identify the initialization problem of 4DGS in fast-moving dynamic regions, where the Structure from Motion (SfM) algorithm fails to provide reliable 3D landmarks. To initialize Gaussian primitives in such regions, we present a dynamic region densification method using the estimated depth maps and scene flow. Our experiments show that the proposed method improves the performance of 4DGS reconstruction from a video captured by a handheld monocular camera and also exhibits promising results in few-shot static scene reconstruction.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene from a casually recorded video requires estimating how it looks from viewpoints the camera never captured. Existing 4D Gaussian Splatting methods can overfit these recordings, especially where observations are sparse. This paper addresses that problem for videos recorded with a single camera.

The method identifies regions where the reconstruction is uncertain because there are few observations. It selectively adds guidance from diffusion models and depth smoothness in those regions. This makes uncertainty determine where additional assumptions influence the reconstruction. The paper also addresses a separate initialization problem: fast motion can prevent Structure from Motion from producing reliable three-dimensional landmarks. Its dynamic region densification method uses estimated depth and scene flow to initialize Gaussian primitives there.

Experiments report improvements in both rendering previously unseen viewpoints and reconstructing the original training images from handheld video. The method also shows promising results for static scenes with few observations. Together, the contributions address insufficient visual evidence and unreliable starting geometry, two obstacles to reconstructing casually recorded scenes.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware regularization and better initialization improve 4D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction from casually recorded single-camera videos.

title: 4D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild with Uncertainty-Aware Regularization

abstract: Recent work has shown that methods that regularize second order information like SAM can improve generalization in deep learning. Seemingly similar methods like weight noise and gradient penalties often fail to provide such benefits. We investigate this inconsistency and reveal its connection to the the structure of the Hessian of the loss. Specifically, its decomposition into the positive semi-definite Gauss-Newton matrix and an indefinite matrix, which we call the Nonlinear Modeling Error (NME) matrix. Previous studies have largely overlooked the significance of the NME in their analysis for various reasons. However, we provide empirical and theoretical evidence that the NME is important to the performance of gradient penalties and explains their sensitivity to activation functions. We also provide evidence that the difference in regularization performance between gradient penalties and weight noise can be explained by the NME. Our findings emphasize the necessity of considering the NME in both experimental design and theoretical analysis for sharpness regularization.

paragraphs: Methods that discourage sharp training-loss behavior can have surprisingly different effects on generalization. SAM often helps, while apparently related approaches involving weight noise or gradient penalties can fail to produce similar benefits. This paper investigates those differences through the Hessian, which describes second-order changes in the loss.

The analysis separates the Hessian into a positive semidefinite Gauss-Newton component and an indefinite component called Nonlinear Modeling Error, or NME. The latter has largely been overlooked in earlier analyses. Treating these components separately allows the authors to examine information that can disappear when sharpness is considered only through the more commonly studied part.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical evidence that NME matters for gradient-penalty performance and explains sensitivity to activation functions. It also presents evidence connecting NME to performance differences between gradient penalties and weight noise. The findings argue for including this component when designing experiments and theories of sharpness regularization, because superficially similar methods can interact differently with the full loss curvature.
summary.tldr: A commonly overlooked Hessian component helps explain why related sharpness-regularization methods differ in their generalization benefits.

title: Neglected Hessian component explains mysteries in sharpness regularization

abstract: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was introduced in the 1980's as a model for Blind Source Separation (BSS), which refers to the process of recovering the sources underlying a mixture of signals, with little knowledge about the source signals or the mixing process. While there are many sophisticated algorithms for estimation, different methods have different shortcomings. In this paper, we develop a nonparametric score to adaptively pick the right algorithm for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise. The novelty of this score stems from the fact that it just assumes a finite second moment of the data and uses the characteristic function to evaluate the quality of the estimated mixing matrix without any knowledge of the parameters of the noise distribution. In addition, we propose some new contrast functions and algorithms that enjoy the same fast computability as existing algorithms like FASTICA and JADE but work in domains where the former may fail. While these also may have weaknesses, our proposed diagnostic, as shown by our simulations, can remedy them. Finally, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze the local and global convergence properties of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks to recover underlying sources from mixed signals with limited knowledge of the sources or mixing process. Many estimation algorithms exist, but their weaknesses differ. This paper develops a diagnostic score for choosing among ICA solutions when the observations contain arbitrary Gaussian noise.

The score evaluates an estimated mixing matrix using the data's characteristic function. It requires a finite second moment but does not require knowing the noise distribution's parameters. This provides a nonparametric way to assess candidate solutions in the noisy setting, making algorithm selection responsive to the observed data rather than assuming one estimator is appropriate throughout.

The authors also introduce contrast functions and algorithms with fast computability comparable to FASTICA and JADE, including applicability in domains where those methods may fail. They acknowledge that the new algorithms can have weaknesses too, and simulations show how the diagnostic can help remedy them through selection. A theoretical framework analyzes local and global convergence, complementing the practical contribution of evaluating alternative solutions.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric diagnostic selects among noisy ICA solutions using finite-second-moment data without knowing Gaussian noise parameters.

title: Nonparametric Evaluation of Noisy ICA Solutions

abstract: Humans can communicate and observe media with different modalities, such as texts, sounds, and images. For robots to be more generalizable embodied agents, they should be capable of following instructions and perceiving the world with adaptation to diverse modalities. Current robotic learning methodologies often focus on single-modal task specification and observation, thereby limiting their ability to process rich multi-modal information. Addressing this limitation, we present an end-to-end general-purpose multi-modal system named Any-to-Policy Embodied Agents. This system empowers robots to handle tasks using various modalities, whether in combinations like text-image, audio-image, text-point cloud, or in isolation. Our innovative approach involves training a versatile modality network that adapts to various inputs and connects with policy networks for effective control. Because of the lack of existing multi-modal robotics datasets for evaluation, we assembled a comprehensive real-world dataset encompassing 30 robotic tasks. Each task in this dataset is richly annotated across multiple modalities, providing a robust foundation for assessment. We conducted extensive validation of our proposed unified modality embodied agent using several simulation benchmarks, including Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, and Maniskill2, as well as in our real-world settings. Our experiments showcase the promising capability of building embodied agents that can adapt to diverse multi-modal in a unified framework.

abstract: We present OSKAR, the first multimodal foundation model based on bootstrapped latent feature prediction. Unlike generative or contrastive methods, it avoids memorizing unnecessary details (e.g., pixels), and does not require negative pairs, large memory banks, or hand-crafted augmentations. We propose a novel pretraining strategy: given masked tokens from multiple modalities, predict a subset of missing tokens per modality, supervised by momentum-updated uni-modal target encoders. This design efficiently utilizes the model capacity in learning high-level representations while retaining modality-specific information. Further, we propose a scalable design which decouples the compute cost from the number of modalities using a fixed representative token budget—in both input and target tokens—and introduces a parameter-efficient cross-attention predictor that grounds each prediction in the full multimodal context. We instantiate OSKAR on video, skeleton, and text modalities. Extensive experimental results show that OSKAR's unified pretrained encoder outperforms models with specialized architectures of similar size in action recognition (rgb, skeleton, frozen, low-shot) and localization, video-text retrieval, and video question answering. Project website: https://multimodal-oskar.github.io

During pretraining, the model receives masked tokens from several modalities and predicts a subset of missing tokens for each. Separate target encoders for individual modalities supply supervision and are updated through momentum. A parameter-efficient cross-attention predictor uses the full multimodal context to inform each prediction, linking modality-specific targets to shared contextual information.

The architecture fixes the budget of representative input and target tokens to decouple computation from the number of modalities. The authors instantiate it with video, skeleton, and text. Their unified pretrained encoder outperforms similarly sized specialized architectures across the reported action recognition, localization, video-text retrieval, and video question-answering evaluations. summary.tldr: OSKAR predicts missing multimodal latent features within a fixed token budget to learn a unified encoder that performs well across video-related tasks.

title: OSKAR: Omnimodal Self-supervised Knowledge Abstraction and Representation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in various domains, showing impressive potential on various tasks. Recently, reasoning LLMs have been proposed to improve the \textit{reasoning} or \textit{thinking} capabilities of LLMs to solve complex problems. Despite the promising results of reasoning LLMs, enhancing the multi-step reasoning capabilities of LLMs still remains a significant challenge. While existing optimization methods have advanced the LLM reasoning capabilities, they often treat reasoning trajectories as a whole, without considering the underlying critical steps within the trajectory. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{G}uided \textbf{P}ivotal \textbf{O}ptimization (GPO), a novel fine-tuning strategy that dives into the reasoning process to enable more effective improvements. GPO first identifies the `critical step' within a reasoning trajectory - a point that the model must carefully proceed so as to succeed at the problem. We locate the critical step by estimating the advantage function. GPO then resets the policy to the critical step and samples the new rollout and prioritizes learning process on those rollouts. This focus allows the model to learn more effectively from pivotal moments within the reasoning process to improve the reasoning performance. We demonstrate that GPO is not a standalone method, but rather a general strategy that can be integrated with various optimization methods to improve reasoning performance. Besides theoretical analysis, our experiments across challenging reasoning benchmarks show that GPO can consistently and significantly enhances the performance of existing optimization methods, showcasing its effectiveness and generalizability in improving LLM reasoning by concentrating on pivotal moments within the generation process.

paragraphs: A long reasoning attempt can contain a pivotal step where the model's next choice strongly affects whether it succeeds. Optimization methods that treat the entire attempt as a single unit may miss this structure. Guided Pivotal Optimization, or GPO, focuses training on these critical points within a generated reasoning trajectory.

GPO estimates an advantage function to locate a critical step. It then returns the generation process to that point, samples new continuations, and prioritizes learning from those rollouts. This gives the optimization procedure additional experience with consequential reasoning decisions. The approach is designed as a general fine-tuning strategy that can be combined with different optimization methods.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks. In those experiments, adding GPO consistently and significantly improves the tested optimization methods. The findings support the idea that where training examples branch within a reasoning process matters: concentrating new continuations around pivotal moments can make the surrounding optimization procedure more effective.
summary.tldr: GPO improves reasoning training by identifying critical steps, sampling new continuations from them, and prioritizing those rollouts.

title: GPO: Learning from Critical Steps to Improve LLM Reasoning

abstract: 3D anomaly detection in point-cloud data is critical for industrial quality control, aiming to identify structural defects with high reliability. However, current memory bank-based methods often suffer from inconsistent feature transformations and limited discriminative capacity, particularly in capturing local geometric details and achieving rotation invariance. These limitations become more pronounced when registration fails, leading to unreliable detection results. We argue that point-cloud registration plays an essential role not only in aligning geometric structures but also in guiding feature extraction toward rotation-invariant and locally discriminative representations. To this end, we propose a registration-induced, rotation-invariant feature extraction framework that integrates the objectives of point-cloud registration and memory-based anomaly detection. Our key insight is that both tasks rely on modeling local geometric structures and leveraging feature similarity across samples. By embedding feature extraction into the registration learning process, our framework jointly optimizes alignment and representation learning. This integration enables the network to acquire features that are both robust to rotations and highly effective for anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on the Anomaly-ShapeNet and Real3D-AD datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing approaches in effectiveness and generalizability.

paragraphs: Detecting defects in three-dimensional point clouds requires distinguishing structural irregularities from changes in how an object is oriented. The paper argues that existing memory-bank methods can struggle with inconsistent feature transformations and insufficient sensitivity to local geometry. Failed registration, the alignment of point clouds, can make detection particularly unreliable.

The proposed framework uses registration as part of learning the features used for anomaly detection. Registration and memory-based detection both depend on local geometric structure and feature similarity across samples, so their objectives are integrated. Jointly learning alignment and representation encourages features that retain useful local distinctions while remaining robust to rotation.

This changes the role of registration from an alignment operation into a source of guidance for the detector's representation. Experiments on Anomaly-ShapeNet and Real3D-AD report consistent improvements over existing approaches in effectiveness and generalizability. The findings support training features around the shared geometric demands of registration and defect detection, rather than relying only on alignment to make comparisons reliable.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning point-cloud registration and anomaly features improves rotation robustness and 3D defect detection in the reported experiments.

title: Registration is a Powerful Rotation-Invariance Learner for 3D Anomaly Detection

abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly enhanced performance on 2D visual tasks. However, improving their spatial intelligence remains a challenge. Existing 3D MLLMs always rely on additional 3D or 2.5D data to incorporate spatial awareness, restricting their utility in scenarios with only 2D inputs, such as images or videos. In this paper, we present Spatial-MLLM, a novel framework for visual-based spatial reasoning from purely 2D observations. Unlike conventional video MLLMs which rely on CLIP-based visual encoders optimized for semantic understanding, our key insight is to unleash the strong structure prior from the feed-forward visual geometry foundation model. Specifically, we propose a dual-encoder architecture: a pretrained 2D visual encoder to extract semantic features, and a 3D spatial encoder—initialized from the backbone of the visual geometry model—to extract 3D structure features. A connector then integrates both features into unified visual tokens for enhanced spatial understanding. Furthermore, we propose a space-aware frame sampling strategy at inference time, which selects the spatially informative frames of a video sequence, ensuring that even under limited token length, the model focuses on frames critical for spatial reasoning. Beyond architecture improvements, we construct a training dataset from multiple sources and train the model on it using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. Extensive experiments on various real-world datasets demonstrate that Spatial-MLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of visual-based spatial understanding and reasoning tasks.

Experiments on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art results across a range of spatial understanding and reasoning tasks. summary.tldr: Spatial-MLLM combines semantic and geometric encoders with spatially informed frame selection to improve spatial reasoning from 2D images and videos.

title: Spatial-MLLM: Boosting MLLM Capabilities in Visual-based Spatial Intelligence

abstract: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values are a widely used method for local feature attribution in interpretable and explainable AI. We propose an efficient two-stage algorithm for computing SHAP values in both black-box setting and tree-based models. Motivated by spectral bias in real-world predictors, we first approximate models using compact Fourier representations, exactly for trees and approximately for black-box models. In the second stage, we introduce a closed-form formula for {\em exactly} computing SHAP values using the Fourier representation, that ``linearizes'' the computation into a simple summation and is amenable to parallelization. As the Fourier approximation is computed only once, our method enables amortized SHAP value computation, achieving significant speedups over existing methods and a tunable trade-off between efficiency and precision.

We propose an efficient two-stage algorithm for computing SHAP values in both black-box setting and tree-based models. Motivated by spectral bias in real-world predictors, we first approximate models using compact Fourier representations, exactly for trees and approximately for black-box models. paragraphs: SHAP values assign credit to input features for a model's individual predictions. Computing these explanations efficiently is the focus of this paper, which proposes a two-stage method for black-box predictors and tree models. The approach separates building a reusable model representation from calculating feature attributions for particular predictions.

First, the method expresses the predictor using a compact Fourier representation, motivated by spectral bias in real-world models. This representation is exact for trees and approximate for black-box predictors. Second, a closed-form formula computes SHAP values exactly from the Fourier representation through a simple summation that can be parallelized.

The distinction between the two stages matters for accuracy: an exact attribution calculation on an approximate black-box representation does not make the representation itself exact. Because the Fourier representation is computed once and reused, its initial cost can be spread over many explanations. The authors report significant speedups over existing methods and a tunable balance between efficiency and precision, making repeated attribution computation the main practical beneficiary.
summary.tldr: A reusable sparse Fourier representation enables fast SHAP computation, with exact attribution summation and a tunable approximation trade-off for black-box models.

title: SHAP values via sparse Fourier representation

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often struggle with culturally specific content — a challenge largely overlooked by existing benchmarks that focus on dominant languages and globalized datasets. We introduce TᴀɪᴡᴀɴVQA, a VQA benchmark designed for Taiwanese culture to evaluate recognition and reasoning in regional contexts. TᴀɪᴡᴀɴVQA contains 2,736 images and 5,472 manually curated questions covering topics such as traditional foods, public signs, festivals, and landmarks. The official benchmark set includes 1,000 images and 2,000 questions for systematic assessment, with the remainder of the data used as training material. Evaluations on state-of-the-art VLMs reveal strong visual recognition but notable weaknesses in cultural reasoning. To address this, we propose a data augmentation strategy that combines human-annotated and synthesized dialogues to enhance cultural understanding. Fine-tuning yields significant gains on TᴀɪᴡᴀɴVQA while maintaining stable performance on other multimodal tasks. To further explore the models’ cultural understanding, we conducted an open-ended question answering experiment. The results indicate a notable decline in cultural knowledge generation ($\approx$10–20\%), suggesting challenges remain. TᴀɪᴡᴀɴVQA offers a scalable framework for building culturally grounded AI models in low-resource cultures, promoting diversity and fairness in multimodal AI. Our dataset and code are publicly available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/hhhuang/TaiwanVQA) and [GitHub](https://github.com/hhhuang/TaiwanVQA).

summary.tldr: TaiwanVQA reveals gaps in Taiwanese cultural reasoning and shows that dialogue-based fine-tuning helps, while open-ended cultural answers remain challenging.

title: TaiwanVQA: Benchmarking and Enhancing Cultural Understanding in Vision-Language Models

abstract: This work introduces a hybrid non-Euclidean optimization method which generalizes gradient norm clipping by combining steepest descent and conditional gradient approaches. The method achieves the best of both worlds by establishing a descent property under a generalized notion of ($L_0$,$L_1$)-smoothness. Weight decay is incorporated in a principled manner by identifying a connection to the Frank-Wolfe short step. In the stochastic case, we show an order optimal $O(n^{-1/4})$ convergence rate by leveraging a momentum based gradient estimator. We discuss how to instantiate the algorithms for deep learning, which we dub Clipped Scion, and demonstrate their properties on image classification and language modeling. The code is available at https://github.com/LIONS-EPFL/ClippedScion.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization method that generalizes gradient norm clipping beyond Euclidean geometry. Its design combines steepest descent and conditional gradient approaches. The aim is to connect these update strategies through a shared mathematical framework, with a descent property established under a generalized form of (L0, L1)-smoothness.

That smoothness condition supplies the setting for the descent guarantee: the result is tied to the stated mathematical assumption. The paper also gives weight decay a principled role by relating it to the Frank-Wolfe short step. This connection places weight decay within the structure of the optimization method rather than presenting it only as an additional tuning choice.

For stochastic optimization, the authors use a momentum-based gradient estimator and prove an order-optimal O(n^(-1/4)) convergence rate. They also describe deep learning versions of the algorithms, named Clipped Scion, and demonstrate their properties on image classification and language modeling. The contribution combines theoretical guarantees with practical instantiations, showing how the generalized clipping framework can be used in neural network training.
summary.tldr: Clipped Scion generalizes gradient clipping through non-Euclidean optimization, with descent and stochastic convergence guarantees under the stated framework.

title: Generalized Gradient Norm Clipping & Non-Euclidean $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness

abstract: Spike camera with high temporal resolution offers a new perspective on high-speed dynamic scene rendering. Most existing rendering methods rely on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for static scenes using a monocular spike camera. However, these methods struggle with dynamic motion, while a single camera suffers from limited spatial coverage, making it challenging to reconstruct fine details in high-speed scenes. To address these problems, we propose Spike4DGS, the first high-speed dynamic scene rendering framework with 4D Gaussian Splatting using spike camera arrays. Technically, we first build a multi-view spike camera array to validate our solution, then establish both synthetic and real-world multi-view spike-based reconstruction datasets. Then, we design a multi-view spike-based dense initialization module that obtains dense point clouds and camera poses from continuous spike streams. Finally, we propose a spike-pixel synergy constraint supervision to optimize Spike4DGS, incorporating both rendered image quality loss and dynamic spatiotemporal spike loss. The results show that our Spike4DGS outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of novel view rendering quality on both synthetic and real-world datasets. More details are available at https://github.com/Qinghongye/Spike4DGS.

paragraphs: Spike cameras provide high temporal resolution, making them attractive for capturing fast motion. Existing approaches using a single spike camera often focus on static scenes and face limited spatial coverage. Spike4DGS combines multiple spike-camera views with 4D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct and render dynamic scenes with greater coverage of their details.

The work includes a physical camera array and both synthetic and real-world datasets for multi-view spike reconstruction. Its initialization module extracts dense point clouds and camera poses from continuous spike streams. These estimates provide the starting scene structure and camera information needed to optimize the dynamic representation.

Training combines supervision for rendered image quality with a loss that captures the spatial and temporal behavior of spikes. This links the appearance of rendered views to the camera signals describing motion over time. On both synthetic and real-world datasets, the method reports better novel-view rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution brings capture hardware, reconstruction data, initialization, and dynamic supervision together in one high-speed scene-rendering framework.
summary.tldr: Spike4DGS combines a spike-camera array with 4D Gaussian Splatting to improve novel-view rendering of fast-moving scenes.

title: Spike4DGS: Towards High-Speed Dynamic Scene Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting via a Spike Camera Array

abstract: Medical imaging super-resolution is critical for improving diagnostic utility and reducing costs, particularly for low-cost modalities such as portable Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT). We propose OCTDiff, a bridged diffusion model designed to enhance image resolution and quality from portable OCT devices. Our image-to-image diffusion framework addresses key challenges in the conditional generation process of denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). We introduce Adaptive Noise Aggregation (ANA), a novel module to improve denoising dynamics within the reverse diffusion process. Additionally, we integrate Multi-Scale Cross-Attention (MSCA) into the U-Net backbone to capture local dependencies across spatial resolutions. To address overfitting on small clinical datasets and to preserve fine structural details essential for retinal diagnostics, we design a customized loss function guided by clinical quality scores. OCTDiff outperforms convolutional baselines and standard DDPMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on clinical portable OCT datasets. Our model and its downstream applications have the potential to generalize to other medical imaging modalities and revolutionize the current workflow of ophthalmic diagnostics. The code is available at https://github.com/AI4VSLab/OCTDiff.

paragraphs: OCTDiff improves the resolution and visual quality of images from portable optical coherence tomography devices. The goal is particularly relevant to lower-cost imaging, where enhancement could improve diagnostic usefulness. The paper uses an image-to-image diffusion framework tailored to portable OCT and the fine retinal structures these images need to preserve.

Its Adaptive Noise Aggregation module improves denoising dynamics during reverse diffusion. A Multi-Scale Cross-Attention component in the U-Net backbone captures local dependencies across spatial resolutions. The training objective also incorporates clinical quality scores, with the stated aims of reducing overfitting on small clinical datasets and retaining structural details important for retinal diagnosis.

On clinical portable OCT datasets, OCTDiff outperforms convolutional baselines and standard denoising diffusion models, achieving the reported state of the art. These findings support the combined architectural and training choices for the evaluated enhancement task. The authors additionally propose that the method could extend to other medical imaging modalities and improve ophthalmic workflows, presenting those broader applications as potential rather than demonstrated outcomes.
summary.tldr: OCTDiff combines specialized diffusion denoising, multiscale attention, and clinically guided training to improve portable OCT image quality.

title: OCTDiff: Bridged Diffusion Model for Portable OCT Super-Resolution and Enhancement

abstract: The sensitivity of optimal transport (OT) to noise has motivated the study of robust variants. In this paper, we study two such formulations of semi-discrete OT in $\mathbb{R}^d$: (i) the $\alpha$-optimal partial transport, which minimizes the cost of transporting a mass of $\alpha$; and (ii) the $\lambda$-robust optimal transport, which regularizes the OT problem using the total variation (TV) distance. First, we provide a novel characterization of the optimal solutions in these settings, showing they can be represented as a restricted Laguerre diagram. Second, we exploit this characterization to establish a strong algorithmic connection between the two problems, showing that any solver for one can be adapted to solve the other with comparable precision. Third, we overcome key challenges posed in extending the cost-scaling paradigm to compute these variants of OT and present an algorithm that computes the exact solution up to $\log (1/\varepsilon)$ bits of precision in $n^{O(d)}\log (1/\varepsilon)$ time, where $n$ is the support size of the discrete distribution. Finally, we present an $n^{1+o(1)}\varepsilon^{-O(d)}$ time approximation algorithm for the above variants of OT.

paragraphs: Optimal transport can be sensitive to noise, motivating formulations that relax how distributions must be matched. This paper studies two such problems in the semi-discrete setting. Partial transport minimizes the cost of moving a specified amount of mass, alpha. Robust transport instead modifies the objective using a total-variation penalty controlled by lambda.

The authors show that optimal solutions to both problems have a shared geometric representation: a restricted Laguerre diagram. This characterization also creates an algorithmic connection. A solver for either formulation can be adapted to solve the other with comparable precision, allowing algorithmic progress on one problem to carry over to its counterpart.

Building on this structure, the paper extends cost-scaling techniques and gives an algorithm computing the solution to log(1/epsilon) bits of precision in n^{O(d)} log(1/epsilon) time. Here n is the discrete support size and d is the dimension. It also gives an approximation algorithm taking n^{1+o(1)} epsilon^{-O(d)} time. These bounds expose different trade-offs between support size, dimension, and precision rather than providing a single uniformly inexpensive solver.
summary.tldr: A shared geometric characterization connects robust and partial semi-discrete optimal transport and enables new precision-sensitive algorithms.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Robust and Partial Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport

abstract: We study the reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP), where an agent explores the environment to maximize the expected cumulative reward while satisfying a single constraint on the expected total utility value in every episode. While this problem is well understood in the tabular setting, theoretical results for function approximation remain scarce. This paper closes the gap by proposing an RL algorithm for linear CMDPs that achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ regret with an episode-wise zero-violation guarantee. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient, scaling polynomially with problem-dependent parameters while remaining independent of the state space size. Our results significantly improve upon recent linear CMDP algorithms, which either violate the constraint or incur exponential computational costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning where an agent must improve rewards while meeting a constraint during every episode of learning. The constraint concerns expected total utility within each episode. This distinction matters: the stated safety guarantee is about that expected quantity, rather than a claim that every individual random outcome satisfies a pathwise safety condition.

The authors work with constrained Markov decision processes using linear function approximation. Their algorithm achieves regret growing approximately with the square root of the number of episodes, suppressing logarithmic factors, while guaranteeing zero episode-wise constraint violation. The result brings together learning efficiency and continued satisfaction of the specified constraint.

The algorithm is also computationally efficient: its cost scales polynomially with problem-dependent parameters and does not depend on the size of the state space. The paper contrasts this combination with recent linear constrained algorithms that either allow violations or require exponential computation. Its contribution is a theoretical guarantee that safe exploration and tractable computation can coexist in the stated linear setting.
summary.tldr: For linear constrained MDPs, the paper gives a polynomial-time learning algorithm with square-root regret and no violations of the per-episode expected-utility constraint.

title: Provably Efficient RL under Episode-Wise Safety in Constrained MDPs with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: We study the problem of causal function estimation in the Proxy Causal Learning (PCL) framework, where confounders are not observed but proxies for the confounders are available. Two main approaches have been proposed: outcome bridge-based and treatment bridge-based methods. In this work, we propose two kernel-based doubly robust estimators that combine the strengths of both approaches, and naturally handle continuous and high-dimensional variables. Our identification strategy builds on a recent density ratio-free method for treatment bridge-based PCL; furthermore, in contrast to previous approaches, it does not require indicator functions or kernel smoothing over the treatment variable. These properties make it especially well-suited for continuous or high-dimensional treatments. By using kernel mean embeddings, we propose the first density-ratio free doubly robust estimators for proxy causal learning, which have closed form solutions and strong uniform consistency guarantees. Our estimators outperform existing methods on PCL benchmarks, including a prior doubly robust method that requires both kernel smoothing and density ratio estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal function estimation when confounding variables are hidden but measurements that serve as proxies for them are available. Within proxy causal learning, two existing approaches use outcome bridges and treatment bridges. The authors develop two kernel-based, doubly robust estimators that combine these approaches while accommodating continuous and high-dimensional variables.

The new estimators also avoid indicator functions and kernel smoothing over the treatment variable. Those features matter particularly for treatments that vary continuously or have many dimensions. Kernel mean embeddings provide the mathematical representation used to construct the estimators, and both have closed-form solutions.

The paper establishes strong uniform consistency guarantees and reports better performance than existing methods on proxy causal learning benchmarks. These comparisons include an earlier doubly robust approach that requires both density-ratio estimation and kernel smoothing. The contribution is a combination of theoretical guarantees and a formulation that removes those estimation components, broadening the practical appeal of combining outcome and treatment bridges.
summary.tldr: Two kernel-based estimators combine outcome and treatment bridges for proxy causal learning without density-ratio estimation or smoothing over treatments.

title: Density Ratio-Free Doubly Robust Proxy Causal Learning

abstract: We introduce MMAR, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the deep reasoning capabilities of Audio-Language Models (ALMs) across massive multi-disciplinary tasks. MMAR comprises 1,000 meticulously curated audio-question-answer triplets, collected from real-world internet videos and refined through iterative error corrections and quality checks to ensure high quality. Unlike existing benchmarks that are limited to specific domains of sound, music, or speech, MMAR extends them to a broad spectrum of real-world audio scenarios, including mixed-modality combinations of sound, music, and speech. Each question in MMAR is hierarchically categorized across four reasoning layers: Signal, Perception, Semantic, and Cultural, with additional sub-categories within each layer to reflect task diversity and complexity. To further foster research in this area, we annotate every question with a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationale to promote future advancements in audio reasoning. Each item in the benchmark demands multi-step deep reasoning beyond surface-level understanding. Moreover, a part of the questions requires graduate-level perceptual and domain-specific knowledge, elevating the benchmark's difficulty and depth. We evaluate MMAR using a broad set of models, including Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), Large Audio Reasoning Models (LARMs), Omni Language Models (OLMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), with audio caption inputs. The performance of these models on MMAR highlights the benchmark's challenging nature, and our analysis further reveals critical limitations of understanding and reasoning capabilities among current models. These findings underscore the urgent need for greater research attention in audio-language reasoning, including both data and algorithm innovation. We hope MMAR will serve as a catalyst for future advances in this important but little-explored area.

paragraphs: MMAR evaluates reasoning about audio across speech, music, other sounds, and combinations of these sources. It contains 1,000 audio-question-answer examples drawn from real-world internet videos and refined through repeated corrections and quality checks. The questions require multiple reasoning steps beyond recognizing a sound or describing an immediately apparent event.

Every example also includes a chain-of-thought rationale. Some questions require graduate-level perceptual or specialized domain knowledge, making the benchmark demanding along both reasoning and knowledge dimensions.

The authors evaluate a broad range of audio, multimodal, language, and reasoning models, including evaluations with audio-caption inputs. Their results and analysis identify shortcomings in current understanding and reasoning capabilities. MMAR consequently offers a structured way to examine challenging audio reasoning across domains, while its mixed audio scenarios broaden evaluation beyond benchmarks restricted to speech, music, or sound alone.
summary.tldr: MMAR provides 1,000 curated, multi-step audio reasoning questions that expose limitations across a broad range of evaluated models.

title: MMAR: A Challenging Benchmark for Deep Reasoning in Speech, Audio, Music, and Their Mix

abstract: Transformer language models have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities in natural language domains, yet we lack a fine-grained understanding of how such generalization arises. In this paper, we investigate length generalization—the ability to extrapolate from shorter to longer inputs—through the lens of \textit{task transfer}. We find that length generalization can be \textit{transferred} across related tasks. That is, training a model with a longer and related auxiliary task can lead the model to generalize to unseen and longer inputs from some other target task. We demonstrate this length generalization transfer across a diverse suite of algorithmic tasks, including arithmetic operations, string transformations, and maze navigation. Our results show that transformer models can inherit generalization capabilities from similar tasks when trained jointly. Moreover, we observe similar transfer effects in pretrained language models, suggesting that pretraining equips models with reusable computational scaffolding that facilitates extrapolation in downstream settings. Finally, we provide initial mechanistic evidence that length generalization transfer correlates with the re-use of the same attention heads between the tasks. Together, our findings deepen our understanding of how transformers generalize to out-of-distribution inputs and highlight the compositional reuse of inductive structure across tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a transformer can learn to handle longer inputs on one task through experience with a related task. The central finding is that training on a longer auxiliary task can enable generalization to previously unseen lengths on a target task. This makes task relationships part of the explanation for length generalization.

The authors demonstrate the transfer across algorithmic problems involving arithmetic, string transformations, and maze navigation. Joint training allows models to inherit some generalization capabilities from similar tasks. Related effects also appear in pretrained language models, suggesting that pretraining can provide reusable computational structure for downstream extrapolation.

An initial mechanistic analysis finds that transfer correlates with reuse of the same attention heads across tasks. This is evidence of an association, rather than a complete causal account of transfer. Taken together, the findings support a view in which transformers can reuse learned computational structure across related tasks, helping explain some successes on inputs longer than those seen for a particular target task.
summary.tldr: Transformers can transfer length generalization from longer related tasks, with initial evidence linking transfer to shared attention heads.

title: Extrapolation by Association: Length Generalization Transfer In Transformers

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate advanced reasoning abilities, enabling robots to understand natural language instructions and generate high-level plans with appropriate grounding. However, LLM hallucinations present a significant challenge, often leading to overconfident yet potentially misaligned or unsafe plans. While researchers have explored uncertainty estimation to improve the reliability of LLM-based planning, existing studies have not sufficiently differentiated between epistemic and intrinsic uncertainty, limiting the effectiveness of uncertainty estimation. In this paper, we present Combined Uncertainty estimation for Reliable Embodied planning (CURE), which decomposes the uncertainty into epistemic and intrinsic uncertainty, each estimated separately. Furthermore, epistemic uncertainty is subdivided into task clarity and task familiarity for more accurate evaluation. The overall uncertainty assessments are obtained using random network distillation and multi-layer perceptron regression heads driven by LLM features. We validated our approach in two distinct experimental settings: kitchen manipulation and tabletop rearrangement experiments. The results show that, compared to existing methods, our approach yields uncertainty estimates that are more closely aligned with the actual execution outcomes. The code is at https://github.com/Firesuiry/CURE.

paragraphs: Language models can turn natural-language instructions into high-level robot plans, but their apparent confidence may accompany misaligned or unsafe plans. This paper studies how to make uncertainty estimates better reflect execution outcomes. Its premise is that different sources of uncertainty should be distinguished when assessing a proposed plan.

CURE separates epistemic uncertainty from intrinsic uncertainty and estimates each independently. It further divides epistemic uncertainty into task clarity and task familiarity, distinguishing whether the task is clearly specified from whether it is familiar. The framework obtains its assessments using random network distillation and multilayer perceptron regression heads driven by language-model features.

The authors evaluate CURE in kitchen manipulation and tabletop rearrangement experiments. Compared with existing methods, its uncertainty estimates align more closely with what happens when plans are executed. This finding supports decomposing uncertainty as a useful route to more informative confidence assessments. The stated result concerns the quality of those assessments, providing a basis for understanding when a language-model-generated robot plan may be unreliable.
summary.tldr: CURE separates sources of uncertainty in LLM-generated robot plans to produce estimates that better match actual execution outcomes.

title: Towards Reliable LLM-based Robots Planning via Combined Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: Modern large-language models often face communication bottlenecks on current hardware rather than computational limitations. *Multi-head latent attention (MLA)* addresses this by compressing the key-value cache using low-rank matrices, while the Absorb operation prevents the KV cache from reverting to its original size, significantly boosting both training and inference speed. Despite the success of DeepSeek V2/V3/R1, most model providers have heavily invested in optimizing GQA-based models and, therefore, lack strong incentives to retrain MLA-based models from scratch. This paper demonstrates that MLA provides superior expressive power compared to GQA with the same KV cache overhead, thereby offering a rationale for transitioning from GQA to MLA. In addition, we introduce TransMLA, a framework that seamlessly converts any GQA-based pre-trained model (e.g., LLaMA, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral/Mixtral) into an MLA-based model. For the first time, our method enables *direct conversion of these models into a format compatible with DeepSeek's codebase*, allowing them to fully leverage the existing, highly-optimized support for the DeepSeek architecture within inference engines like vLLM and SGlang. By compressing 93\% of the KV cache in LLaMA-2-7B, we achieve a **10x speedup** with an 8K context length while maintaining meaningful output. Moreover, the model requires only **6B tokens** for fine-tuning to recover comparable performance across multiple benchmarks. TransMLA provides a practical path for migrating GQA-based models to the MLA structure, and when combined with DeepSeek’s advanced optimizations—such as FP8 quantization and Multi-Token Prediction—further inference acceleration can be achieved.

paragraphs: Language-model speed can be limited by moving stored information through hardware. Multi-head latent attention, or MLA, addresses this by compressing the key-value cache with low-rank matrices. Its Absorb operation preserves that compressed form. TransMLA offers a way to move pretrained grouped-query attention models into this architecture without beginning training from scratch.

The paper establishes greater expressive power for MLA than grouped-query attention at the same cache overhead. It then introduces a conversion framework that produces models compatible with DeepSeek’s codebase. That compatibility matters because converted models can use existing optimized inference support in engines such as vLLM and SGlang, linking the architectural change with practical deployment infrastructure.

For LLaMA-2-7B, the authors report 93% cache compression and a tenfold speedup at an 8K context length while retaining meaningful output. Recovering comparable performance across multiple benchmarks requires six billion fine-tuning tokens. These are distinct reported milestones: meaningful generation after compression and benchmark recovery through fine-tuning. The authors also describe further acceleration opportunities through additional DeepSeek optimizations.
summary.tldr: TransMLA converts pretrained grouped-query attention models to compressed latent attention compatible with DeepSeek infrastructure, with fine-tuning used to recover comparable benchmark performance.

title: TransMLA: Migrating GQA Models to MLA with Full DeepSeek Compatibility and Speedup

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved considerable accuracy in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) from static images. However, their efficacy in video OCR is significantly diminished due to factors such as motion blur, temporal variations, and visual effects inherent in video content. To provide clearer guidance for training practical MLLMs, we introduce MME-VideoOCR benchmark, which encompasses a comprehensive range of video OCR application scenarios. MME-VideoOCR features 10 task categories comprising 25 individual tasks and spans 44 diverse scenarios. These tasks extend beyond text recognition to incorporate deeper comprehension and reasoning of textual content within videos. The benchmark consists of 1,464 videos with varying resolutions, aspect ratios, and durations, along with 2,000 meticulously curated, manually annotated question-answer pairs. We evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs on MME-VideoOCR, revealing that even the best-performing model (Gemini-2.5 Pro) achieves only an accuracy of 73.7%. Fine-grained analysis indicates that while existing MLLMs demonstrate strong performance on tasks where relevant texts are contained within a single or few frames, they exhibit limited capability in effectively handling tasks that demand holistic video comprehension. These limitations are especially evident in scenarios that require spatio-temporal reasoning, cross-frame information integration, or resistance to language prior bias. Our findings also highlight the importance of high-resolution visual input and sufficient temporal coverage for reliable OCR in dynamic video scenarios.

paragraphs: Reading text in video involves more than recognizing letters in a still image. Motion blur, changing appearances, and visual effects can interfere with recognition, while some questions require combining information across time. MME-VideoOCR evaluates both text reading and deeper understanding of textual content within videos.

The benchmark contains 1,464 videos and 2,000 manually annotated question-answer pairs. Its coverage includes 10 task categories, 25 tasks, and 44 scenarios, with videos varying in resolution, shape, and duration. This variety supports analysis of where models succeed or fail across different demands of video-based text understanding.

Across 18 evaluated multimodal models, the highest accuracy is 73.7%, achieved by Gemini-2.5 Pro. Models perform relatively well when relevant text appears in one or a few frames, but struggle more with holistic understanding, spatial and temporal reasoning, and combining information across frames. The analysis also identifies difficulty resisting language-based expectations. The findings emphasize the value of sufficiently detailed visual inputs and enough temporal coverage to support reliable answers about video text.
summary.tldr: MME-VideoOCR reveals that strong text recognition in individual frames does not reliably extend to understanding text across a video.

title: MME-VideoOCR: Evaluating OCR-Based Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs in Video Scenarios

abstract: Graph Neural Networks \texttt{(GNNs)} excel at jointly modeling node features and topology, yet their \emph{black-box} nature limits their adoption in real-world applications where interpretability is desired. Inspired by the success of interpretable Neural Additive Models \texttt{(NAM)} for tabular data, Graph Neural Additive Network \texttt{(GNAN)} extends the additive modeling approach to graph data to overcome limitations of GNNs. While being interpretable, \texttt{GNAN} representation learning overlooks the importance of local aggregation and more importantly suffers from parameter complexity. To mitigate the above challenges, we introduce Graph Neural Additive Model with Random Fourier Features (\texttt{G-NAMRFF}), a lightweight, self‐interpretable graph additive architecture. \texttt{G-NAMRFF} represents each node embedding as the sum of feature‐wise contributions where contributions are modeled via a \emph{Gaussian process} \texttt{(GP)} with a graph- and feature-aware kernel. Specifically, we construct a kernel using Radial Basis Function (\texttt{RBF}) with graph structure induced by Laplacian and learnable Finite Impulse Response (\texttt{FIR}) filter. We approximate the kernel using Random Fourier Features (\texttt{RFFs}) which transforms the \texttt{GP} prior to a Bayesian formulation, which are subsequently learnt using a single layer neural network with size equal to number of \texttt{RFF} features. \texttt{G-NAMRFF} is light weight with $168\times$ fewer parameters compared to \texttt{GNAN}. Despite its compact size, \texttt{G-NAMRFF} matches or outperforms state-of-the-art \texttt{GNNs} and \texttt{GNAN} on node and graph classification tasks, delivering real-time interpretability without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph models combine node attributes with connections between nodes, but their predictions can be difficult to interpret. Additive graph models make individual feature contributions more explicit, yet the prior GNAN approach has substantial parameter demands and overlooks local aggregation. G-NAMRFF aims to preserve that interpretability while improving efficiency and the use of graph structure.

Each node representation is expressed as a sum of feature-specific contributions. These contributions are modeled through a Gaussian process with a kernel that incorporates both features and graph information. The kernel combines a radial basis function with structure induced by the graph Laplacian and a learnable finite impulse response filter. Random Fourier features approximate this kernel, producing a Bayesian formulation learned with a single-layer neural network.

The authors report 168 times fewer parameters than GNAN. Despite its smaller size, G-NAMRFF matches or exceeds state-of-the-art GNNs and GNAN on evaluated node and graph classification tasks. Its additive construction also provides real-time interpretability. The results suggest that explicit feature contributions and graph-aware modeling can coexist with compact representations and competitive classification performance.
summary.tldr: G-NAMRFF combines interpretable feature contributions with graph-aware kernels, reporting competitive accuracy with 168 times fewer parameters than GNAN.

title: Interpretable and Parameter Efficient Graph Neural Additive Models with Random Fourier Features

abstract: Monitoring chemical processes is essential to prevent catastrophic failures, optimize costs and profits, and ensure the safety of employees and the environment. A key component of modern monitoring systems is the automated detection of anomalies in sensor data over time, called time series, enabling partial automation of plant operation and adding additional layers of supervision to crucial components. The development of anomaly detection methods in this domain is challenging, since real chemical process data are usually proprietary, and simulated data are generally not a sufficient replacement. In this paper, we present NoBOOM, the first collection of datasets for anomaly detection in real-world chemical process data, including labeled data from a running process at our industry partner BASF SE — one of the world’s leading chemical companies — and several chemical processes run in laboratory‑scale and pilot‑scale plants. While we are not able to share every detail about the industrial process, for the laboratory‑ and pilot‑scale plants, we provide comprehensive information on plant configuration, process operation, and, in particular, anomaly events, enabling a differentiated analysis of anomaly detection methods. To demonstrate the complexity of the benchmark, we analyze the data with regard to common issues of time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) benchmarks, including potential triviality and bias.

For the smaller plants, the authors provide detailed information about equipment configuration, process operation, and anomaly events. This context supports more differentiated analysis of detection methods by connecting sensor patterns to the processes and events that produced them.

The contribution supplies real-process evidence and contextual documentation for studying anomaly detection in a domain where representative public data are difficult to obtain.
summary.tldr: NoBOOM supplies labeled real chemical-process data and process context for evaluating industrial anomaly detection.

title: NoBOOM: Chemical Process Datasets for Industrial Anomaly Detection

abstract: The rapid extension of context windows in large vision-language models has given rise to long-context vision-language models (LCVLMs), which are capable of handling hundreds of images with interleaved text tokens in a single forward pass. In this work, we introduce MMLongBench, the first benchmark covering a diverse set of long-context vision-language tasks, to evaluate LCVLMs effectively and thoroughly. MMLongBench is composed of 13,331 examples spanning five different categories of downstream tasks, such as Visual RAG and Many-Shot ICL. It also provides broad coverage of image types, including various natural and synthetic images. To assess the robustness of the models to different input lengths, all examples are delivered at five standardized input lengths (8K-128K tokens) via a cross-modal tokenization scheme that combines vision patches and text tokens. Through a thorough benchmarking of 46 closed-source and open-source LCVLMs, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the current models' vision-language long-context ability. Our results show that: i) performance on a single task is a weak proxy for overall long-context capability; ii) both closed-source and open-source models face challenges in long-context vision-language tasks, indicating substantial room for future improvement; iii) models with stronger reasoning ability tend to exhibit better long-context performance. By offering wide task coverage, various image types, and rigorous length control, MMLongBench provides the missing foundation for diagnosing and advancing the next generation of LCVLMs.

Both groups struggle, while stronger reasoning ability tends to accompany better long-context performance. This relationship is an observed tendency. The benchmark's breadth and length controls make it useful for identifying which abilities hold up as mixed visual and textual inputs grow.
summary.tldr: MMLongBench tests long-context vision-language models across varied tasks and input lengths, revealing uneven capabilities and substantial remaining challenges.

title: MMLongBench: Benchmarking Long-Context Vision-Language Models Effectively and Thoroughly

abstract: Unlocking deep and interpretable biological reasoning from complex genomic data remains a major AI challenge limiting scientific progress. While current DNA foundation models excel at representing sequences, they struggle with multi-step reasoning and lack transparent, biologically meaningful explanations. BioReason addresses this by tightly integrating a DNA foundation model with a large language model (LLM), enabling the LLM to directly interpret and reason over genomic information. Through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, BioReason learns to produce logical, biologically coherent deductions. It achieves major performance gains, boosting KEGG-based disease pathway prediction accuracy from 86% to 98% and improving variant effect prediction by an average of 15% over strong baselines. BioReason can reason over unseen biological entities and explain its decisions step by step, offering a transformative framework for interpretable, mechanistic AI in biology. All data, code, and checkpoints are available at [https://github.com/bowang-lab/BioReason](https://github.com/bowang-lab/BioReason).

paragraphs: DNA foundation models can represent genomic sequences effectively, but those representations do not by themselves provide multistep biological reasoning or understandable explanations. BioReason tackles this gap by tightly combining a DNA foundation model with a large language model. The language model can then interpret genomic information as part of its reasoning process.

The system is trained through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to produce deductions that are logical and biologically coherent. This connects sequence representation with explanations of biological predictions. The intended benefit is a model that can work through relationships in genomic information and present its decisions as a sequence of reasoning steps.

The authors report that accuracy on KEGG-based disease pathway prediction rises from 86% to 98%, alongside an average 15% improvement in variant effect prediction over strong baselines. They also report reasoning over biological entities not seen during training and step-by-step explanations. These findings support the approach as a way to combine improved predictive performance with more interpretable biological reasoning on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: BioReason integrates a DNA model with an LLM to improve biological predictions and produce step-by-step explanations.

title: BioReason: Incentivizing Multimodal Biological Reasoning within a DNA-LLM Model

abstract: Real-world scenes, such as those in ScanNet, are difficult to capture, with highly limited data available. Generating realistic scenes with varied object poses remains an open and challenging task. In this work, we propose FactoredScenes, a framework that synthesizes realistic 3D scenes by leveraging the underlying structure of rooms while learning the variation of object poses from lived-in scenes. We introduce a factored representation that decomposes scenes into hierarchically organized concepts of room programs and object poses. To encode structure, FactoredScenes learns a library of functions capturing reusable layout patterns from which scenes are drawn, then uses large language models to generate high-level programs, regularized by the learned library. To represent scene variations, FactoredScenes learns a program-conditioned model to hierarchically predict object poses, and retrieves and places 3D objects in a scene. We show that FactoredScenes generates realistic, real-world rooms that are difficult to distinguish from real ScanNet scenes.
