paragraphs: Real indoor scenes are difficult to capture, leaving limited data for learning how to generate believable rooms. A useful generator must represent both room organization and variation in how objects are positioned. FactoredScenes addresses these requirements by separating high-level room programs from object poses within a hierarchical scene representation.

To learn room structure, the framework builds a library of functions representing reusable layout patterns. A language model generates high-level programs, with the learned library regularizing those programs toward the captured patterns. This gives scene generation a structured vocabulary for organizing rooms rather than treating every arrangement as an unrelated example.

A separate model learns pose variation from lived-in scenes and predicts object poses hierarchically, conditioned on the room program. The system then retrieves three-dimensional objects and places them in the scene. The authors report generated rooms that are difficult to distinguish from real ScanNet scenes. Their results support combining reusable layout structure with learned pose variation as a way to synthesize realistic indoor environments from limited real-world data.
summary.tldr: FactoredScenes generates realistic rooms by combining language-model programs grounded in learned layout libraries with hierarchical object-pose prediction.

title: From Programs to Poses: Factored Real-World Scene Generation via Learned Program Libraries

abstract: Recent studies reveal that Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong sequential reasoning capabilities, allowing them to replace specialized time-series models and serve as foundation models for complex time-series analysis. To activate the capabilities of LLMs for time-series tasks, numerous studies have attempted to bridge the gap between time series and linguistics by aligning textual representations with time-series patterns. However, it is a non-trivial endeavor to losslessly capture the infinite time-domain variability using natural language, leading to suboptimal alignment performance. Beyond representation, contextual differences, where semantics in time series are conveyed by consecutive points, unlike in text by individual tokens, are often overlooked by existing methods. To address these, we propose S$^2$TS-LLM, a simple yet effective framework to repurpose LLMs for universal time series analysis through the following two main paradigms: (i) a spectral symbolization paradigm transforms time series into frequency-domain representations characterized by a fixed number of components and prominent amplitudes, which enables a limited set of symbols to effectively abstract key frequency features; (ii) a contextual segmentation paradigm partitions the sequence into blocks based on temporal patterns and reassigns positional encodings accordingly, thereby mitigating the structural mismatch between time series and natural language. Together, these paradigms bootstrap the LLMs' perception of temporal patterns and structures, effectively bridging time series and linguistics. Extensive experiments show that S$^2$TS-LLM can serve as a powerful time series analyzer, outperforming state-of-the-art methods across time series tasks.

paragraphs: S²TS-LLM addresses a mismatch between language models and time series: meaningful temporal patterns often span consecutive measurements, whereas text is organized around tokens. Simply describing measurements in words can also struggle to capture the variety of possible signals. The paper therefore changes both how a time series is represented and how its context is organized before asking a language model to analyze it.

The first component converts the signal into frequency-domain features, using a fixed number of components and prominent amplitudes. A limited vocabulary of symbols can then summarize key frequency patterns. The second component groups the sequence into blocks according to temporal patterns and adjusts positional encodings to reflect those groups. Together, these steps make signal content and temporal organization more compatible with the model's input structure.

The reported experiments find that this framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods across time-series tasks. The contribution is a coordinated representation strategy: symbolization abstracts frequency information, while segmentation addresses how neighboring observations carry meaning. These findings support repurposing language models for time-series analysis through both changes.
summary.tldr: S²TS-LLM combines frequency-based symbols and temporal segmentation to improve language-model analysis of time series.

title: Bridging Time and Linguistics: LLMs as Time Series Analyzer through Symbolization and Segmentation

abstract: People continuously perceive and interact with their surroundings based on underlying intentions that drive their exploration and behaviors. While research in egocentric user and scene understanding has focused primarily on motion and contact-based interaction, forecasting human visual perception itself remains less explored despite its fundamental role in guiding human actions and its implications for AR/VR and assistive technologies. We address the challenge of egocentric 3D visual span forecasting, predicting where a person's visual perception will focus next within their three-dimensional environment. To this end, we propose EgoSpanLift, a novel method that transforms egocentric visual span forecasting from 2D image planes to 3D scenes. EgoSpanLift converts SLAM-derived keypoints into gaze-compatible geometry and extracts volumetric visual span regions. We further combine EgoSpanLift with 3D U-Net and unidirectional transformers, enabling spatio-temporal fusion to efficiently predict future visual span in the 3D grid. In addition, we curate a comprehensive benchmark from raw egocentric multisensory data, creating a testbed with 364.6K samples for 3D visual span forecasting. Our approach outperforms competitive baselines for egocentric gaze anticipation and 3D localization, while achieving comparable results even when projected back onto 2D image planes without additional 2D-specific training.

paragraphs: This paper predicts where a person’s visual attention will focus next in their three-dimensional surroundings. It extends egocentric understanding beyond motion and physical interaction to forecasting visual perception itself. The task is relevant to systems such as augmented reality, virtual reality, and assistive technologies that could benefit from anticipating what a user will look at.

It converts keypoints obtained through simultaneous localization and mapping into geometry compatible with gaze, then extracts volumetric regions representing visual span. The authors also build a benchmark containing 364.6 thousand samples from raw egocentric multisensory data. Their method outperforms competitive baselines for gaze anticipation and three-dimensional localization. When its predictions are projected back onto image planes, it achieves comparable results without additional training specific to two-dimensional prediction. This suggests that the three-dimensional formulation can support scene-level forecasting while retaining usefulness for image-based evaluation.
summary.tldr: EgoSpanLift forecasts future visual attention in 3D by combining gaze-compatible scene geometry with spatial and temporal modeling.

title: Gaze Beyond the Frame: Forecasting Egocentric 3D Visual Span

abstract: Generative modeling, representation learning, and classification are three core problems in machine learning (ML), yet their state-of-the-art (SoTA) solutions remain largely disjoint. In this paper, we ask: Can a unified principle address all three? Such unification could simplify ML pipelines and foster greater synergy across tasks. We introduce Latent Zoning Network (LZN) as a step toward this goal. At its core, LZN creates a shared Gaussian latent space that encodes information across all tasks. Each data type (e.g., images, text, labels) is equipped with an encoder that maps samples to disjoint latent zones, and a decoder that maps latents back to data. ML tasks are expressed as compositions of these encoders and decoders: for example, label-conditional image generation uses a label encoder and image decoder; image embedding uses an image encoder; classification uses an image encoder and label decoder. We demonstrate the promise of LZN in three increasingly complex scenarios: (1) LZN can enhance existing models (image generation): When combined with the SoTA Rectified Flow model, LZN improves FID on CIFAR10 from 2.76 to 2.59—without modifying the training objective. (2) LZN can solve tasks independently (representation learning): LZN can implement unsupervised representation learning without auxiliary loss functions, outperforming the seminal MoCo and SimCLR methods by 9.3% and 0.2%, respectively, on downstream linear classification on ImageNet. (3) LZN can solve multiple tasks simultaneously (joint generation and classification): With image and label encoders/decoders, LZN performs both tasks jointly by design, improving FID and achieving SoTA classification accuracy on CIFAR10. The code and trained models are available at https://github.com/microsoft/latent-zoning-networks. The project website is at https://zinanlin.me/blogs/latent_zoning_networks.html.

paragraphs: Generation, representation learning, and classification often rely on separate model designs. Latent Zoning Network explores a shared organizing principle for all three. It creates a Gaussian latent space with disjoint zones, using an encoder and decoder for each data type, such as images or labels.

Tasks become different combinations of those components. A label encoder followed by an image decoder generates a class-conditioned image. An image encoder produces a representation, while an image encoder followed by a label decoder performs classification. This makes the relationship among tasks explicit within the architecture instead of treating each as an unrelated pipeline.

The authors demonstrate three uses. Added to Rectified Flow, LZN improves CIFAR10 FID from 2.76 to 2.59 without changing the training objective. For unsupervised representation learning, it outperforms MoCo and SimCLR on downstream ImageNet linear classification without auxiliary losses. A joint image-and-label version also improves generation FID and achieves state-of-the-art CIFAR10 classification accuracy. These results establish the promise of the shared design across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Latent Zoning Network combines encoders and decoders in a shared latent space to support generation, representation learning, and classification.

title: Latent Zoning Network: A Unified Principle for Generative Modeling, Representation Learning, and Classification

abstract: When dealing with subjective, noisy, or otherwise nebulous features, the “wisdom of crowds” suggests that one may benefit from multiple judgments of the same feature on the same object. We give theoretically-motivated ""feature multi-selection"" algorithms that choose, among a large set of candidate features, not only which features to judge but how many times to judge each one. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for linear regression on a crowdsourced learning task of predicting people’s height and weight from photos, using features such as ""gender"" and ""estimated weight"" as well as culturally fraught ones such as ""attractive"".
originalAbstract: When dealing with subjective, noisy, or otherwise nebulous features, the “wisdom of crowds” suggests that one may benefit from multiple judgments of the same feature on the same object. We give theoretically-motivated ""feature multi-selection"" algorithms that choose, among a large set of candidate features, not only which features to judge but how many times to judge each one. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for linear regression on a crowdsourced learning task of predicting people’s height and weight from photos, using features such as ""gender"" and ""estimated weight"" as well as culturally fraught ones such as ""attractive"".

paragraphs: Some learning features come from human judgments rather than precise measurements. Such judgments can be subjective, noisy, or difficult to define consistently. The paper starts from the possibility that asking several people to judge the same feature on the same object can be useful. This makes repeated measurement a meaningful part of feature selection.

The proposed feature multi-selection algorithms make two connected decisions: which features to obtain and how many judgments to collect for each. The authors describe these algorithms as theoretically motivated. Their formulation extends the usual choice of a feature subset by allowing different amounts of repetition across features, so selecting a feature does not settle how it should be measured.

The approach is demonstrated with linear regression on a crowdsourced task predicting height and weight from photographs. The candidate features include gender judgments, estimated weight, and culturally subjective attractiveness judgments. The reported results demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in that task. They support considering repeated judgments during selection without establishing that every subjective feature benefits equally from repetition.
summary.tldr: Feature multi-selection chooses both which subjective features to collect and how many judgments to obtain for each.

title: Feature Multi-Selection among Subjective Features

abstract: The semi-supervised support vector machine (S3VM) is a maximum-margin classification algorithm based on both labeled and unlabeled data. Training S3VM involves either a combinatorial or non-convex optimization problem and thus finding the global optimal solution is intractable in practice. It has been demonstrated that a key to successfully find a good (local) solution of S3VM is to gradually increase the effect of unlabeled data, a la annealing. However, existing algorithms suffer from the trade-off between the resolution of annealing steps and the computation cost. In this paper, we go beyond this trade-off by proposing a novel training algorithm that efficiently performs annealing with an infinitesimal resolution. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed infinitesimal annealing algorithm tends to produce better solutions with less computation time than existing approaches.

Training S3VM involves either a combinatorial or non-convex optimization problem and thus finding the global optimal solution is intractable in practice. It has been demonstrated that a key to successfully find a good (local) solution of S3VM is to gradually increase the effect of unlabeled data, a la annealing. However, existing algorithms suffer from the trade-off between the resolution of annealing steps and the computation cost. paragraphs: Semi-supervised support vector machines learn maximum-margin classifiers from both labeled and unlabeled examples. Their training problems are combinatorial or non-convex, making global optimization impractical. The paper focuses on finding good local solutions by controlling how strongly unlabeled examples influence training as optimization proceeds.

Gradually increasing that influence, through annealing, had already been shown to help. Existing methods, however, face a trade-off: finer annealing steps require more computation. The authors propose a training algorithm that performs annealing efficiently at infinitesimal resolution, addressing the tension between a gradual progression and the expense of implementing many small steps.

Experiments show that the proposed method tends to find better solutions in less computation time than existing approaches. This is an empirical tendency, rather than a guarantee of reaching a global optimum. The contribution is a way to improve the optimization path for a difficult semi-supervised objective while reducing the computational cost associated with finely resolved annealing.
summary.tldr: Infinitesimal annealing trains semi-supervised SVMs with a gradual unlabeled-data influence and tends to find better solutions faster in experiments.

title: Infinitesimal Annealing for Training Semi-Supervised Support Vector Machines

abstract: This work proposes a simple and computationally efficient estimator for linear regression, and other smooth and strongly convex loss minimization problems. We prove loss approximation guarantees that hold for general distributions, including those with heavy tails. All prior results only hold for estimators which either assume bounded or subgaussian distributions, require prior knowledge of distributional properties, or are not known to be computationally tractable. In the special case of linear regression with possibly heavy-tailed responses and with bounded and well-conditioned covariates in d-dimensions, we show that a random sample of size \tildeO(d\log(1/δ)) suffices to obtain a constant factor approximation to the optimal loss with probability 1-δ, a minimax optimal sample complexity up to log factors. The core technique used in the proposed estimator is a new generalization of the median-of-means estimator to arbitrary metric spaces.

The core technique used in the proposed estimator is a new generalization of the median-of-means estimator to arbitrary metric spaces.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed data challenge learning guarantees that rely on bounded observations or subgaussian distributions. This paper proposes a computationally efficient estimator for linear regression and other smooth, strongly convex loss-minimization problems. Its loss-approximation guarantees cover general distributions, including heavy-tailed ones, broadening the settings in which efficient estimation has theoretical support.

The main technique generalizes the median-of-means estimator to arbitrary metric spaces. This extends a robust estimation principle beyond settings where estimates are simply numbers. The authors position the method against earlier results that required stronger distributional assumptions, prior knowledge of distributional properties, or estimators without established computational tractability.

A specific regression guarantee allows heavy-tailed responses but requires bounded, well-conditioned covariates in d dimensions. Under those conditions, roughly d log(1/δ) samples, up to additional logarithmic factors, suffice for a constant-factor approximation to optimal loss with probability 1−δ. This sample complexity is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. The distinction matters: the stated result controls achieved loss and retains explicit conditions on the covariates.
summary.tldr: A metric-space generalization of median-of-means enables efficient regression with loss guarantees for heavy-tailed data.

title: Heavy-tailed regression with a generalized median-of-means

abstract: We solve principal component regression (PCR), up to a multiplicative accuracy $1+\gamma$, by reducing the problem to $\tilde{O}(\gamma^{-1})$ black-box calls of ridge regression. Therefore, our algorithm does not require any explicit construction of the top principal components, and is suitable for large-scale PCR instances. In contrast, previous result requires $\tilde{O}(\gamma^{-2})$ such black-box calls. We obtain this result by developing a general stable recurrence formula for matrix Chebyshev polynomials, and a degree-optimal polynomial approximation to the matrix sign function. Our techniques may be of independent interests, especially when designing iterative methods.

paragraphs: Principal component regression is commonly associated with finding leading principal components before performing regression. This paper gives an approximation algorithm that avoids explicitly constructing those components. Instead, it reduces the task to repeated calls to a ridge-regression solver, treating that solver as a reusable computational building block.

For multiplicative accuracy 1+gamma, the algorithm requires roughly gamma to the power of minus one ridge-regression calls, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The previous result required roughly gamma to the power of minus two calls under the same notation. The improvement therefore concerns how the number of solver calls grows as the requested accuracy becomes tighter.

The authors obtain the reduction through two approximation tools: a stable recurrence for matrix Chebyshev polynomials and a degree-optimal polynomial approximation to the matrix sign function. Avoiding explicit principal-component construction makes the approach suitable for large-scale PCR instances. The polynomial techniques also have potential independent value, especially for designing iterative methods, although that broader usefulness is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: A stable polynomial construction reduces approximate principal component regression to fewer ridge-regression calls without explicitly computing principal components.

title: Faster Principal Component Regression and Stable Matrix Chebyshev Approximation

abstract: We develop differentially private hypothesis testing methods for the small sample regime. Given a sample $\mathcal{D}$ from a categorical distribution $p$ over some domain $\Sigma$, an explicitly described distribution $q$ over $\Sigma$, some privacy parameter $\epsilon$, accuracy parameter $\alpha$, and requirements $\beta_\mathrm{I}$ and $\beta_\mathrm{II}$ for the type I and type II errors of our test, the goal is to distinguish between $p=q$ and $d_\mathrm{tv}(p,q) \ge \alpha$. We provide theoretical bounds for the sample size $|\mathcal{D}|$ so that our method both satisfies $(\epsilon,0)$-differential privacy, and guarantees $\beta_\mathrm{I}$ and $\beta_\mathrm{II}$ type I and type II errors. We show that differential privacy may come for free in some regimes of parameters, and we always beat the sample complexity resulting from running the $\chi^2$-test with noisy counts, or standard approaches such as repetition for endowing non-private $\chi^2$-style statistics with differential privacy guarantees. We experimentally compare the sample complexity of our method to that of recently proposed methods for private hypothesis testing.

paragraphs: Identity testing asks whether observations come from a specified reference distribution. This paper studies categorical data when the sample is small and the test must also protect privacy. The task is to distinguish exact agreement with the reference from a difference of at least alpha in total variation distance.

The authors give sample-size bounds that jointly ensure pure differential privacy and specified limits on both kinds of testing error. Those errors correspond to rejecting a correct reference distribution and failing to detect a sufficiently different one. The analysis therefore links the amount of data needed to privacy, separation, and error requirements.

In some parameter regimes, privacy may come without an additional sample-complexity cost. The proposed bounds also improve on applying a chi-squared test to noisy counts or using standard repetition approaches to privatize chi-squared-style statistics. The paper experimentally compares sample requirements with recently proposed private tests. Its contribution is a testing method designed around the privacy constraint while keeping data requirements small.
summary.tldr: Private identity tests achieve strong sample-efficiency guarantees, with no additional privacy-related sample cost in some parameter regimes.

title: Priv’IT: Private and Sample Efficient Identity Testing

abstract: Gaussian process modulated Poisson processes provide a flexible framework for modeling spatiotemporal point patterns. So far this had been restricted to one dimension, binning to a pre-determined grid, or small data sets of up to a few thousand data points. Here we introduce Cox process inference based on Fourier features. This sparse representation induces global rather than local constraints on the function space and is computationally efficient. This allows us to formulate a grid-free approximation that scales well with the number of data points and the size of the domain. We demonstrate that this allows MCMC approximations to the non-Gaussian posterior. In practice, we find that Fourier features have more consistent optimization behavior than previous approaches. Our approximate Bayesian method can fit over 100 000 events with complex spatiotemporal patterns in three dimensions on a single GPU.

We demonstrate that this allows MCMC approximations to the non-Gaussian posterior. In practice, we find that Fourier features have more consistent optimization behavior than previous approaches. paragraphs: Gaussian-process-modulated Poisson processes model patterns of events across space and time. Their flexibility comes with difficult inference, and the paper describes earlier approaches as restricted to one dimension, predetermined grids, or datasets containing only a few thousand points. It introduces Fourier-feature-based Cox process inference to extend the scale of this modeling framework.

The Fourier features provide a sparse representation that imposes global constraints on the function space rather than local ones. This representation supports a computationally efficient approximation without dividing the domain into a fixed grid. The authors report that the approach scales well with both the number of observed events and the size of the domain.

The method also permits Markov chain Monte Carlo approximations to the non-Gaussian posterior. In practice, its optimization behavior is more consistent than that of previous approaches. The authors demonstrate fitting more than 100,000 events with complex three-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns on a single GPU. This result shows how the representation can make approximate Bayesian inference feasible for substantially larger event-pattern datasets.
summary.tldr: A sparse Fourier representation enables grid-free Cox process inference for more than 100,000 spatiotemporal events on a single GPU.

title: Large-Scale Cox Process Inference using Variational Fourier Features

abstract: Recent years have seen a flurry of activities in designing provably efficient nonconvex optimization procedures for solving statistical estimation problems. For various problems like phase retrieval or low-rank matrix completion, state-of-the-art nonconvex procedures require proper regularization (e.g. trimming, regularized cost, projection) in order to guarantee fast convergence. When it comes to vanilla procedures such as gradient descent, however, prior theory either recommends highly conservative learning rates to avoid overshooting, or completely lacks performance guarantees. This paper uncovers a striking phenomenon in several nonconvex problems: even in the absence of explicit regularization, gradient descent follows a trajectory staying within a basin that enjoys nice geometry, consisting of points incoherent with the sampling mechanism. This “implicit regularization” feature allows gradient descent to proceed in a far more aggressive fashion without overshooting, which in turn results in substantial computational savings. Focusing on two statistical estimation problems, i.e. solving random quadratic systems of equations and low-rank matrix completion, we establish that gradient descent achieves near-optimal statistical and computational guarantees without explicit regularization. As a byproduct, for noisy matrix completion, we demonstrate that gradient descent enables optimal control of both entrywise and spectral-norm errors.

paragraphs: Nonconvex methods for statistical estimation often use explicit safeguards such as trimming, projection, or regularized objectives to obtain fast-convergence guarantees. For plain gradient descent, earlier theory sometimes required very conservative learning rates or offered no guarantee. This paper explains how gradient descent itself can exhibit a stabilizing effect in several nonconvex estimation problems.

The key finding concerns the path taken by the iterates. Even without explicit regularization, gradient descent stays within a region with favorable geometry whose points remain incoherent with the sampling mechanism. This implicit regularization allows more aggressive progress without overshooting. The explanation links fast convergence to the behavior of the whole optimization trajectory, rather than to an added corrective step.

For noisy matrix completion, they additionally obtain optimal control of entrywise errors and spectral-norm error. These conclusions concern the studied statistical problems. They show why explicit regularization can be unnecessary for strong guarantees in these settings and why plain gradient descent can save substantial computation.
summary.tldr: In the studied nonconvex estimation problems, gradient descent implicitly stays in favorable regions and achieves strong guarantees without explicit regularization.

title: Implicit Regularization in Nonconvex Statistical Estimation: Gradient Descent Converges Linearly for Phase Retrieval and Matrix Completion

abstract: Mean embeddings provide an extremely flexible and powerful tool in machine learning and statistics to represent probability distributions and define a semi-metric (MMD, maximum mean discrepancy; also called N-distance or energy distance), with numerous successful applications. The representation is constructed as the expectation of the feature map defined by a kernel. As a mean, its classical empirical estimator, however, can be arbitrary severely affected even by a single outlier in case of unbounded features. To the best of our knowledge, unfortunately even the consistency of the existing few techniques trying to alleviate this serious sensitivity bottleneck is unknown. In this paper, we show how the recently emerged principle of median-of-means can be used to design estimators for kernel mean embedding and MMD with excessive resistance properties to outliers, and optimal sub-Gaussian deviation bounds under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the sensitivity of kernel mean embeddings to outliers. A mean embedding represents a probability distribution by averaging the features defined by a kernel. These representations also support maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, which measures differences between distributions. Their flexibility makes the reliability of the estimated average an important concern.

When features are unbounded, the usual empirical mean can be distorted arbitrarily severely by even one outlier. The authors replace reliance on that ordinary average with estimators based on the median-of-means principle. They develop this approach for both the kernel mean embedding itself and the associated MMD quantity, addressing robustness at both levels.

The resulting estimators have strong resistance to outliers and optimal sub-Gaussian deviation bounds under mild assumptions. Such bounds control how estimation error behaves probabilistically, giving the robustness claim a theoretical foundation. The contribution is to make distribution representations and comparisons more resistant to corrupted observations while retaining a rigorous statement about estimation accuracy under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Median-of-means estimators make kernel mean embeddings and MMD resistant to outliers, with optimal sub-Gaussian deviation bounds under mild assumptions.

title: MONK Outlier-Robust Mean Embedding Estimation by Median-of-Means

abstract: Experience replay (ER) is a fundamental component of off-policy deep reinforcement learning (RL). ER recalls experiences from past iterations to compute gradient estimates for the current policy, increasing data-efficiency. However, the accuracy of such updates may deteriorate when the policy diverges from past behaviors and can undermine the performance of ER. Many algorithms mitigate this issue by tuning hyper-parameters to slow down policy changes. An alternative is to actively enforce the similarity between policy and the experiences in the replay memory. We introduce Remember and Forget Experience Replay (ReF-ER), a novel method that can enhance RL algorithms with parameterized policies. ReF-ER (1) skips gradients computed from experiences that are too unlikely with the current policy and (2) regulates policy changes within a trust region of the replayed behaviors. We couple ReF-ER with Q-learning, deterministic policy gradient and off-policy gradient methods. We find that ReF-ER consistently improves the performance of continuous-action, off-policy RL on fully observable benchmarks and partially observable flow control problems.

paragraphs: Experience replay improves data efficiency by reusing past interactions to update a reinforcement-learning policy. However, those interactions may become less suitable as the current policy moves away from the behavior that generated them. This paper addresses the resulting deterioration in update accuracy by actively managing the relationship between the policy and replayed experience.

Remember and Forget Experience Replay uses two mechanisms. It skips gradients from experiences that are too unlikely under the current policy, and it constrains policy changes within a trust region of replayed behaviors. The first mechanism filters unsuitable updates; the second regulates how far learning moves away from the experience being reused.

The authors combine the method with Q-learning, deterministic policy gradients, and off-policy gradient methods. They find consistent improvements for continuous-action, off-policy learning on fully observable benchmarks and partially observable flow-control problems. These results support controlling policy–experience compatibility as a useful way to improve replay. The method addresses both which past experiences contribute gradients and how rapidly the policy changes.
summary.tldr: ReF-ER improves experience replay by filtering unlikely past experiences and keeping policy changes close to replayed behaviors.

title: Remember and Forget for Experience Replay

abstract: Ensuring that classifiers are non-discriminatory or fair with respect to a sensitive feature (e.g., race or gender) is a topical problem. Progress in this task requires fixing a definition of fairness, and there have been several proposals in this regard over the past few years. Several of these, however, assume either binary sensitive features (thus precluding categorical or real-valued sensitive groups), or result in non-convex objectives (thus adversely affecting the optimisation landscape). In this paper, we propose a new definition of fairness that generalises some existing proposals, while allowing for generic sensitive features and resulting in a convex objective. The key idea is to enforce that the expected losses (or risks) across each subgroup induced by the sensitive feature are commensurate. We show how this relates to the rich literature on risk measures from mathematical finance. As a special case, this leads to a new convex fairness-aware objective based on minimising the conditional value at risk (CVaR).

paragraphs: Fair classification requires a concrete definition of what fairness means. This paper focuses on the expected prediction losses experienced by groups defined through a sensitive feature, such as race or gender. Its central proposal is that those group-level risks should be commensurate, making differences in predictive loss the basis for the fairness objective.

The formulation addresses two restrictions found in some existing proposals. Definitions built around binary sensitive features do not directly cover more general categories or real-valued features. Other formulations introduce nonconvex objectives that complicate optimization. The authors propose a definition that generalizes some earlier ideas, accommodates generic sensitive features, and yields a convex objective.

They connect this approach to mathematical finance, where risk measures summarize exposure to unfavorable outcomes. That connection provides a framework for constructing fairness-aware learning objectives. One special case minimizes conditional value at risk, or CVaR, and remains convex. The contribution therefore links a particular view of group fairness with an optimization framework that can express it tractably.
summary.tldr: The paper defines fairness through comparable subgroup risks and derives convex learning objectives, including one based on CVaR.

title: Fairness risk measures

abstract: Recent work has argued that neural networks can be understood theoretically by taking the number of channels to infinity, at which point the outputs become Gaussian process (GP) distributed. However, we note that infinite Bayesian neural networks lack a key facet of the behaviour of real neural networks: the fixed kernel, determined only by network hyperparameters, implies that they cannot do any form of representation learning. The lack of representation or equivalently kernel learning leads to less flexibility and hence worse performance, giving a potential explanation for the inferior performance of infinite networks observed in the literature (e.g. Novak et al. 2019). We give analytic results characterising the prior over representations and representation learning in finite deep linear networks. We show empirically that the representations in SOTA architectures such as ResNets trained with SGD are much closer to those suggested by our deep linear results than by the corresponding infinite network. This motivates the introduction of a new class of network: infinite networks with bottlenecks, which inherit the theoretical tractability of infinite networks while at the same time allowing representation learning.

paragraphs: Infinite-width limits make neural networks easier to analyze by relating their outputs to Gaussian processes. The paper identifies a missing capability in infinite Bayesian networks with fixed kernels: they cannot learn representations from data. Their kernels depend only on network hyperparameters, restricting the flexibility available during learning.

The authors suggest this loss of representation learning as a possible explanation for inferior infinite-network performance reported in prior work. They derive analytic results for the distribution of representations and for representation learning in finite deep linear networks. These results describe aspects of finite networks that the corresponding fixed-kernel infinite limit does not retain.

Empirical comparisons show that representations in architectures such as ResNets trained with SGD are closer to those suggested by the finite deep linear analysis than by the corresponding infinite network. Motivated by this evidence, the authors introduce infinite networks with bottlenecks. These models are intended to retain the analytical tractability of infinite networks while allowing representations to be learned.
summary.tldr: Finite-network representation learning helps explain a limitation of fixed-kernel infinite networks and motivates infinite networks with learnable bottleneck representations.

title: Why bigger is not always better: on finite and infinite neural networks

abstract: Modern machine learning models are often trained on examples with noisy labels that hurt performance and are hard to identify. In this paper, we provide an empirical study showing that a simple $k$-nearest neighbor-based filtering approach on the logit layer of a preliminary model can remove mislabeled training data and produce more accurate models than many recently proposed methods. We also provide new statistical guarantees into its efficacy.
originalAbstract: Modern machine learning models are often trained on examples with noisy labels that hurt performance and are hard to identify. In this paper, we provide an empirical study showing that a simple $k$-nearest neighbor-based filtering approach on the logit layer of a preliminary model can remove mislabeled training data and produce more accurate models than many recently proposed methods. We also provide new statistical guarantees into its efficacy.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can reduce a model's accuracy, but identifying those mistakes is itself difficult. This paper investigates a simple filtering approach that uses a preliminary trained model to help locate mislabeled examples. The central idea is to examine neighborhoods in a representation produced by that model, making the model part of the process for improving its training data.

The method applies k-nearest neighbors to the preliminary model's logit layer, the layer containing its prediction scores. This supplies a space in which examples can be compared for filtering. The paper studies whether this neighborhood-based procedure can remove incorrectly labeled training data and thereby support more accurate models. Its focus is a straightforward data-filtering step built around an existing model representation.

The empirical study reports that this approach removes mislabeled examples and produces more accurate models than many recently proposed methods. The authors also provide new statistical guarantees supporting its efficacy. Together, these contributions give both empirical and theoretical support for the filtering strategy, while the comparative accuracy claim remains a finding of the reported study.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor filtering in a preliminary model's logit space can remove mislabeled training examples and improve accuracy.

title: Deep k-NN for Noisy Labels

abstract: Running Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in a decentralized fashion has shown promising results. In this paper we propose Moniqua, a technique that allows decentralized SGD to use quantized communication. We prove in theory that Moniqua communicates a provably bounded number of bits per iteration, while converging at the same asymptotic rate as the original algorithm does with full-precision communication. Moniqua improves upon prior works in that it (1) requires zero additional memory, (2) works with 1-bit quantization, and (3) is applicable to a variety of decentralized algorithms. We demonstrate empirically that Moniqua converges faster with respect to wall clock time than other quantized decentralized algorithms. We also show that Moniqua is robust to very low bit-budgets, allowing $1$-bit-per-parameter communication without compromising validation accuracy when training ResNet20 and ResNet110 on CIFAR10.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent distributes training across participants that exchange information. Reducing the precision of those messages can lower communication costs, but the resulting quantization must still support effective optimization. Moniqua is a technique for adding quantized communication to a variety of decentralized training algorithms.

The authors prove that Moniqua uses a bounded number of communicated bits per iteration while preserving the original algorithm's asymptotic convergence rate with full-precision communication. It requires no additional memory and can operate with one-bit quantization. These properties address communication, storage, and optimization behavior together rather than judging compression by message size alone.

Experiments show faster convergence in wall-clock time than other quantized decentralized algorithms. In training ResNet20 and ResNet110 on CIFAR10, one bit per parameter is sufficient without compromising validation accuracy. This accuracy finding is tied to those experiments, while the convergence result concerns asymptotic rates. Together, they support very low-precision communication as a practical option for the evaluated decentralized training settings.
summary.tldr: Moniqua enables low-bit decentralized SGD communication while preserving asymptotic convergence rates and reporting faster wall-clock convergence.

title: Moniqua: Modulo Quantized Communication in Decentralized SGD

abstract: The multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem is a classical learning task that exemplifies the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. However, standard formulations do not take into account risk. In online decision making systems, risk is a primary concern. In this regard, the mean-variance risk measure is one of the most common objective functions. Existing algorithms for mean-variance optimization in the context of MAB problems have unrealistic assumptions on the reward distributions. We develop Thompson Sampling-style algorithms for mean-variance MAB and provide comprehensive regret analyses for Gaussian and Bernoulli bandits with fewer assumptions. Our algorithms achieve the best known regret bounds for mean-variance MABs and also attain the information-theoretic bounds in some parameter regimes. Empirical simulations show that our algorithms significantly outperform existing LCB-based algorithms for all risk tolerances.

paragraphs: Standard multi-armed bandit formulations emphasize reward while balancing exploration and exploitation. In applications where variability matters, the average reward alone may not capture the decision maker's objective. This paper studies mean-variance bandits, which incorporate risk through an objective that accounts for both expected reward and reward variation.

The authors develop Thompson Sampling-style algorithms for this setting and analyze their regret for Gaussian and Bernoulli reward distributions. Their motivation includes reducing the unrealistic distributional assumptions used by existing mean-variance methods. The analysis therefore addresses both how the algorithms learn and what assumptions support their performance guarantees within these two distribution families.

The algorithms achieve the best known regret bounds reported for mean-variance bandits and reach information-theoretic bounds in some parameter regimes. This optimality claim is restricted to those regimes. Empirical simulations show substantial improvements over existing lower-confidence-bound algorithms across all risk tolerances evaluated. The work extends sampling-based exploration to risk-sensitive objectives while supporting it with both regret analysis and numerical comparisons.
summary.tldr: Thompson Sampling-style methods improve mean-variance bandit regret guarantees and outperform LCB methods in the reported simulations.

title: Thompson Sampling Algorithms for Mean-Variance Bandits

abstract: Agents that learn to select optimal actions represent a prominent focus of the sequential decision-making literature. In the face of a complex environment or constraints on time and resources, however, aiming to synthesize such an optimal policy can become infeasible. These scenarios give rise to an important trade-off between the information an agent must acquire to learn and the sub-optimality of the resulting policy. While an agent designer has a preference for how this trade-off is resolved, existing approaches further require that the designer translate these preferences into a fixed learning target for the agent. In this work, leveraging rate-distortion theory, we automate this process such that the designer need only express their preferences via a single hyperparameter and the agent is endowed with the ability to compute its own learning targets that best achieve the desired trade-off. We establish a general bound on expected discounted regret for an agent that decides what to learn in this manner along with computational experiments that illustrate the expressiveness of designer preferences and even show improvements over Thompson sampling in identifying an optimal policy.

paragraphs: Learning an optimal policy can require more information, time, or resources than an agent can afford. This paper treats the choice of what to learn as part of the decision problem. The goal is to balance the information acquired against the performance lost by accepting a policy that may be suboptimal.

The method uses rate-distortion theory to turn a designer's preference about this trade-off into learning targets. Instead of manually specifying a fixed target, the designer sets a single hyperparameter and the agent computes targets suited to that preference. This moves part of the design burden into the agent's own learning procedure.

The authors establish a general bound on expected discounted regret for agents that select learning targets this way. Computational experiments illustrate how the parameter expresses different preferences and also show improvements over Thompson sampling in identifying an optimal policy. Those experimental improvements suggest that choosing information targets carefully can help even when optimal behavior remains the eventual objective; they are not a universal comparison across all environments.
summary.tldr: A rate-distortion approach lets agents choose learning targets from a single parameter balancing information acquisition against policy suboptimality.

title: Deciding What to Learn: A Rate-Distortion Approach

abstract: We present a novel approach to Bayesian inference and general Bayesian computation that is defined through a sequential decision loop. Our method defines a recursive partitioning of the sample space. It neither relies on gradients nor requires any problem-specific tuning, and is asymptotically exact for any density function with a bounded domain. The output is an approximation to the whole density function including the normalisation constant, via partitions organised in efficient data structures. Such approximations may be used for evidence estimation or fast posterior sampling, but also as building blocks to treat a larger class of estimation problems. The algorithm shows competitive performance to recent state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world problems including parameter inference for gravitational-wave physics.

paragraphs: Bayesian computation often requires both understanding a probability distribution and generating samples from it. This paper approaches those tasks by constructing an approximation to the entire density function, including its normalization constant. That constant supplies the scale needed to turn an unnormalized density into a probability distribution, and is also useful for evidence estimation.

The algorithm operates through a sequence of decisions that recursively partition the sample space. It stores the resulting partitions in efficient data structures, producing a reusable representation of the density. The procedure requires neither gradients nor tuning specific to the problem. For densities defined on bounded domains, the authors establish asymptotic exactness: the approximation becomes exact in the limiting regime.

The resulting representation can support fast posterior sampling, evidence estimation, and other estimation procedures that use density approximations as components. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems, including gravitational-wave parameter inference, show competitive performance against recent leading methods. These findings support recursive partitioning as a practical approach to Bayesian computation, alongside its bounded-domain asymptotic guarantee.
summary.tldr: Recursive partitioning estimates whole probability densities without gradients or problem-specific tuning, with asymptotic exactness on bounded domains.

title: Black-box density function estimation using recursive partitioning

abstract: Multi-modal distributions are commonly used to model clustered data in statistical learning tasks. In this paper, we consider the Mixed Linear Regression (MLR) problem. We propose an optimal transport-based framework for MLR problems, Wasserstein Mixed Linear Regression (WMLR), which minimizes the Wasserstein distance between the learned and target mixture regression models. Through a model-based duality analysis, WMLR reduces the underlying MLR task to a nonconvex-concave minimax optimization problem, which can be provably solved to find a minimax stationary point by the Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) algorithm. In the special case of mixtures of two linear regression models, we show that WMLR enjoys global convergence and generalization guarantees. We prove that WMLR’s sample complexity grows linearly with the dimension of data. Finally, we discuss the application of WMLR to the federated learning task where the training samples are collected by multiple agents in a network. Unlike the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, WMLR directly extends to the distributed, federated learning setting. We support our theoretical results through several numerical experiments, which highlight our framework’s ability to handle the federated learning setting with mixture models.

paragraphs: Mixed linear regression models data generated by several different linear relationships. The challenge is to learn those relationships within a shared mixture model. This paper introduces Wasserstein Mixed Linear Regression, which measures the discrepancy between learned and target mixture regression models using a distance from optimal transport.

The authors use a model-based duality analysis to turn this fitting problem into a minimax optimization problem. Its structure is nonconvex in one part and concave in the other. They prove that gradient descent ascent can reach a minimax stationary point. For the special case of two linear regression components, they establish stronger global convergence and generalization guarantees, and show sample complexity growing linearly with data dimension.

The framework also extends directly to distributed federated learning, where multiple agents hold training samples. The abstract contrasts this extension with expectation-maximization. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and illustrate the framework’s ability to learn mixture models in this distributed setting.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein-based mixture regression supports provable minimax optimization and federated learning, with stronger guarantees for two-component mixtures.

title: A Wasserstein Minimax Framework for Mixed Linear Regression

abstract: Recently, particle-based variational inference (ParVI) methods have gained interest because they can avoid arbitrary parametric assumptions that are common in variational inference. However, many ParVI approaches do not allow arbitrary sampling from the posterior, and the few that do allow such sampling suffer from suboptimality. This work proposes a new method for learning to approximately sample from the posterior distribution. We construct a neural sampler that is trained with the functional gradient of the KL-divergence between the empirical sampling distribution and the target distribution, assuming the gradient resides within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Our generative ParVI (GPVI) approach maintains the asymptotic performance of ParVI methods while offering the flexibility of a generative sampler. Through carefully constructed experiments, we show that GPVI outperforms previous generative ParVI methods such as amortized SVGD, and is competitive with ParVI as well as gold-standard approaches like Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for fitting both exactly known and intractable target distributions.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference approximates a target distribution without the arbitrary parametric assumptions common in other variational methods. However, many particle methods do not provide a way to draw arbitrary new posterior samples. This paper introduces Generative Particle Variational Inference, or GPVI, to combine particle-based inference with a learned generative sampler.

GPVI trains a neural sampler using the functional gradient of the KL divergence between its empirical sampling distribution and the target. The construction assumes that this gradient belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The resulting method maintains the asymptotic performance of particle-based variational inference while providing the flexibility to generate samples through a neural model.

Experiments cover both exactly known and intractable target distributions. GPVI outperforms earlier generative particle methods, including amortized SVGD, and is competitive with particle-based inference and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. These results support the proposed combination in the tested settings: a sampler that can generate additional approximate posterior draws while retaining the distribution-fitting strengths associated with particle-based methods.
summary.tldr: GPVI learns a neural posterior sampler using functional gradients, combining generative sampling flexibility with the asymptotic performance of particle-based inference.

title: Generative Particle Variational Inference via Estimation of Functional Gradients

abstract: Attention-based neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art results on a wide range of tasks. Most such models use deterministic attention while stochastic attention is less explored due to the optimization difficulties or complicated model design. This paper introduces Bayesian attention belief networks, which construct a decoder network by modeling unnormalized attention weights with a hierarchy of gamma distributions, and an encoder network by stacking Weibull distributions with a deterministic-upward-stochastic-downward structure to approximate the posterior. The resulting auto-encoding networks can be optimized in a differentiable way with a variational lower bound. It is simple to convert any models with deterministic attention, including pretrained ones, to the proposed Bayesian attention belief networks. On a variety of language understanding tasks, we show that our method outperforms deterministic attention and state-of-the-art stochastic attention in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, generalization across domains, and robustness to adversarial attacks. We further demonstrate the general applicability of our method on neural machine translation and visual question answering, showing great potential of incorporating our method into various attention-related tasks.

paragraphs: This paper replaces fixed attention weights with a probabilistic model of attention. Most attention networks deterministically decide how much weight to assign to different inputs. The authors investigate stochastic attention, where those weights have distributions, while addressing the optimization difficulties and complicated designs that have made this approach less common.

Their Bayesian attention belief network models unnormalized attention weights through a hierarchy of gamma distributions. A corresponding encoder uses stacked Weibull distributions to approximate the posterior, combining a deterministic upward computation with a stochastic downward computation. This construction supports differentiable optimization through a variational lower bound. The authors also describe conversion of existing deterministic attention models, including pretrained models.

On the language understanding tasks studied, the method improves over deterministic attention and leading stochastic attention approaches in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, cross-domain generalization, and resistance to adversarial attacks. Additional experiments on translation and visual question answering demonstrate applicability beyond language understanding. These findings support probabilistic attention as a practical modeling choice across several attention-based tasks.
summary.tldr: Bayesian attention belief networks make attention probabilistic through a trainable distribution hierarchy, improving several reported measures across attention-based tasks.

title: Bayesian Attention Belief Networks

abstract: We study the problem of learning general {—} i.e., not necessarily homogeneous {—} halfspaces with adversarial label noise under the Gaussian distribution. Prior work has provided a sophisticated polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. In this work, we show that the problem can be solved directly via online gradient descent applied to a sequence of natural non-convex surrogates. This approach yields a simple iterative learning algorithm for general halfspaces with near-optimal sample complexity, runtime, and error guarantee. At the conceptual level, our work establishes an intriguing connection between learning halfspaces with adversarial noise and online optimization that may find other applications.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of learning general {—} i.e., not necessarily homogeneous {—} halfspaces with adversarial label noise under the Gaussian distribution. Prior work has provided a sophisticated polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. In this work, we show that the problem can be solved directly via online gradient descent applied to a sequence of natural non-convex surrogates. This approach yields a simple iterative learning algorithm for general halfspaces with near-optimal sample complexity, runtime, and error guarantee. At the conceptual level, our work establishes an intriguing connection between learning halfspaces with adversarial noise and online optimization that may find other applications.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when some training labels may be adversarially corrupted. It allows general halfspaces, so the boundary need not pass through the origin. The theoretical setting assumes Gaussian-distributed inputs, making that distribution assumption part of the problem addressed by the guarantees.

Earlier work supplied a sophisticated polynomial-time algorithm for this task. The authors show that online gradient descent can instead be applied directly to a sequence of natural nonconvex surrogate objectives. The resulting procedure is a simple iterative learning algorithm, connecting a noisy classification problem to tools from online optimization.

The algorithm achieves near-optimal sample complexity, runtime, and error guarantees. These three aspects concern how much data it needs, how much computation it requires, and the prediction quality it can attain. The broader conceptual contribution is the connection between adversarially noisy halfspace learning and online optimization, which the authors suggest may be useful elsewhere while establishing results for the Gaussian setting studied here.
summary.tldr: Online gradient descent learns general halfspaces under Gaussian inputs and adversarial label noise with near-optimal guarantees.

title: Learning General Halfspaces with Adversarial Label Noise via Online Gradient Descent

abstract: Despite the ubiquitous use of stochastic optimization algorithms in machine learning, the precise impact of these algorithms and their dynamics on generalization performance in realistic non-convex settings is still poorly understood. While recent work has revealed connections between generalization and heavy-tailed behavior in stochastic optimization, they mainly relied on continuous-time approximations; and a rigorous treatment for the original discrete-time iterations is yet to be performed. To bridge this gap, we present novel bounds linking generalization to the lower tail exponent of the transition kernel associated with the optimizer around a local minimum, in both discrete- and continuous-time settings. To achieve this, we first prove a data- and algorithm-dependent generalization bound in terms of the celebrated Fernique-Talagrand functional applied to the trajectory of the optimizer. Then, we specialize this result by exploiting the Markovian structure of stochastic optimizers, and derive bounds in terms of their (data-dependent) transition kernels. We support our theory with empirical results from a variety of neural networks, showing correlations between generalization error and lower tail exponents.

paragraphs: The path taken by a stochastic optimizer may matter for how well a trained model performs beyond its training data. Earlier work connected generalization to heavy-tailed optimization behavior, largely through continuous-time approximations. This paper develops a treatment that also covers the discrete updates used by the original optimization algorithms.

The analysis first bounds generalization using a mathematical quantity called the Fernique-Talagrand functional applied to the optimizer’s trajectory. This makes the bound depend on both the data and the algorithm. The authors then use the optimizer’s Markov structure to express bounds through its transition kernel, which describes how one optimization state leads probabilistically to another.

The resulting bounds connect generalization with the transition kernel’s lower tail exponent around a local minimum, in both discrete and continuous time. Experiments across several neural networks show correlations between these exponents and generalization error. Those correlations support the theoretical direction without establishing that the exponent alone determines performance. The contribution provides a more direct mathematical connection between optimization dynamics and generalization.
summary.tldr: New bounds connect generalization to stochastic optimizer transition kernels and their lower tail exponents, including for discrete-time updates.

title: Generalization Bounds using Lower Tail Exponents in Stochastic Optimizers

abstract: Recent work by Baratin et al. (2021) sheds light on an intriguing pattern that occurs during the training of deep neural networks: some layers align much more with data compared to other layers (where the alignment is defined as the normalize euclidean product of the tangent features matrix and the data labels matrix). The curve of the alignment as a function of layer index (generally) exhibits a ascent-descent pattern where the maximum is reached for some hidden layer. In this work, we provide the first explanation for this phenomenon. We introduce the Equilibrium Hypothesis which connects this alignment pattern to signal propagation in deep neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate an excellent match with the theoretical predictions.

(2021) sheds light on an intriguing pattern that occurs during the training of deep neural networks: some layers align much more with data compared to other layers (where the alignment is defined as the normalize euclidean product of the tangent features matrix and the data labels matrix). The curve of the alignment as a function of layer index (generally) exhibits a ascent-descent pattern where the maximum is reached for some hidden layer. In this work, we provide the first explanation for this phenomenon. We introduce the Equilibrium Hypothesis which connects this alignment pattern to signal propagation in deep neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate an excellent match with the theoretical predictions.

paragraphs: Different layers of a deep neural network can become aligned with the training labels to different degrees. The paper investigates a previously observed pattern: alignment generally rises through part of the network and then falls, reaching its highest value at an intermediate hidden layer. This makes the distribution of learning across depth an explanatory question.

Here, alignment has a specific mathematical meaning. It is measured through a normalized Euclidean product between a layer's tangent-feature matrix and the label matrix. The phenomenon therefore concerns a defined relationship between features and labels, rather than a claim that one layer is universally the most useful. The authors introduce the Equilibrium Hypothesis to connect this pattern with signal propagation through the network.

The paper presents this connection as an explanation for the rise-and-fall shape across layers. Its experiments closely match the theoretical predictions. These findings support studying feature learning together with how signals propagate through depth, because the observed alignment pattern is linked to that propagation rather than described only as an isolated training behavior.
summary.tldr: The Equilibrium Hypothesis links signal propagation to the observed tendency for feature-label alignment to peak at an intermediate network layer.

title: Feature Learning and Signal Propagation in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Accurately estimating personalized treatment effects within a study site (e.g., a hospital) has been challenging due to limited sample size. Furthermore, privacy considerations and lack of resources prevent a site from leveraging subject-level data from other sites. We propose a tree-based model averaging approach to improve the estimation accuracy of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) at a target site by leveraging models derived from other potentially heterogeneous sites, without them sharing subject-level data. To our best knowledge, there is no established model averaging approach for distributed data with a focus on improving the estimation of treatment effects. Specifically, under distributed data networks, our framework provides an interpretable tree-based ensemble of CATE estimators that joins models across study sites, while actively modeling the heterogeneity in data sources through site partitioning. The performance of this approach is demonstrated by a real-world study of the causal effects of oxygen therapy on hospital survival rate and backed up by comprehensive simulation results.

paragraphs: Estimating how a treatment affects different kinds of patients is difficult when a hospital has only a small study population. Other hospitals could provide useful evidence, but privacy considerations and limited resources can prevent sharing individual patient records. This paper proposes combining treatment-effect models across sites to improve estimates for a particular target site.

The method estimates conditional average treatment effects: average treatment effects for people with particular observed characteristics. It combines estimators in an interpretable, tree-based ensemble. Crucially, it also partitions sites to account for differences between their data sources. The approach therefore treats variation across hospitals as something to model explicitly when combining their estimates.

The evidence includes simulations and a real-world study of oxygen therapy's causal effects on hospital survival. These demonstrate the approach's performance in the settings studied. Its practical contribution is a way for a target hospital to benefit from models developed elsewhere without requiring those hospitals to share subject-level data.
summary.tldr: A tree-based ensemble combines treatment-effect models from heterogeneous sites to improve target-site estimates without sharing individual records.

title: A Tree-based Model Averaging Approach for Personalized Treatment Effect Estimation from Heterogeneous Data Sources

abstract: Most of the existing methods for estimating the local intrinsic dimension of a data distribution do not scale well to high dimensional data. Many of them rely on a non-parametric nearest neighbours approach which suffers from the curse of dimensionality. We attempt to address that challenge by proposing a novel approach to the problem: Local Intrinsic Dimension estimation using approximate Likelihood (LIDL). Our method relies on an arbitrary density estimation method as its subroutine, and hence tries to sidestep the dimensionality challenge by making use of the recent progress in parametric neural methods for likelihood estimation. We carefully investigate the empirical properties of the proposed method, compare them with our theoretical predictions, show that LIDL yields competitive results on the standard benchmarks for this problem, and that it scales to thousands of dimensions. What is more, we anticipate this approach to improve further with the continuing advances in the density estimation literature.

paragraphs: Local intrinsic dimension concerns the effective dimensionality of a data distribution near a particular location. Estimating it becomes difficult when observations have many coordinates. Many existing estimators rely on nonparametric nearest-neighbor methods, which struggle with the curse of dimensionality as the surrounding data space grows.

LIDL approaches the problem through approximate likelihood and uses a density estimator as a subroutine. The framework can work with an arbitrary density-estimation method, allowing it to draw on progress in parametric neural likelihood estimation. Its strategy is to use those modeling capabilities to address a scaling problem that affects neighborhood-based approaches.

The authors investigate empirical behavior and compare it with their theoretical predictions. They report competitive results on standard benchmarks and show that the method scales to thousands of dimensions. They also anticipate further gains as density estimation improves. That last point is an expectation about future progress; the demonstrated contribution is the likelihood-based approach and its observed performance at high dimensionality.
summary.tldr: LIDL uses approximate likelihood to estimate local intrinsic dimension, achieving competitive benchmark results and scaling to thousands of dimensions.

title: LIDL: Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation Using Approximate Likelihood

abstract: Label noise in real-world datasets encodes wrong correlation patterns and impairs the generalization of deep neural networks (DNNs). It is critical to find efficient ways to detect corrupted patterns. Current methods primarily focus on designing robust training techniques to prevent DNNs from memorizing corrupted patterns. These approaches often require customized training processes and may overfit corrupted patterns, leading to a performance drop in detection. In this paper, from a more data-centric perspective, we propose a training-free solution to detect corrupted labels. Intuitively, “closer” instances are more likely to share the same clean label. Based on the neighborhood information, we propose two methods: the first one uses “local voting" via checking the noisy label consensuses of nearby features. The second one is a ranking-based approach that scores each instance and filters out a guaranteed number of instances that are likely to be corrupted. We theoretically analyze how the quality of features affects the local voting and provide guidelines for tuning neighborhood size. We also prove the worst-case error bound for the ranking-based method. Experiments with both synthetic and real-world label noise demonstrate our training-free solutions consistently and significantly improve most of the training-based baselines. Code is available at github.com/UCSC-REAL/SimiFeat.

paragraphs: Incorrect labels can teach neural networks misleading relationships. Detecting those labels through model training creates a difficulty: the model may itself memorize the corruption. This paper instead studies detection directly from neighborhood relationships in the available features, avoiding the need to train a predictive model for that detection task.

The first method uses local voting, checking whether an example's noisy label agrees with labels of nearby examples. It rests on the intuition that nearby feature representations are more likely to share a clean label. The second method ranks examples by a score and filters a guaranteed number of examples considered likely to be corrupted; this does not imply every filtered label is wrong.

The authors analyze how feature quality affects local voting, give guidance for choosing neighborhood size, and establish a worst-case error bound for ranking. Experiments with synthetic and real-world noise report consistent, substantial improvements over most training-based baselines. The findings make neighborhood information a useful basis for label inspection when its relationship to clean labels is informative.
summary.tldr: Feature-neighborhood voting and ranking detect corrupted labels without training a predictive model for detection.

title: Detecting Corrupted Labels Without Training a Model to Predict

abstract: We propose constrained causal Bayesian optimization (cCBO), an approach for finding interventions in a known causal graph that optimize a target variable under some constraints. cCBO first reduces the search space by exploiting the graph structure and, if available, an observational dataset; and then solves the restricted optimization problem by modelling target and constraint quantities using Gaussian processes and by sequentially selecting interventions via a constrained expected improvement acquisition function. We propose different surrogate models that enable to integrate observational and interventional data while capturing correlation among effects with increasing levels of sophistication. We evaluate cCBO on artificial and real-world causal graphs showing successful trade off between fast convergence and percentage of feasible interventions.
