title: WildActor: Unconstrained Identity-Preserving Video Generation

abstract: Recent developments in large language models have shown advantages in reallocating a notable share of computational resource from training time to inference time. However, the principles behind inference time scaling are not well understood. In this paper, we introduce an analytically tractable model of inference-time scaling: Bayesian linear regression with a reward-weighted sampler, where the reward is determined from a linear model, modeling LLM-as-a-judge scenario. We study this problem in the high-dimensional regime, where the deterministic equivalents dictate a closed-form expression for the posterior predictive mean and variance. We analyze the generalization error when training data are sampled from a teacher model. We draw $k$ inference-time samples and select via softmax at a temperature applied to a quadratic reward. When the reward is not too different from the teacher, the generalization error decreases monotonically with increasing inference time samples $k$. However, the specific reward that optimizes inference-time selection generally differs from the teacher. In contrast, substantial reward misspecification induces a finite optimal $k$ beyond which more sampling can increase the generalization error. For fixed $k$, there exists an optimal sampling temperature. We experimentally verify these facts in large language model inference with an additional large language model as a judge. In the “best-of-$k$" limit with the teacher as reward, we theoretically show that the generalization error decays as $\Theta(1/k^2)$ and determine the leading coefficient via extreme value theory. These formulas delineate domains where scaling inference-time computation is provably preferable to collecting more data. Finally, we demonstrate that when task difficulty increases, the previously mentioned advantage of inference-time compute degrades.

paragraphs: Generating more candidate answers and asking a judge to select one can improve predictions, but the benefit depends on the judge's reward. This paper analyzes that dependence using Bayesian linear regression with reward-weighted sampling. In a high-dimensional setting, the model yields closed-form expressions for predictive quantities and supports analysis of generalization error.

The authors study selection among k samples using a softmax temperature and a quadratic reward. When the reward is sufficiently close to the data-generating teacher, error decreases as k grows. Substantial reward misspecification instead produces a finite best sample count, beyond which more sampling can worsen error. The best selection reward generally differs from the teacher, and each fixed k has an optimal temperature.

Experiments with language models and a language-model judge verify these behaviors. In the theoretical best-of-k setting with the teacher as reward, error decreases at a rate proportional to 1/k². The analysis identifies conditions where spending computation at inference is preferable to collecting more training data, while showing that this advantage weakens as task difficulty increases.
summary.tldr: A tractable model shows when judge-based sampling improves predictions and when reward mismatch makes additional samples harmful.

title: Demystifying LLM-as-a-Judge: Analytically Tractable Model for Inference-Time Scaling

abstract: With the advance of generative AI, the text-to-image (T2I) model has the ability to generate various contents. However, T2I models still can generate unsafe contents. To alleviate this issue, various concept erasing methods are proposed. However, existing methods tend to excessively erase unsafe concepts and suppress benign concepts contained in harmful prompts, which can negatively affect model utility. In this paper, we focus on eliminating unsafe content while maintaining model capability in safe semantic meaning interpretation by optimizing the concept erasing reward (CER) with reinforcement learning. To avoid overly content erasure, we introduce the Safe Adapter to project partial text embedding for efficient concept regulation in cross-attention layers. Extensive experiments conducted on different datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in alleviating unsafe content generation while preserving the high fidelity of benign images compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) concept erasing methods. In terms of robustness, our method outperforms counterparts against red-teaming tools. Moreover, we showcase the proposed approach is more effective in emerging image-to-image (I2I) scenarios compared with others. Lastly, we extend our method to erase general concepts, such as artistic styles and objects. Disclaimer: This paper includes discussions of sexually explicit content that may be offensive to certain readers. All images used in this work are synthesized or from public datasets.

paragraphs: Removing unsafe concepts from an image generator can also damage its handling of harmless content. A prompt may mix unsafe and benign meanings, and broad erasure can suppress both. ForceForget targets this trade-off by seeking to reduce unsafe generation while retaining the model's ability to interpret safe parts of a prompt.

The method uses reinforcement learning to optimize a concept-erasing reward. It also introduces a Safe Adapter that projects part of the text embedding to regulate concepts within cross-attention layers. This provides a more selective way to influence the connection between text and image generation, with the stated aim of avoiding excessive removal of content.

Experiments across different datasets report reduced unsafe generation while preserving the fidelity of benign images compared with existing leading erasure methods. The method also performs better against the evaluated red-teaming tools and in the studied image-to-image scenarios. Finally, the authors extend it to removing artistic styles and objects. Together, these findings support selective concept regulation across several settings, without establishing that unsafe outputs are impossible.
summary.tldr: ForceForget combines reinforcement learning with selective text-feature regulation to reduce unsafe image generation while preserving benign content.

title: ForceForget: Reinforcement Concept Removal for Enhancing Safety in Text-to-Image Models

abstract: Machine unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of specific data from trained models to safeguard privacy. However, this presents a significant challenge in the context of continual learning (CL), where models update sequentially on dynamic datasets. A major limitation is that current certified unlearning algorithms fail to account for the complex, cumulative model evolution inherent to CL framework. In this work, we establish the first theoretical foundation bridging CL and machine unlearning. We formulate the CL’s unlearning objective as the minimization of post-unlearning excess risk, which decomposes into CL excess risk and unlearning loss, characterizing the fundamental trade-off between preserving historical knowledge and targeted forgetting. Under mild assumptions, we first establish an upper bound for the CL excess risk in non-convex models. We then adapt two certified unlearning approaches, gradient-based and Hessian-based, to the CL framework. Our analysis reveals that while the gradient-based approach is less effective than the Hessian-based method in minimizing unlearning loss, it offers the distinct advantage of nearly zero storage overhead for enabling unlearning. This insight motivates a hybrid strategy that reduces storage costs while maintaining post-unlearning performance. Experimental results further validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Removing selected training data’s influence becomes more complicated when a model has learned through a sequence of tasks. Earlier updates affect later ones, so unlearning must account for accumulated model evolution. This paper develops a theoretical framework connecting certified unlearning with continual learning and the need to retain useful historical knowledge.

The authors express post-unlearning excess risk as a combination of continual-learning excess risk and unlearning loss. This separates errors associated with sequential learning from the cost of targeted forgetting. Under assumptions described as mild, they establish an upper bound for continual-learning excess risk in non-convex models, then adapt gradient-based and Hessian-based certified unlearning approaches to this setting.

Their analysis finds that the gradient-based approach is less effective at minimizing unlearning loss but requires nearly zero storage overhead to enable unlearning. The Hessian-based approach offers a different performance–storage balance. This motivates a hybrid method that reduces storage costs while maintaining post-unlearning performance. Experiments support the theoretical findings, making storage requirements an explicit part of the forgetting–retention trade-off.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes unlearning in continual learning and develops a hybrid approach balancing targeted forgetting, retained performance, and storage cost.

title: The Forgetting-Retention Dilemma: Certified Unlearning Theory in Continual Learning

abstract: Automatic verification is a critical component in building math-solving agents and reinforcement learning, yet it often falls short in generalizability, performance, and cost-efficiency. Identifying that the primary bottleneck of verification lies in error detection capability, we propose pessimistic verification, a paradigm of agentic workflows that rejects a solution if any of multiple parallel verifiers identifies a flaw. We further introduce progressive pessimistic verification, which employs fine-grained proof decomposition to significantly enhance verification accuracy and efficiency. Our approach surpasses the performance and token efficiency of extended long chain-of-thought (long CoT) and mainstream verification workflows, crucially, our analysis reveals that existing benchmarks underestimate its effectiveness on stronger models due to inherent annotation errors. To further validate the effectiveness of our method, we applied a verification-based solving workflow on the IMO 2025 and MathArena Apex 2025 datasets, where the workflow with progressive pessimistic verification exhibits remarkable improvements in both efficiency and accuracy on highly challenging contest-level math problems with state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: Checking an open-ended mathematical solution requires detecting flaws in its reasoning. This paper identifies error detection as the main bottleneck in automatic verification and proposes a workflow organized around finding any reason to reject a candidate. Multiple verifiers operate in parallel, and a flaw identified by any one of them causes rejection.

The progressive version combines this pessimistic decision rule with fine-grained decomposition of proofs. Breaking the argument into smaller components makes verification more focused. The authors report that this approach improves both verification accuracy and token efficiency compared with extended chains of thought and mainstream verification workflows.

Their analysis also finds annotation errors in existing benchmarks that cause those benchmarks to underestimate the method’s effectiveness with stronger models. To test verification within a broader solving process, they apply it to IMO 2025 and MathArena Apex 2025 problems using state-of-the-art models. They report substantial gains in efficiency and accuracy. The contribution connects targeted error detection with practical improvements in solving difficult mathematical problems, while highlighting how benchmark labels can distort evaluation.
summary.tldr: Parallel flaw detection and fine-grained proof decomposition improve reported mathematical verification accuracy and token efficiency.

title: Pessimistic Verification for Open-Ended Math Questions

abstract: We investigate which models admit a collapse of the expected information gain (EIG) and its derivative from a doubly intractable to a singly intractable expression. We prove that a sufficient condition is that the posterior distribution belongs to an exponential family (EF) and depends on the experimental design and data only through its natural parameters, and derive corresponding singly intractable and unbiased estimators for the $\operatorname{EIG}$ and its (reparameterized) gradient. We further show that this is achieved when using a likelihood of an analogous form and any arbitrary prior. This is complemented by a theoretical analysis of certain degenerate behaviors that may arise when optimizing the $\operatorname{EIG}$ for EF-modeled experiments. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the benefits of using our singly intractable estimators, showing superior convergence rates, and substantial performance gains for sequential design problems compared to using standard nested estimators.

paragraphs: Expected information gain measures how informative a proposed experiment is expected to be. Computing it, or its derivative for optimization, can require difficult nested calculations. This paper identifies a sufficient condition under which that doubly intractable calculation can be reduced to a singly intractable expression.

The condition concerns posteriors in an exponential family whose dependence on the experimental design and observed data occurs only through their natural parameters. Under this condition, the authors derive unbiased estimators for expected information gain and its reparameterized gradient. They also show how a likelihood with an analogous form and an arbitrary prior can achieve the stated reduction.

The analysis additionally examines certain degenerate behaviors that can occur when optimizing information gain in exponential-family experiment models. Empirical comparisons show faster convergence and substantial gains in sequential design relative to standard nested estimators. The contribution is both a structural criterion for simplifying the computation and estimators that make that simplification useful for experimental design.
summary.tldr: A sufficient exponential-family condition simplifies expected information gain and its gradient, enabling unbiased estimators with improved empirical convergence.

title: Tractable Expected Information Gains for Exponential Family Posteriors

abstract: Constitutional AI has focused on single-model alignment using fixed principles. However, multi-agent systems create novel alignment challenges through emergent social dynamics. We present Constitutional Evolution, a framework for automatically discovering behavioral norms in multi-agent LLM systems. Using a grid-world simulation with survival pressure, we study the tension between individual and collective welfare, quantified via a Societal Stability Score $\mathcal{S} \in [0,1]$ that combines productivity, survival, and conflict metrics. Adversarial constitutions lead to societal collapse ($\mathcal{S}=0$), while vague prosocial principles (”be helpful, harmless, honest”) produce inconsistent coordination ($\mathcal{S}=0.249$). Even constitutions designed by Claude 4.5 Opus with explicit knowledge of the objective achieve only moderate performance ($\mathcal{S}=0.332$). Using LLM-driven genetic programming with multi-island evolution, we evolve constitutions maximizing social welfare without explicit guidance toward cooperation. The evolved constitution $\mathcal{C}^*$ achieves $\mathcal{S}=0.556\pm0.008$ (123% higher than human-designed baselines, $N=10$), eliminates conflict, and discovers that minimizing communication (0.9% vs 62.2% social actions) outperforms verbose coordination. Our interpretable rules demonstrate that cooperative norms can be discovered rather than prescribed.

paragraphs: Rules that guide one language model may not produce a stable society of interacting agents. This paper studies that problem in a grid-world simulation with survival pressure. It evaluates constitutions—behavioral rules for agents—using a Societal Stability Score that combines productivity, survival, and conflict, exposing tension between individual behavior and collective welfare.

The proposed Constitutional Evolution framework uses language-model-driven genetic programming with multiple evolving populations to discover interpretable rules. The objective rewards social welfare without explicitly directing the search toward cooperation. Adversarial rules produce collapse, vague prosocial rules achieve a score of 0.249, and rules designed by an objective-informed Claude 4.5 Opus achieve 0.332.

The evolved constitution reaches 0.556 ± 0.008, reported as 123% higher than human-designed baselines across ten runs, and eliminates conflict. It also sharply reduces social actions: 0.9% compared with 62.2%, with less communication outperforming verbose coordination in this setting. The results show that effective cooperative norms can emerge through optimization in the simulation rather than needing to be specified beforehand.
summary.tldr: Evolutionary search discovers interpretable agent rules that improve simulated social welfare, eliminate conflict, and favor minimal communication.

title: Evolving Interpretable Constitutions for Multi-Agent Coordination

abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to explain how neural networks implement their capabilities, but the scale of Large Language Models (LLMs) has limited prior MI work in Machine Translation (MT) to word-level analyses. We study sentence-level MT from a mechanistic perspective by analyzing attention heads to understand how LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions. We decompose MT into two subtasks: producing text in the target language (i.e. target language identification) and preserving the input sentence’s meaning (i.e. sentence equivalence). Across three families of open-source models and 20 translation directions, we find that distinct, sparse sets of attention heads specialize in each subtask. Based on this insight, we construct subtask-specific steering vectors and show that modifying just 1% of the relevant heads enables instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting, while ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.

paragraphs: Translating a sentence requires both producing the requested language and preserving the original meaning. This paper examines whether those functions correspond to different internal components of language models. It moves mechanistic analysis beyond individual words by studying attention heads involved in sentence-level translation.

Across three open-source model families and 20 translation directions, the authors find distinct, sparse sets of heads specializing in target-language identification and sentence equivalence. They use this separation to construct steering vectors for each subtask. Modifying just 1% of the relevant heads enables translation without instructions at performance comparable to instruction-based prompting.

The study also removes the identified heads and observes selective disruption of their associated translation functions. Together, steering and ablation provide evidence that these head sets play functionally distinct roles in the evaluated models. The findings make translation behavior more interpretable by separating the machinery associated with language choice from the machinery associated with preserving a sentence’s meaning.
summary.tldr: Distinct sparse attention-head sets support language choice and meaning preservation, enabling targeted steering of sentence translation.

title: Translation Heads: Disentangling meaning from language in LLM-based machine translation

abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RRL) aims to tackle unexpected environmental changes by optimizing policies against the worst case. However, RRL remains impractical due to the cost of the Max-Min optimization, where it suffers from the exhaustive query complexity for finding the worst-case (dubbed ’Min’) within the environmental uncertainty set $\mathcal{U}$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{U}|)$. By viewing this via a lens of quantum perspective, we raise a pivotal question: If we can query from the environment with quantum superpositions, is it possible to accelerate the Max-Min optimization of RRL? Our answer is ’Yes’. Our method, called quantum robust inner minimization (QRIM), encodes the uncertainty set with quantum superposition and amplifies low-return cases, thus enabling RL for solving the robust (i.e., worst-case) Bellman equation. Importantly, QRIM achieves a quadratic speed-up in query complexity without altering the outer RL pipeline, i.e., $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{|\mathcal{U}|})$. Validated through classical simulations to real quantum hardware execution, QRIM learns more robust policies with quadratically reduced queries than classical RL.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that perform well against adverse environmental conditions. Its optimization contains an inner search for the worst case within an uncertainty set. Exhaustively querying that set costs an amount proportional to its size, which can make robust learning expensive even before accounting for the outer policy-learning process.

Quantum Robust Inner Minimization, or QRIM, addresses this search under the assumption that the environment can be queried in quantum superposition. It encodes the uncertainty set as a superposition and amplifies cases with low returns. This supplies the worst-case component needed for the robust Bellman equation while leaving the outer reinforcement learning pipeline unchanged.

The stated query complexity improves from linear in the uncertainty-set size to its square root, a quadratic speed-up in queries. Validation spans classical simulations and execution on real quantum hardware, with more robust learned policies and quadratically fewer queries than classical reinforcement learning. The speed-up concerns query complexity under the quantum-access assumption; it is not a claim about every component of end-to-end runtime.
summary.tldr: Given quantum-superposition access to the environment, QRIM quadratically reduces the queries needed for robust reinforcement learning’s worst-case search.

title: Quantum Robust Inner Minimization for Reinforcement Learning with Quadratic Speed-Up in Query Complexity

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) extend large language models with visual reasoning, but their multimodal design also introduces new, underexplored vulnerabilities. Existing multimodal red-teaming methods largely rely on brittle templates, focus on single-attack settings, and expose only a narrow subset of vulnerabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce VERA-V, a variational inference framework that recasts multimodal jailbreak discovery as learning a joint posterior distribution over paired text-image prompts. This probabilistic view captures complex cross-modal interactions, enabling stealthy, coordinated adversarial inputs that bypass model guardrails. We train a lightweight attacker to approximate the posterior, allowing efficient sampling of diverse jailbreaks and providing distributional insights into vulnerabilities. VERA-V further integrates three complementary strategies: (i) typography-based text prompts that embed harmful cues, (ii) diffusion-based image synthesis that introduces adversarial signals, and (iii) structured distractors to fragment VLM attention. Experiments on HarmBench and HADES benchmarks show that VERA-V consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both open-source and frontier VLMs, achieving up to 53.75% higher attack success rate (ASR) over the best baseline on GPT-4o. We include the code on the project page available here: https://github.com/kxwhiowo/VERA-V

paragraphs: VERA-V studies vulnerabilities that arise when vision-language models process text and images together. The authors argue that fixed attack templates and isolated attack examples reveal only a narrow portion of this behavior. Their framework instead models a distribution over paired text–image prompts, aiming to capture how the two modalities interact.

Using variational inference, a lightweight attacker learns to approximate a joint posterior over adversarial prompt pairs. It can then sample diverse examples and provide a distribution-level view of vulnerabilities. The framework combines typography-based cues, diffusion-generated visual signals, and structured distractions that divide model attention. These components are studied as coordinated sources of multimodal pressure on model guardrails.

On HarmBench and HADES, VERA-V consistently outperforms the reported state-of-the-art baselines across open-source and frontier vision-language models. The authors report an attack-success-rate improvement of up to 53.75% over the best baseline on GPT-4o. The findings indicate that probabilistic modeling of paired inputs can expose vulnerabilities beyond those captured by brittle templates or individual attack settings.
summary.tldr: VERA-V models distributions of coordinated text–image attacks to uncover a broader range of vision-language-model vulnerabilities.

title: VERA-V: Variational Inference Framework for Jailbreaking Vision-Language Models

abstract: We generalize the attention mechanism by viewing it through the lens of Entropic Optimal Transport, revealing that standard attention corresponds to a transport problem regularized by an implicit uniform prior. We introduce Generalized Optimal transport Attention with Trainable priors (GOAT), a new attention mechanism that replaces this naive assumption with a learnable, continuous prior. This prior maintains full compatibility with optimized kernels such as FlashAttention. GOAT also provides an EOT-based explanation of attention sinks and materializes a solution for them, avoiding the representational trade-offs of standard attention. Finally, by absorbing spatial information into the core attention computation, GOAT learns an extrapolatable prior that combines the flexibility of learned positional embeddings with the length generalization of fixed encodings.

paragraphs: This paper reinterprets attention through entropic optimal transport, a framework for distributing mass under a regularized matching objective. From this perspective, standard attention includes an implicit uniform prior. The authors use that connection to ask whether attention can benefit from learning the prior that shapes its allocation of attention.

GOAT replaces the uniform assumption with a trainable continuous prior while retaining compatibility with optimized kernels such as FlashAttention. The same optimal-transport interpretation provides an explanation of attention sinks and leads to a proposed solution that avoids the representational trade-offs attributed to standard attention. The prior therefore changes the core attention formulation while preserving compatibility with efficient computation.

GOAT also incorporates spatial information directly into attention. The resulting learned prior can extrapolate, combining the flexibility associated with learned positional embeddings and the length generalization associated with fixed encodings. The contribution ties attention allocation, attention sinks, and positional information to one formulation. Its stated benefits arise from making the prior explicit and learnable within the attention operation.
summary.tldr: GOAT replaces attention’s implicit uniform prior with a learnable continuous prior that addresses attention sinks and supports positional extrapolation.

title: You Need Better Attention Priors

abstract: Retina-like event cameras and brain-inspired Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) demonstrate exceptional energy efficiency through bio-inspired sensing and computation. While SNNs are naturally well-suited to the asynchronous nature of event data, their practical applications face the following challenges: sensitivity to noise, dense representations that disrupt spike pathways, and insufficient multi-scale feature perception. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a bio-vision-inspired object detection method motivated by biological (bio) vision systems. First, at the micro level, this paper proposes a noise-filtering STATNF-Neuron architecture to address the current sensitivity of basic neurons to noise. Based on STATNF-Neurons, the paper introduces two bio-vision-inspired macro-structures: Events-to-Spikes Representation (E2S), which preserves spiking characteristics while mimicking the memory and noise-filtering abilities of retinal neurons; Bidirectional Multi-Scale Spiking Network (BiSNet), which simulates cortical information flow pathways to integrate multi-scale features in both directions, enhancing the network’s ability to perceive information at multiple scales. Extensive experiments show that the proposed bio-vision-inspired method achieving state-of-the-art performance. Notably, it reaches 96.1% accuracy on NCAR, 63.5% mAP(50) on N-Caltech101, and 69.1% mAP(50) on Gen1.

paragraphs: Event cameras and spiking neural networks both support efficient processing inspired by biological vision. Their compatibility does not automatically solve object detection, however. The paper identifies three obstacles: sensitivity to noise, dense representations that interfere with spike pathways, and inadequate integration of visual features at different scales.

The proposed method addresses these obstacles at multiple architectural levels. STATNF-Neurons provide noise filtering within the neuron design. An Events-to-Spikes representation builds on those neurons to preserve spiking characteristics while incorporating memory and noise filtering inspired by retinal neurons. A Bidirectional Multi-Scale Spiking Network then combines features across scales in both directions, drawing inspiration from information flow in the cortex.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance in their experiments, including 96.1% accuracy on NCAR, 63.5% mAP at a 0.50 threshold on N-Caltech101, and 69.1% on Gen1 using the same detection measure. The findings support coordinating neuron behavior, event representation, and feature integration within one detection system. Each component targets a stated obstacle to making spiking computation useful for event-based visual recognition.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired spiking detector combines noise filtering, spike-preserving representations, and multiscale processing to achieve strong reported event-camera results.

title: Bio-Vision-Inspired Spiking Neural Networks for Object Detection with Event Cameras

abstract: Effective demonstration selection is crucial for maximizing large language model (LLM) performance in few-shot in-context learning. Because of effects such as recency bias, the effectiveness of demonstrations depends heavily on their contextual relationship to the specific query and on the ordering in which they are presented, making demonstration selection a complex combinatorial problem. To address these two challenges, we introduce AutoSelect, a novel framework that formulates demonstration selection as an auto-regressive sequential decision process. At each step, AutoSelect embeds the query and previously selected demonstrations into matrix representations to preserve structural information, and a trainable policy model sequentially selects the next best exemplar. To navigate the factorial space of demonstration permutations, our framework formulates a Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized optimization problem, from which an optimal policy induces an optimal Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking over all possible demonstration sequences. We prove that minimizing a tractable policy-level cross-entropy (CE) loss provably bounds the worst-case discrepancy between our policy’s induced PL ranking and the optimal one, enabling tractable prioritization of high-quality sequences. Empirically, AutoSelect outperforms existing heuristic and learning-based methods across nine diverse datasets, achieving up to an 11% improvement over the strongest baseline. Analytical studies and a case study further highlight AutoSelect’s key properties, as well as its transferability and generalizability.
originalAbstract: Effective demonstration selection is crucial for maximizing large language model (LLM) performance in few-shot in-context learning. Because of effects such as recency bias, the effectiveness of demonstrations depends heavily on their contextual relationship to the specific query and on the ordering in which they are presented, making demonstration selection a complex combinatorial problem. To address these two challenges, we introduce AutoSelect, a novel framework that formulates demonstration selection as an auto-regressive sequential decision process. At each step, AutoSelect embeds the query and previously selected demonstrations into matrix representations to preserve structural information, and a trainable policy model sequentially selects the next best exemplar. To navigate the factorial space of demonstration permutations, our framework formulates a Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized optimization problem, from which an optimal policy induces an optimal Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking over all possible demonstration sequences. We prove that minimizing a tractable policy-level cross-entropy (CE) loss provably bounds the worst-case discrepancy between our policy’s induced PL ranking and the optimal one, enabling tractable prioritization of high-quality sequences. Empirically, AutoSelect outperforms existing heuristic and learning-based methods across nine diverse datasets, achieving up to an 11% improvement over the strongest baseline. Analytical studies and a case study further highlight AutoSelect’s key properties, as well as its transferability and generalizability.

paragraphs: Examples placed in a language model’s prompt can help it answer a new question, but their usefulness depends on both relevance and order. AutoSelect treats choosing these demonstrations as a sequence of decisions. Each choice considers the query together with the examples already selected, allowing the framework to account for their combined context.

The method represents that context using matrices intended to preserve structural information, then trains a policy to choose the next example. Its optimization includes a KL regularization term and connects the optimal policy to a Plackett-Luce ranking of demonstration sequences. The authors prove that a tractable cross-entropy training loss bounds the worst-case discrepancy between the learned ranking and the optimal ranking.

This connection matters because the number of possible example orderings grows factorially, making exhaustive comparison impractical. Across nine datasets, AutoSelect beats heuristic and learned selection methods, with improvements reaching 11% over the strongest baseline. Additional analyses support its transferability and generalizability, while the theoretical result explains how a manageable training objective can guide selection among many possible sequences.
summary.tldr: AutoSelect learns to choose prompt examples sequentially, accounting for their context and order while improving performance across nine datasets.

title: Auto-regressive In-context Demonstration Selection

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable potential in role-playing tasks but frequently suffer from personality decay—termed "Out-of-Character" (OOC) behavior—during prolonged interactions. While heuristic strategies exist to align model behaviors, the internal computational dynamics driving personality expression remain opaque. A fundamental barrier to decoding these mechanisms is a metric gap: while standard causal attribution paradigms target atomic, single-token outcomes, personality manifests as a holistic, multi-token behavioral tendency. We bridge this gap via the Latent Persona Vector, a differentiable proxy enabling the first fine-grained causal tracing of personality circuits. This metric reveals a structured "Preparation-Establishment-Expression" dynamic and identifies a mechanistic contributor to OOC behavior: competition between persona-specific signals and an assistant-like default direction during the critical "Establishment" phase. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose surgically recalibrating the signal magnitude in fewer than $5%$ of attention heads. This targeted intervention effectively strengthens the persona signal, significantly restoring character consistency while preserving general reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Language models can drift out of character during extended role-playing conversations. Understanding why is difficult because personality appears across many tokens and behaviors, whereas standard causal attribution methods often target a single token. The paper develops a measurable proxy that makes this broader behavioral tendency accessible to fine-grained causal analysis.

The analysis reveals three stages: preparation, establishment, and expression. During establishment, persona-specific signals compete with a default assistant-like direction. The authors identify this competition as a mechanistic contributor to personality decay.

The contribution links a behavioral measurement problem to an internal mechanism and a targeted intervention. It explains one contributor to out-of-character behavior through the balance of competing signals at a particular stage of processing.
summary.tldr: A Latent Persona Vector reveals competition behind character drift and guides a small attention-head intervention that improves persona consistency.

title: Tracing the Persona Circuit: How Large Language Models Encode and Express Character Traits

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on sensitive datasets raises privacy concerns, as training data extraction (TDE) attacks can expose highly confidential information. Existing defenses against such attacks either lack formal privacy guarantees or incur substantial utility degradation. We observe that fine-tuning induces widespread probability shifts, yet preserving only a small subset of influential token-level deviations is sufficient; the remaining shifts can be aggressively smoothed with minimal impact on utility. Motivated by this insight, we propose SCP-$\Delta_r$, a Near Access Freeness (NAF)-based algorithm that operates on relative probabilities and explicitly smooths low-impact tokens using a base model. SCP-$\Delta_r$ achieves orders-of-magnitude better theoretical bounds than existing NAF based methods and provides strong empirical protection against TDE attacks with minimal performance loss.

Its starting observation is that fine-tuning shifts many token probabilities, but retaining only a small subset of influential changes can be sufficient for utility.

The proposed SCP-Δr algorithm works with relative probabilities and uses the base model to smooth low-impact token changes. It preserves the deviations that matter most while aggressively reducing others. The method is based on Near Access Freeness, which supplies the formal framework for analyzing protection against training-data extraction.

The authors report theoretical bounds that improve by orders of magnitude over existing methods based on the same framework. Empirical evaluations also show strong protection against extraction attacks with minimal performance loss. The contribution connects selective preservation of fine-tuning changes with both formal analysis and practical utility, demonstrating that widespread probability changes need not all be retained to obtain the benefits of specialization.
summary.tldr: SCP-Δr smooths low-impact fine-tuning changes to strengthen extraction protection while preserving utility in the reported evaluations.

title: Provably Protecting Fine-Tuned LLMs from Training Data Extraction while Preserving Utility

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for long-context question answering is bottlenecked by inference-time prefilling over large retrieved contexts. A common strategy is to precompute key–value (KV) caches for individual documents and selectively recompute a small subset of tokens to restore global causal dependencies, but existing methods rely on heuristics or representation discrepancies without modeling whether selected tokens can effectively influence generation. We cast selective KV recomputation as an information flow problem and show that a simple attention-norm signal from the query reliably identifies tokens that are both semantically relevant and structurally positioned to propagate information, when computed under an inference-consistent RoPE geometry. We therefore reconstruct global positional assignments for retrieved chunks and introduce an information-flow–guided chunk reordering strategy. Experiments on Large Language Model and Vision-Language Model benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over prior methods under comparable latency.

paragraphs: Long-context retrieval-augmented generation spends substantial inference time processing retrieved documents before answering. Precomputing each document's key–value cache reduces that work, but separately processed documents lack some dependencies that arise when they appear together. Selective recomputation attempts to restore these dependencies by updating only a small number of tokens.

InfoFlow KV frames token selection around information flow. A useful token must be relevant to the question and positioned so that its information can influence generation. The authors show that a simple query-derived attention-norm signal reliably identifies such tokens when the positional geometry matches inference. Their method reconstructs global positions for retrieved chunks using the appropriate rotary positional geometry and reorders chunks to guide information flow.

Experiments on language-model and vision-language-model benchmarks report consistent improvements over prior methods at comparable latency. The findings indicate that selecting tokens by relevance alone misses part of the problem: information must also propagate through the combined context. The approach uses that relationship to improve the value of a limited recomputation budget.
summary.tldr: InfoFlow KV improves selective cache recomputation by identifying relevant tokens that can effectively influence generation.

title: InfoFlow KV: Information-Flow-Aware KV Recomputation for Long Context

abstract: Discrete flow models offer a powerful framework for learning distributions over discrete state spaces and have demonstrated superior performance compared to the discrete diffusion models. However, their convergence properties and error analysis remain largely unexplored. In this work, we develop a unified framework grounded in stochastic calculus theory to systematically investigate the theoretical properties of discrete flow models. Specifically, by leveraging a Girsanov-type theorem for the path measures of two continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs), we present a comprehensive error analysis that accounts for both transition rate estimation error and early stopping error. In fact, the estimation error of transition rates has received little attention in existing works. Unlike discrete diffusion models, discrete flow incurs no initialization error caused by truncating the time horizon in the noising process. Building on generator matching and uniformization, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds for distribution estimation without the boundedness condition on oracle transition rates. Furthermore, we derive a faster rate of total variation convergence for the estimated distribution with the boundedness condition, yielding a nearly optimal rate in terms of sample size. Our results provide the first error analysis for discrete flow models. We also investigate model performance under different settings based on simulation results.

This paper develops a stochastic-calculus framework that accounts for inaccurate transition-rate estimates and stopping the process early. The analysis compares the path distributions of two continuous-time Markov chains using a Girsanov-type theorem. summary.tldr: A unified analysis bounds discrete-flow estimation and early-stopping errors, with nearly optimal sample-size convergence under an additional boundedness condition.

title: Error Analysis of Discrete Flow with Generator Matching

abstract: Unlearnable examples (UEs) aim to compromise model training by injecting imperceptible perturbations to clean samples. However, existing UE schemes exhibit limited robustness against advanced defenses due to their heuristic design or narrowly scoped domain perturbations. To address this, we propose DUNE, a Dual-branch UNlearnable Ensemble perturbation optimization approach. Specifically, DUNE separately optimizes perturbations in the spatial and color domains to establish the mapping between perturbations and shift-induced labels. This design extends the perturbation domain to increase noise intensity for improving robustness and drives the models to learn perturbation-oriented features with degraded generalization, thereby achieving unlearnability. To strengthen DUNE’s performance, we further propose an unlearnability-enhancing ensemble strategy that aggregates diverse pre-trained models during the dual-branch optimization. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet verify that DUNE’s robustness outperforms 12 SOTA UE schemes under 7 mainstream defenses, yielding a lower average test accuracy of 14.95% to 50.82%.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples contain visually imperceptible changes intended to undermine models trained on them. Their effectiveness depends on whether those changes remain disruptive when training defenses are applied. The paper argues that existing methods often lose robustness because they rely on heuristic designs or restrict perturbations to a narrow domain.

DUNE optimizes two perturbation branches separately, one in the spatial domain and one in the color domain. It links these perturbations to labels induced by shifts, encouraging a model to learn features tied to the perturbations that generalize poorly. Expanding the perturbation domain is intended to strengthen the disruptive signal. An additional ensemble strategy brings diverse pretrained models into the optimization to further improve unlearnability.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet compare DUNE with 12 state-of-the-art schemes under seven mainstream defenses. The authors report stronger robustness and lower average test accuracies, with reported values ranging from 14.95% to 50.82%. Here, lower accuracy is the desired outcome: it indicates that training on the perturbed examples leaves the resulting model less able to generalize.
summary.tldr: DUNE combines spatial and color perturbations with model ensembling to make unlearnable examples more robust against training defenses.

title: Dual-branch Robust Unlearnable Examples

abstract: Large language models have demonstrated remarkable performance; however, their massive parameter counts make deployment highly expensive. Low-rank approximation offers a promising compression solution, yet existing approaches have two main limitations: (1) They focus on minimizing the output error of individual linear layers, without considering the architectural characteristics of Transformers, and (2) they decompose a large weight matrix into two small low-rank matrices. Consequently, these methods often fall short compared to other compression techniques like pruning and quantization, and introduce runtime overhead such as the extra GEMM kernel launches and memory operations for decomposed small matrices. To address these limitations, we propose $A^3$, a post-training low-rank approximation framework. $A^3$ splits a Transformer layer into three functional components, namely $\texttt{QK}$, $\texttt{OV}$, and $\texttt{MLP}$ and provides analytical solutions that reduces the hidden dimension size inside each component while minimizing the component’s functional loss. This approach directly reduces model sizes, KV cache sizes, and FLOPs without introducing any runtime overheads. Through extensive experiments, we show that $A^3$ maintains superior performance compared to SoTAs. For example, under the same reduction budget in computation and memory, our low-rank approximated LLaMA 3.1-70B achieves a perplexity of 4.69 on WikiText-2, outperforming the previous SoTA’s 7.87 by 3.18. We also show versatile applications of $A^3$ in KV cache compression, integration with quantization, fine-tuning and mixed-rank assignments. We open-sourced our framework at https://github.com/DeepWok/a3.

title: A3: an Analytical Low-Rank Approximation Framework for Attention

abstract: Although recent video generative models are getting more capable of following external camera controls, imposed by either text descriptions or camera trajectories, they still struggle to generalize to unconventional camera motions, which is crucial in creating truly original and artistic videos. The challenge lies in finding sufficient training videos with the intended uncommon camera motions. To this end, we propose VividCam, a training paradigm that enables diffusion models to learn complex camera motions from synthetic videos, releasing the reliance on collecting realistic training videos. VividCam incorporates multiple disentanglement strategies that isolate camera motion learning from synthetic appearance artifacts, ensuring more robust motion representation and mitigating domain shift. We show that our design synthesizes a wide range of precisely controlled camera motions using surprisingly simple synthetic data. Notably, this synthetic data often consists of basic geometries within a low-poly 3D scene and can be efficiently rendered by engines like Unity. Our video results can be found in https://wuqiuche.github.io/VividCamDemoPage/.

VividCam addresses this data problem by teaching diffusion models camera motion using synthetic videos. The approach reduces reliance on collecting realistic videos containing the particular uncommon movements a creator wants.

The important design challenge is separating the camera's movement from the artificial appearance of those scenes. VividCam uses multiple disentanglement strategies to isolate motion learning, aiming for robust motion representations while reducing the shift between synthetic training imagery and generated video.

The contribution is a training paradigm that extracts useful camera-control information from readily rendered scenes while mitigating their visual artifacts.
summary.tldr: VividCam teaches diffusion video models uncommon camera movements from simple synthetic scenes while separating motion from artificial appearance.

title: VividCam: Learning Unconventional Camera Motions from Virtual Synthetic Videos

abstract: Instruction tuning (IT) is a central mechanism for aligning large language models (LLMs) with user intent. In practice, randomly shuffling the training set is a simple yet surprisingly strong baseline. However, it overlooks latent structure, such as domain and reasoning depth, and thus interleaves heterogeneous objectives, which can induce gradient conflicts and diminish effective optimization progress. To this end, we propose EP-Order, an embedding-proximity-based data-ordering paradigm for IT of LLMs. Unlike previous paradigms that derive order from per-example scores, EP-Order explicitly accounts for inter-sample correlations by operating in representation space. EP-Order trains a warm-up model on a small subset of data (e.g., 10%), embeds all training samples for clustering, and ranks these clusters according to embedding proximity. To handle sharp gradient changes at cluster transitions and alleviate catastrophic forgetting under cluster-based training, we introduce mixed regions that interleave samples from the previous, current, and next clusters, thereby stabilizing learning. Extensive experiments on 14 benchmarks spanning vision-language, text-only, and hybrid thinking/no-thinking scenarios show that EP-Order achieves broadly consistent improvements over random shuffling. These results suggest that exploiting embedding-level data structure offers an effective and general direction for improving IT on complex, high-conflict training data.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuning datasets can mix examples from different domains and with different reasoning demands. Randomly shuffling them is a strong baseline, but it can place conflicting training objectives next to one another. EP-Order investigates whether ordering related examples together can make optimization more effective by accounting for relationships within the dataset.

The method first trains a warm-up model on a small subset, such as ten percent of the data. It uses that model to embed all training examples, groups them into clusters, and orders those clusters by embedding proximity. Across fourteen benchmarks covering vision-language, text-only, and hybrid thinking settings, it delivers broadly consistent improvements over random shuffling. The findings suggest that both grouping related data and smoothing transitions between groups can improve instruction tuning.
summary.tldr: EP-Order improves instruction tuning by arranging related training examples into nearby groups and blending examples at group transitions.

title: Group-wise Data Ordering: Enhancing Instruction Tuning of Large Language Models via Embedding Proximity

abstract: Decentralized class continual learning refers to a paradigm where distributed clients continuously acquire new classes while retaining previously learned information without relying on a central server. With increasing emphasis on privacy preservation, there is a growing need for on-demand unlearning, introducing two key challenges: Historical Class Unlearning and Network-Wide Knowledge Entanglement. In this work, we propose a decentralized continual learning framework with on-demand unlearning (DCU), which is the first attempt at achieving class continual learning and arbitrary-time class unlearning in a distributed setting. Specifically, our proposed DCU comprises three main stages: prototypes extraction, prototype-guided continual learning, and unlearning with disposable prototypes. Firstly, the prototypes extraction mechanism is designed to capture the class-specific concepts as lightweight, disposable embeddings. Then, the synthetic data guided by these prototypes can be combined with real data to achieve incremental learning through distillation. Besides, synthetic samples with noisy label are used to guide the adjustment of the model’s decision boundary, effectively erasing the influence of the target class while preserving other classes’ knowledge. Extensive experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our DCU in dynamic learning and target class unlearning.

paragraphs: Decentralized continual learning lets distributed clients acquire new classes while retaining earlier knowledge without a central server. Supporting requests to forget a class adds two difficulties: the class may have been learned long ago, and its influence may be entangled with knowledge throughout the network. DCU combines continued learning with class unlearning requested at arbitrary times.

The framework first extracts lightweight class prototypes, embeddings that capture class-specific concepts and can later be discarded. These prototypes guide synthetic-data generation. Combining synthetic and real data through distillation supports incremental learning, giving the system a way to preserve earlier class knowledge as new classes arrive.

For unlearning, synthetic samples with noisy labels guide changes to the model’s decision boundary, removing the target class’s influence while preserving knowledge of other classes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate effectiveness in both dynamic learning and targeted forgetting. The approach makes disposable class representations central to managing knowledge over time, connecting the mechanisms for retaining useful information and removing selected information within a decentralized system.
summary.tldr: DCU uses disposable class prototypes and synthetic data to support continual learning and on-demand class forgetting without a central server.

title: Forgetting Whenever You Want: A Decentralized Continual Learning Framework with On-Demand Unlearning

abstract: Adaptive testing is widely adopted in AI-driven educational assessment systems (e.g., GRE), where the goal is to select an optimal subset of questions from a large question pool to accurately estimate an examinee’s ability. A fundamental challenge is that: optimal question subsets are inherently personalized, and solving for them is NP-hard. Recently, it has been framed as a gradient matching problem: aligning gradients between selected subsets and the full question set across the entire ability parameter space. However, such global alignment on entire space is computationally expensive and difficult to scale. In this work, we propose GPM (Gradient Path Matching), a novel framework that instead aligns gradients along possible optimization paths toward the final estimate. By leveraging intermediate gradients as supervision, GPM learns an explicit and generalizable selection algorithm from large-scale data. We provide theoretical analysis on its convergence and scalability. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that it achieves the same estimation accuracy using, on average, 20% fewer questions.

We provide theoretical analysis on its convergence and scalability. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that it achieves the same estimation accuracy using, on average, 20% fewer questions.

paragraphs: Adaptive testing aims to estimate a person’s ability from a carefully chosen subset of questions. The best subset depends on the examinee, and finding an optimal one is computationally difficult. Previous gradient-matching formulations try to make a subset behave like the full question pool across the entire space of possible ability estimates, which is expensive.

Gradient Path Matching, or GPM, narrows that alignment problem to possible optimization paths toward the final estimate. Rather than matching learning signals everywhere, it uses intermediate gradients along those paths as supervision. From large-scale data, it learns an explicit selection algorithm intended to generalize across testing cases. This focuses selection on the process by which an ability estimate is actually refined.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of convergence and scalability. In experiments on real and synthetic datasets, GPM reaches the same estimation accuracy with 20% fewer questions on average. That result links the computational reformulation to a practical testing benefit: obtaining an equally accurate estimate while asking examinees fewer questions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: GPM learns question selection by matching gradients along estimation paths, achieving the same accuracy with 20% fewer questions on average.

title: Efficient Adaptive Testing via Gradient Path Matching Subset Selection for AI Education

abstract: We derive a novel PAC-Bayesian generalization bound for reinforcement learning that explicitly accounts for Markov dependencies in the data, through the chain’s mixing time. This contributes to overcoming challenges in obtaining generalization guarantees for reinforcement learning, where the sequential nature of data breaks the independence assumptions underlying classical bounds. The new bound provides non-vacuous certificates for modern off-policy algorithms such as Soft Actor-Critic. We demonstrate the practical utility of the bound through PB-SAC, a novel algorithm that optimizes the bound during training to guide exploration. Experiments across several continuous control tasks show that the proposed approach provides meaningful confidence certificates while maintaining competitive performance.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning observations arrive in sequences, so nearby data points can depend on one another. This complicates generalization guarantees built around independent samples. The paper derives a PAC-Bayesian bound that explicitly accounts for Markov dependence through the chain’s mixing time, bringing the temporal structure of reinforcement-learning data into the guarantee.

The resulting bound provides non-vacuous certificates for modern off-policy algorithms such as Soft Actor-Critic. A non-vacuous certificate is informative rather than a mathematically valid statement too loose to be useful. The contribution is therefore not only a formal bound, but one intended to produce meaningful confidence information for contemporary learning algorithms.

The authors turn the bound into a training method called PB-SAC, which optimizes it to guide exploration. Experiments on several continuous-control tasks show meaningful confidence certificates alongside competitive task performance. These results suggest that a dependence-aware generalization bound can serve two connected purposes: assessing a learned policy and influencing the learning process that produces it.
summary.tldr: PB-SAC uses a PAC-Bayesian bound that accounts for temporal dependence to guide exploration and provide meaningful generalization certificates.

title: PAC-Bayesian Reinforcement Learning Trains Generalizable Policies

abstract: As generative AI faces intensifying legal challenges, the machine learning community has increasingly relied on post-hoc opt-out—especially inference-time guardrails and parameter modifications—to argue for compliance. This paper argues that such post-hoc opt-out methods cannot retroactively cure liability from unlawful data acquisition and training ingestion, because compliance hinges on data lineage, not the outputs. Our argument has three parts. First, unauthorized copying/ingestion can be a legally complete completed act, and model weights may operate as fixed copies that retain training-derived expressive value, making later filtering beside the point for infringement. Second, contract and tort/unfair-competition rules—via licenses, terms of service, and anti-free-riding principles—can independently restrict access and use, often bypassing copyright defenses (e.g., fair use or TDM exceptions). Third, since value from protected inputs can persist in weights, remedies such as unjust enrichment and disgorgement may require stripping gains and, in some cases, reaching the model itself. We therefore argue for a shift from Post-Hoc Opt-Out to verifiable Ex-Ante Process Compliance.

paragraphs: The paper challenges the argument that changes made after training can resolve liability arising from unlawfully acquired or ingested training data. Its position is that compliance depends on the history of the data’s acquisition and use. Filtering outputs or modifying parameters later cannot retroactively change an earlier act of unauthorized copying that may already constitute infringement.

The authors develop three connected arguments. First, unauthorized ingestion can be a completed legal act, and weights may retain protected expressive value as fixed copies. Second, licenses, terms of service, and contract or unfair-competition rules can independently constrain access and use, even where copyright defenses are invoked. These are presented as legal arguments rather than universal findings about every model.

Third, the paper argues that retained value from protected inputs may support remedies aimed at removing gains, potentially reaching the model itself in some cases. It consequently advocates verifiable compliance before acquisition and training. The proposed shift directs attention to data lineage and process evidence when assessing whether model development was lawful.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that post-training changes cannot retroactively resolve liability from unlawful data acquisition and ingestion.

abstract: Even though several techniques have been proposed in the literature for achieving multiclass classification using Support Vector Machine(SVM), the scalability aspect of these approaches to handle large data sets still needs much of exploration. Core Vector Machine(CVM) is a technique for scaling up a two class SVM to handle large data sets. In this paper we propose a Multiclass Core Vector Machine(MCVM). Here we formulate the multiclass SVM problem as a Quadratic Programming(QP) problem defining an SVM with vector valued output. This QP problem is then solved using the CVM technique to achieve scalability to handle large data sets. Experiments done with several large synthetic and real world data sets show that the proposed MCVM technique gives good generalization performance as that of SVM at a much lesser computational expense. Further, it is observed that MCVM scales well with the size of the data set.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can be extended to classification with multiple classes, but handling large datasets remains a computational concern. Core Vector Machines provide a technique for scaling two-class SVMs. This paper brings that technique to multiclass learning, aiming to preserve the predictive behavior of an SVM while reducing the expense of training on large collections of examples.

The proposed Multiclass Core Vector Machine begins by expressing the multiclass SVM as a quadratic programming problem. Its SVM has vector-valued output, providing a formulation for the multiclass task. The authors then solve this optimization problem using the Core Vector Machine technique, connecting the multiclass formulation to an existing route for scalable SVM computation.

Experiments use several large synthetic and real-world datasets. The authors report generalization performance comparable to an SVM at substantially lower computational expense, along with good scaling as dataset size grows. These are empirical findings about the tested problems. They support the proposed formulation as a practical way to extend the computational benefits of Core Vector Machines to multiclass classification.
summary.tldr: The Multiclass Core Vector Machine extends scalable SVM training to multiple classes with comparable generalization at lower experimental computational cost.

title: Multiclass core vector machine

abstract: We present a principled Bayesian framework for modeling partial memberships of data points to clusters. Unlike a standard mixture model which assumes that each data point belongs to one and only one mixture component, or cluster, a partial membership model allows data points to have fractional membership in multiple clusters. Algorithms which assign data points partial memberships to clusters can be useful for tasks such as clustering genes based on microarray data and global positioning and orbit determination. Our Bayesian Partial Membership Model (BPM) uses exponential family distributions to model each cluster, and a product of these distibtutions, with weighted parameters, to model each datapoint. Here the weights correspond to the degree to which the datapoint belongs to each cluster. All parameters in the BPM are continuous, so we can use Hybrid Monte Carlo to perform inference and learning. We discuss relationships between the BPM and Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Mixed Membership models, Exponential Family PCA, and fuzzy clustering. Lastly, we show some experimental results and discuss nonparametric extensions to our model.

Here the weights correspond to the degree to which the datapoint belongs to each cluster. All parameters in the BPM are continuous, so we can use Hybrid Monte Carlo to perform inference and learning. paragraphs: A standard mixture model assigns each data point to one underlying component, even when that assignment is uncertain. This paper develops a Bayesian model in which a point can instead have fractional membership in several clusters. Such a representation is useful when partial belonging is part of what the model is intended to describe.

The Bayesian Partial Membership Model represents clusters with exponential-family distributions. Each data point is modeled through a product of these distributions with weighted parameters, where the weights express its degree of membership in each cluster. All model parameters are continuous, allowing the authors to use Hybrid Monte Carlo for inference and learning.

The paper relates the framework to Latent Dirichlet Allocation, mixed-membership models, Exponential Family PCA, and fuzzy clustering. It also presents experimental results and discusses nonparametric extensions. Gene clustering from microarray measurements and positioning or orbit determination are named as possible application areas. The contribution is a principled probabilistic construction for partial membership, rather than merely a procedure that outputs fractional cluster assignments.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian partial-membership model represents each data point through weighted contributions from multiple exponential-family clusters.

title: Statistical models for partial membership

abstract: This paper proposes a general framework, called EigenTransfer, to tackle a variety of transfer learning problems, e.g. cross-domain learning, self-taught learning, etc. Our basic idea is to construct a graph to represent the target transfer learning task. By learning the spectra of a graph which represents a learning task, we obtain a set of eigenvectors that reflect the intrinsic structure of the task graph. These eigenvectors can be used as the new features which transfer the knowledge from auxiliary data to help classify target data. Given an arbitrary non-transfer learner (e.g. SVM) and a particular transfer learning task, EigenTransfer can produce a \emph{transfer learner} accordingly for the target transfer learning task. We apply EigenTransfer on three different transfer learning tasks, cross-domain learning, cross-category learning and self-taught learning, to demonstrate its unifying ability, and show through experiments that EigenTransfer can greatly outperform several representative non-transfer learners.
