By learning the spectra of a graph which represents a learning task, we obtain a set of eigenvectors that reflect the intrinsic structure of the task graph. These eigenvectors can be used as the new features which transfer the knowledge from auxiliary data to help classify target data. Given an arbitrary non-transfer learner (e.g. SVM) and a particular transfer learning task, EigenTransfer can produce a \emph{transfer learner} accordingly for the target transfer learning task. We apply EigenTransfer on three different transfer learning tasks, cross-domain learning, cross-category learning and self-taught learning, to demonstrate its unifying ability, and show through experiments that EigenTransfer can greatly outperform several representative non-transfer learners.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses auxiliary data to help with a target prediction task. EigenTransfer proposes a common framework for several forms of this problem. Its starting point is a graph representing the transfer task, allowing the structure relevant to that task to be expressed before choosing the final classifier.

The framework learns spectral information from the graph and obtains eigenvectors reflecting its intrinsic structure. These eigenvectors become new features through which auxiliary knowledge can help classify target data. A conventional learner, such as a support vector machine, can then operate on the resulting representation. This gives the framework a way to turn a non-transfer learner into a learner suited to a particular transfer task.

The authors apply EigenTransfer to cross-domain, cross-category, and self-taught learning, demonstrating the breadth of the construction. Experiments show that it can substantially outperform several representative non-transfer learners. The reported results support the usefulness of graph-derived representations in these settings, while the unifying contribution is the same feature-construction strategy across different kinds of transfer.
summary.tldr: EigenTransfer converts graph eigenvectors into features that let conventional classifiers use auxiliary knowledge across several transfer-learning settings.

title: EigenTransfer: a unified framework for transfer learning

abstract: Given a large-scale linked document collection, such as a collection of blog posts or a research literature archive, there are two fundamental problems that have generated a lot of interest in the research community. One is to identify a set of high-level topics covered by the documents in the collection; the other is to uncover and analyze the social network of the authors of the documents. So far these problems have been viewed as separate problems and considered independently from each other. In this paper we argue that these two problems are in fact inter-dependent and should be addressed together. We develop a Bayesian hierarchical approach that performs topic modeling and author community discovery in one unified framework. The effectiveness of our model is demonstrated on two blog data sets in different domains and one research paper citation data from CiteSeer.
originalAbstract: Given a large-scale linked document collection, such as a collection of blog posts or a research literature archive, there are two fundamental problems that have generated a lot of interest in the research community. One is to identify a set of high-level topics covered by the documents in the collection; the other is to uncover and analyze the social network of the authors of the documents. So far these problems have been viewed as separate problems and considered independently from each other. In this paper we argue that these two problems are in fact inter-dependent and should be addressed together. We develop a Bayesian hierarchical approach that performs topic modeling and author community discovery in one unified framework. The effectiveness of our model is demonstrated on two blog data sets in different domains and one research paper citation data from CiteSeer.

paragraphs: A linked document collection contains information about both subject matter and the people producing it. Topic modeling seeks the major themes in the documents, while author-community discovery seeks structure among their authors. This paper argues that these questions are interdependent and should be handled together when analyzing collections such as blogs or research literature.

The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that unifies topic discovery and author-community discovery. Putting both into one framework allows the analysis to account for their relationship instead of treating each as an isolated task. The resulting approach aims to describe what a collection discusses alongside the social organization associated with its authors.

The model is evaluated on two blog datasets from different domains and a CiteSeer research-paper citation dataset. The authors report that these applications demonstrate its effectiveness. The main contribution is a joint modeling perspective on content and author structure, supported by evaluations across both blogs and research literature rather than by a claim that either source of information always determines the other.
summary.tldr: Topic-link LDA jointly models document topics and author communities, with effectiveness demonstrated on blog and research-citation datasets.

title: Topic-link LDA: joint models of topic and author community

abstract: The goal of transfer learning is to improve the learning of a new target concept given knowledge of related source concept(s). We introduce the first boosting-based algorithms for transfer learning that apply to regression tasks. First, we describe two existing classification transfer algorithms, ExpBoost and TrAdaBoost, and show how they can be modified for regression. We then introduce extensions of these algorithms that improve performance significantly on controlled experiments in a wide range of test domains.
originalAbstract: The goal of transfer learning is to improve the learning of a new target concept given knowledge of related source concept(s). We introduce the first boosting-based algorithms for transfer learning that apply to regression tasks. First, we describe two existing classification transfer algorithms, ExpBoost and TrAdaBoost, and show how they can be modified for regression. We then introduce extensions of these algorithms that improve performance significantly on controlled experiments in a wide range of test domains.

paragraphs: Transfer learning aims to improve learning on a new target problem by using knowledge from related source problems. This paper addresses that goal for regression, where the prediction is a numerical value. Its stated contribution is the first set of boosting-based transfer learning algorithms that applies to regression tasks.

The authors begin with ExpBoost and TrAdaBoost, two existing transfer algorithms for classification. They explain how these methods can be modified for regression, extending their use beyond predicting categories. This provides a route from established classification transfer methods to the numerical prediction setting, while retaining boosting as the basis of the algorithms.

The paper then introduces extensions to the adapted methods and reports significant performance improvements in controlled experiments across a wide range of test domains. Those findings support the value of the proposed extensions in the evaluated settings. The overall contribution has two parts: making boosting-based transfer available for regression and improving those methods through further algorithmic development.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts boosting-based transfer methods to regression and introduces extensions that significantly improve performance in controlled experiments.

title: Boosting for Regression Transfer

abstract: We demonstrate efficient approximate inference for the Dirichlet Diffusion Tree, a Bayesian nonparametric prior over tree structures. Although DDTs provide a powerful and elegant approach for modeling hierarchies they haven't seen much use to date. One problem is the computational cost of MCMC inference. We provide the first deterministic approximate inference methods for DDT models and show excellent performance compared to the MCMC alternative. We present message passing algorithms to approximate the Bayesian model evidence for a specific tree. This is used to drive sequential tree building and greedy search to find optimal tree structures, corresponding to hierarchical clusterings of the data. We demonstrate appropriate observation models for continuous and binary data. The empirical performance of our method is very close to the computationally expensive MCMC alternative on a density estimation problem, and significantly outperforms kernel density estimators.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate efficient approximate inference for the Dirichlet Diffusion Tree, a Bayesian nonparametric prior over tree structures. Although DDTs provide a powerful and elegant approach for modeling hierarchies they haven't seen much use to date. One problem is the computational cost of MCMC inference. We provide the first deterministic approximate inference methods for DDT models and show excellent performance compared to the MCMC alternative. We present message passing algorithms to approximate the Bayesian model evidence for a specific tree. This is used to drive sequential tree building and greedy search to find optimal tree structures, corresponding to hierarchical clusterings of the data. We demonstrate appropriate observation models for continuous and binary data. The empirical performance of our method is very close to the computationally expensive MCMC alternative on a density estimation problem, and significantly outperforms kernel density estimators.

paragraphs: The Dirichlet Diffusion Tree is a Bayesian nonparametric prior for modeling tree structures and hierarchies. Its practical use has been hindered in part by the computational expense of Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. The paper introduces deterministic approximate inference methods intended to make this hierarchical model more computationally accessible.

The authors develop message-passing algorithms that approximate the Bayesian model evidence for a given tree. This quantity then guides sequential tree construction and greedy search over candidate structures. The resulting trees correspond to hierarchical clusterings of the observations. The paper also presents observation models suitable for both continuous and binary data.

On a density-estimation problem, the approximate method performs very close to the computationally expensive MCMC alternative and significantly better than kernel density estimators. These results support the practical value of deterministic approximation for the tested task. The contribution connects an approximate way to score individual trees with procedures for exploring the space of hierarchical structures.
summary.tldr: Deterministic message passing makes Dirichlet Diffusion Tree inference efficient while closely matching MCMC performance on a density-estimation problem.

title: Message Passing Algorithms for the Dirichlet Diffusion Tree

abstract: We show the equivalence of the herding procedure of Welling (2009) with a standard convex optimization algorithm–namely a conditional gradient algorithm minimizing a quadratic moment discrepancy. This link enables us to harness convergence results from convex optimization as well as suggest faster alternatives for the task of approximating integrals in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We study the behavior of the different variants with numerical simulations. The experiments indicate that while we can improve on the task of approximating integrals, the original herding algorithm tends to approach more often the maximum entropy distribution, shedding more light on the learning bias behind herding.
originalAbstract: We show the equivalence of the herding procedure of Welling (2009) with a standard convex optimization algorithm–namely a conditional gradient algorithm minimizing a quadratic moment discrepancy. This link enables us to harness convergence results from convex optimization as well as suggest faster alternatives for the task of approximating integrals in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We study the behavior of the different variants with numerical simulations. The experiments indicate that while we can improve on the task of approximating integrals, the original herding algorithm tends to approach more often the maximum entropy distribution, shedding more light on the learning bias behind herding.

paragraphs: The paper establishes that herding can be understood as a standard conditional gradient algorithm for convex optimization. In this formulation, the algorithm minimizes a quadratic discrepancy between moments. The equivalence turns a procedure for constructing approximations into an optimization method with a recognizable objective and access to an existing body of convergence analysis.

This connection lets the authors apply convergence results from convex optimization and propose faster alternatives for approximating integrals in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The practical question becomes how different optimization variants behave on the integration task. The paper investigates these alternatives through numerical simulations, using the shared formulation to compare their behavior.

The experiments indicate that integral approximation can be improved, while original herding more often approaches the maximum entropy distribution. These are distinct observed tendencies: improving the integration objective does not necessarily preserve the original procedure’s distributional preference. The result therefore clarifies both how herding can be accelerated for one task and what its original learning behavior appears to favor.
summary.tldr: Viewing herding as conditional gradient optimization yields convergence tools and faster integration variants while revealing differences in distributional bias.

title: On the Equivalence between Herding and Conditional Gradient Algorithms
